1.0: Scene. — Mount Aetna in Sicily, before the cave of the Cyclops. Silenus
1.1: O Bromius, unnumbered are the toils I bear because of thee, no less now than when I was young and hale; first, when thou wert driven mad by Hera and didst leave the mountain nymphs, thy nurses;
1.5: next, when in battle with earth-born spearmen I stood beside thee on the right as squire, and slew Enceladus, smiting him full in the middle of his targe with my spear. Come, though, let me see; must I confess ’twas all a dream? No, by Zeus! since I really showed his spoils to the Bacchic god.
1.10: And now am I enduring to the full a toil still worse than those. For when Hera sent forth a race of Tyrrhene pirates against thee, that thou mightest be smuggled far away, I, as soon as the news reached me, sailed in quest of thee with my children; and, taking the helm
1.15: myself, I stood on the end of the stern and steered our trim craft; and my sons, sitting at the oars, made the grey billows froth and foam as they sought thee, my liege. But just as we had come nigh Malea in our course, an east-wind blew upon the ship
1.20: and drove us hither to the rock of Aetna, where in lonely caverns dwell the one-eyed children of ocean’s god, the murdering Cyclopes. Captured by one of them we are slaves in his house; Polyphemus they call him whom we serve;
1.25: and instead of Bacchic revelry we are herding a godless Cyclops’s flocks; and so it is my children, striplings as they are, tend the young thereof on the edge of the downs; while my appointed task is to stay here and fill the troughs and sweep out the cave,
1.30: or wait upon the ungodly Cyclops at his impious feasts. His orders now compel obedience; I have to scrape out his house with the rake you see, so as to receive the Cyclops, my absent master,
1.35: and his sheep in clean caverns.
1.36: But already I see my children driving their browsing flocks towards me.
1.37: What means this? is the beat of feet in the Sicinnis dance the same to you now as when ye attended the Bacchic god in his revelries
1.40:
and made your way with dainty steps to the mask of lyres to the halls of Althaea?
Chorus
1.41: Offspring of well-bred sires and dams, pray whither wilt thou be gone from me to the rocks? Hast thou not here a gentle breeze,
1.45:
and grass to browse, and water from the eddying stream set near the cave in troughs? and are not thy young ones bleating for thee?
Chorus
1.49: Pst! pst! wilt thou not browse here,
1.50:
here on the dewy slope? Ho? ho! ere long will I cast a stone at thee. Away, away! O horned one, to the fold-keeper of the Cyclops, the country-ranging shepherd.
Chorus
1.55: Loosen thy bursting udder; welcome to thy teats the kids, whom thou leavest in the lambkins’ pens. Those little bleating kids, asleep the livelong day, miss thee;
1.60:
wilt then leave at last the rich grass pastures on the peaks of Aetna and enter the fold?
Chorus
1.63: Here we have no Bromian god; no dances here, or Bacchantes thyrsus-bearing;
1.65: no roll of drums, or drops of sparkling wine by gurgling founts; nor is it now with Nymphs in Nysa I sing a song of Bacchus, Bacchus!
1.70: to the queen of love, in quest of whom I once sped on with Bacchantes, white of foot.
1.73: Dear friend, dear Bacchic god, whither art roaming alone,
1.75: waving thy auburn locks, while I, thy minister, do service to the one-eyed Cyclops, a slave and wanderer I,
1.80:
clad in this wretched goat-skin dress, severed from thy love?
Silenus
1.82:
Hush, children! and bid our servants fold the flocks in the rock-roofed cavern.
Chorus
1.84:
(To Servants.) Away! (To Silenus.) But prithee, why such haste, father?
Silenus
1.85: I see the hull of a ship from Hellas at the shore, and men, that wield the oar, on their way to this cave with some chieftain. About their necks they carry empty vessels and pitchers for water; they are in want of food. Luckless strangers!
1.90: who can they be? They know not what manner of man our master Polyphemus is, to have set foot here in his cheerless abode and come to the jaws of the cannibal Cyclops in an evil hour. But hold ye your peace, that we may inquire
1.95:
whence they come to the peak of Sicilian Aetna.
Odysseus
1.96: Pray tell us, sirs, of some river-spring whence we might draw a draught to slake our thirst, or of someone willing to sell victuals to mariners in need.
1.99: Why, what is this? We seem to have chanced upon a city of the Bromian god;
1.100:
here by the caves I see a group of Satyrs. To the eldest first I bid All hail!
Silenus
1.102:
All hail, sir! tell me who thou art, and name thy country.
Odysseus
1.103:
Odysseus of Ithaca, king of the Cephallenians’ land.
Silenus
1.104:
I know him for a prating knave, one of Sisyphus’ shrewd offspring.
Odysseus
1.105:
I am the man; abuse me not.
Silenus
1.106:
Whence hast thou sailed hither to Sicily?
Odysseus
1.107:
From Ilium and the toils of Troy.
Silenus
1.108:
How was that? didst thou not know the passage to thy native land?
Odysseus
1.109:
Tempestuous winds drove me hither against my will.
Silenus
1.110:
God wot! thou art in the same plight as I am.
Odysseus
1.111:
Why, wert thou too drifted hither against thy will?
Silenus
1.112:
I was, as I pursued the pirates who carried Bromius off.
Odysseus
1.113:
What land is this and who are its inhabitants?
Silenus
1.114:
This is mount Aetna, the highest point in Sicily.
Odysseus
1.115:
But where are the city-walls and ramparts?
Silenus
1.116:
There are none; the headlands, sir, are void of men.
Odysseus
1.117:
Who then possess the land? the race of wild creatures?
Silenus
1.118:
The Cyclopes, who have caves, not roofed houses.
Odysseus
1.119:
Obedient unto whom? or is the power in the people’s hands?
Silenus
1.120:
They are rovers; no man obeys another in anything.
Odysseus
1.121:
Do they sow Demeter’s grain, or on what do they live?
Silenus
1.122:
On milk and cheese and flesh of sheep.
Odysseus
1.123:
Have they the drink of Bromius, the juice of the vine?
Silenus
1.124:
No indeed! and thus it is a joyless land they dwell in.
Odysseus
1.125:
Are they hospitable and reverent towards strangers?
Silenus
1.126:
Strangers, they say, supply the daintiest meat.
Odysseus
1.127:
What, do they delight in killing men and eating them?
Silenus
1.128:
No one has ever arrived here without being butchered.
Odysseus
1.129:
Where is the Cyclops himself? inside his dwelling?
Silenus
1.130:
He is gone hunting wild beasts with hounds on Aetna.
Odysseus
1.131:
Dost know then what to do, that we may be gone from the land?
Silenus
1.132:
Not I, Odysseus; but I would do anything for thee.
Odysseus
1.133:
Sell us food, of which we are in need.
Silenus
1.134:
There is nothing but flesh, as I said.
Odysseus
1.135:
Well, even that is a pleasant preventive of hunger.
Silenus
1.136:
And there is cheese curdled with fig-juice, and the milk of kine.
Odysseus
1.137:
Bring them out; a man should see his purchases.
Silenus
1.138:
But tell me, how much gold wilt thou give me in exchange?
Odysseus
1.139:
No gold bring I, but Dionysus’ drink.
Silenus
1.140:
Most welcome words! I have long been wanting that.
Odysseus
1.141:
Yes, it was Maron, the god’s son, who gave me a draught.
Silenus
1.142:
What! Maron whom once I dandled in these arms?
Odysseus
1.143:
The son of the Bacchic god, that thou mayst learn more certainly.
Silenus
1.144:
Is it inside the ship, or hast thou it with thee?
Odysseus
1.145:
This, as thou seest, is the skin that holds it, old sir.
Silenus
1.146:
Why, that would not give me so much as a mouthful.
Odysseus
1.147:
This, and twice as much again as will run from the skin.
Silenus
1.148:
Fair the rill thou speakest of, delicious to me.
Odysseus
1.149:
Shall I let thee taste the wine unmixed, to start with?
Silenus
1.150:
A reasonable offer; for of a truth a taste invites the purchase.
Odysseus
1.151:
Well, I haul about a cup as well as the skin.
Silenus
1.152:
Come, let it gurgle in, that I may revive my memory by a pull at it.
Odysseus
1.153:
There then!
Silenus
Ye gods! what a delicious scent it has!
Odysseus
1.154:
What! didst thou see it?
Silenus
No, i’ faith, but I smell it.
Odysseus
1.155:
Taste it then, that thy approval may not stop at words.
Silenus
1.156:
Zounds! Bacchus is inviting me to dance; ha! ha!
Odysseus
1.158:
Did it not gurgle finely down thy throttle?
Silenus
1.159:
Aye that it did, to the ends of my fingers.
Odysseus
1.160:
Well, we will give thee money besides.
Silenus
1.161:
Only undo the skin, and never mind the money.
Odysseus
1.162:
Bring out the cheeses then and lambs.
Silenus
1.163: I will do so, with small thought of any master. For let me have a single cup of that and I would turn madman,
1.165: giving in exchange for it the flocks of every Cyclops and then throwing myself into the sea from the Leucadian  rock, once I have been well drunk and smoothed out my wrinkled brow. For if a man rejoice not in his drinking, he is mad; for in drinking there is love
1.170:
with all its frolic, and dancing withal, and oblivion of woe. Shall not I then purchase so rare a drink, bidding the senseless Cyclops and his central eye go hang? Exit Silenus.
Chorus
1.175:
Hearken, Odysseus, let us hold some converse with thee.
Odysseus
1.176:
Well, do so; ours is a meeting of friends.
Chorus
1.177:
Did you take Troy and capture the famous Helen?
Odysseus
1.178:
Aye, and we destroyed the whole family of Priam.
Chorus
1.180: were all of you in turn her lovers? for she likes variety in husbands; the traitress! the sight of a man with embroidered breeches on his legs and a golden chain about his neck so fluttered her,
1.185:
that she left Menelaus, her excellent little husband. Would there had never been a race of women born into the world at all, unless it were for me alone!
Silenus
1.188: (reappearing with food.) Lo! I bring you fat food from the flocks, king Odysseus, the young of bleating sheep
1.190:
and cheeses of curdled milk without stint. Carry them away with you and be gone from the cave at once, after giving me a drink of merry grape-juice in exchange.
Chorus
1.193:
Alack! yonder comes the Cyclops; what shall we do?
Odysseus
1.194:
Then truly are we lost, old sir! whither must we fly?
Silenus
1.195:
Inside this rock, for there ye may conceal yourselves.
Odysseus
1.196:
Dangerous advice of thine, to run into the net!
Silenus
1.197:
No danger; there are ways of escape in plenty in the rock.
Odysseus
1.198: No, never that; for surely Troy will groan and loudly too, if we flee from a single man, when I have oft withstood
1.200:
with my shield a countless host of Phrygians. Nay, if die we must, we will die a noble death; or, if we live, we will maintain our old renown at least with credit.
Cyclops
1.203: A light here! hold it up! what is this? what means this idleness, your Bacchic revelry? Here have we no Dionysus,
1.205: nor clash of brass, nor roll of drums. Pray, how is it with my newly-born lambs in the caves? are they at the teat, running close to the side of their dams? Is the full amount of milk for cheeses milked out in baskets of rushes?
1.210:
How now? what say you? One of ye will soon be shedding tears from the weight of my club; look up, not down.
Chorus
1.212:
There! my head is bent back till I see Zeus himself; I behold both the stars and Orion.
Cyclops
1.214:
Is my breakfast quite ready?
Chorus
1.215:
’Tis laid; be thy throat only ready.
Cyclops
1.216:
Are the bowls too full of milk?
Chorus
1.217:
Aye, so that thou canst swill off a whole hogshead, so it please thee.
Cyclops
1.218:
Sheeps’ milk or cows’ milk or a mixture of both?
Chorus
1.219:
Whichever thou wilt; don’t swallow me, that’s all.
Cyclops
1.220: Not I; for you would start kicking in the pit of my stomach and kill me by your antics. (Catching sight of Odysseus and his followers.) Ha! what is this crowd I see near the folds? Some pirates or robbers have put in here. Yes, I really see the lambs from my caves
1.225:
tied up there with twisted osiers, cheese-presses scattered about, and old Silenus with his bald pate all swollen with blows.
Silenus
1.228:
Oh! oh! poor wretch that I am, pounded to a fever.
Cyclops
1.229:
By whom? who has been pounding thy head, old sirrah?
Silenus
1.230:
These are the culprits, Cyclops, all because I refused to let them plunder thee.
Cyclops
1.231:
Did they not know I was a god and sprung from gods?
Silenus
1.232: That was what I told them, but they persisted in plundering thy goods, and, in spite of my efforts, they actually began to eat the cheese and carry off the lambs; and they said they would
1.235: tie thee in a three-cubit pillory and tear out thy bowels by force at thy navel, and flay thy back thoroughly with the scourge; and then, after binding thee, fling thy carcase down among the benches of their ship to sell to some one
1.240:
for heaving up stones, or else throw thee into a mill.
Cyclops
1.241: Oh, indeed! Be off then and sharpen my cleavers at once; heap high the faggots and light them; for they shall be slain forthwith and fill this maw of mine,
1.245:
what time I pick my feast hot from the coals, waiting not for carvers, and fish up the rest from the cauldron boiled and sodden; for I have had my fill of mountain-fare and sated myself with banquets of lions and stags, but ’tis long I have been without human flesh.
Silenus
1.250:
Truly, master, a change like this is all the sweeter after everyday fare; for just of late there have been no fresh arrivals of strangers at these caves.
Odysseus
1.253: Hear the strangers too in turn, Cyclops. We had come near the cave from our ship,
1.255: wishing to procure provisions by purchase, when this fellow sold us the lambs and handed them over for a stoup of wine to drink himself,—a voluntary act on both sides,—there was no violence employed at all. No, there is not a particle of truth in the story he tells,
1.260:
now that he has been caught selling thy property behind thy back.
Silenus
1.261:
I? Perdition catch thee!
Odysseus
If I am lying, yes.
Silenus
1.262: O Cyclops, by thy sire Poseidon, by mighty Triton and Nereus, by Calypso and the daughters of Nereus,
1.265:
by the sacred billows and all the race of fishes! I swear to thee, most noble sir, dear little Cyclops, master mine, it is not I who sell thy goods to strangers, else may these children, dearly as I love them, come to an evil end.
Chorus
1.270:
Keep that for thyself; with my own eyes I saw thee sell the goods to the strangers; and if I lie, perdition catch my sire! but injure not the strangers.
Cyclops
1.273: Ye lie; for my part I put more faith in him than Rhadamanthus, declaring him more just.
1.275:
But I have some questions to ask. Whence sailed ye, strangers? of what country are you? what city was it nursed your childhood?
Odysseus
1.277:
We are Ithacans by birth, and have been driven from our course by the winds of the sea on our way from Ilium, after sacking its citadel.
Cyclops
1.280:
Are ye the men who visited on Ilium, that bordereth on Scamander’s wave, the rape of Helen, worst of women?
Odysseus
1.282:
We are; that was the fearful labour we endured.
Cyclops
1.283:
A sorry expedition yours, to have sailed to the land of Phrygia for the sake of one woman!
Odysseus
1.285: It was a god’s doing; blame not any son of man. But thee do we implore, most noble son of Ocean’s god, speaking as free-born men; be not so cruel as to slay thy friends on their coming to thy cave, nor regard us as food for thy jaws, an impious meal;
1.290: for we preserved thy sire, O king, in possession of his temple-seats deep in the nooks of Hellas; and the sacred port of Taenarus and Malea’s furthest coves remain unharmed; and Sunium’s rock, the silver-veined, sacred to Zeus-born Athena, still is safe,
1.295: and Geraestus, the harbour of refuge; and we did not permit Phrygians to put such an intolerable reproach on Hellas. Now in these things thou too hast a share, for thou dwellest in a corner of the land of Hellas beneath Aetna’s fire-streaming rock; and although thou turn from arguments,
1.300: still it is a custom amongst mortal men to receive shipwrecked sailors as their suppliants and show them hospitality and help them with raiment; not that these should fill thy jaws and belly, their limbs transfixed with spits for piercing ox-flesh. The land of Priam hath emptied Hellas quite enough,
1.305: drinking the blood of many whom the spear laid low, with the ruin it has brought on widowed wives, on aged childless dames, and hoary-headed sires; and if thou roast and consume the remnant,—a meal thou wilt rue,—why, where shall one turn? Nay, be persuaded by me, Cyclops;
1.310:
forego thy ravenous greed and choose piety rather than wickedness; for on many a man ere now unrighteous gains have brought down retribution.
Silenus
1.313: ..... I will give thee a word of advice! as for his flesh, leave not a morsel of it, and if thou eat his tongue,
1.315:
Cyclops, thou wilt become a monstrous clever talker.
Cyclops
1.316: Wealth, manikin, is the god for the wise; all else is mere vaunting and fine words. Plague take the headlands by the sea, on which my father seats himself! Why hast thou put forward these arguments?
1.320: I shudder not at Zeus’s thunder, nor know I wherein Zeus is a mightier god than I, sir stranger; what is more, I reck not of him; my reasons hear. When he pours down the rain from above, here in this rock in quarters snug,
1.325: feasting on roast calf’s flesh or some wild game and moistening well my upturned paunch with deep draughts from a tub of milk, I rival the thunderclaps of Zeus with my artillery; and when the north-wind blows from Thrace and sheddeth snow,
1.330: I wrap my carcase in the hides of beasts and light a fire, and what care I for snow? The earth perforce, whether she like it or not, produces grass and fattens my flocks, which I sacrifice to no one save myself
1.335: and this belly, the greatest of deities; but to the gods, not I! For surely to eat and drink one’s fill from day to day and give oneself no grief at all, this is the king of gods for your wise man, but lawgivers go hang, chequering, as they do, the life of man!
1.340: And so I will not cease from  indulging myself by devouring thee; and thou shalt receive this stranger’s gift, that I may be free of blame,—fire and my father’s element yonder, and a cauldron to hold thy flesh and boil it nicely in collops.
1.345:
So in with you, that ye may feast me well, standing round the altar to honour the cavern’s god. [Enters his cave.
Odysseus
1.347: Alas! escaped from the troubles of Troy and the sea, my barque now strands upon the whim and forbidding heart of this savage.
1.350: O Pallas, mistress mine, goddess-daughter of Zeus, help me, help me now; for I am come to toils and depths of peril worse than all at Ilium; and thou, O Zeus, the stranger’s god, who hast thy dwelling ’mid the radiant stars, behold these things;
1.355:
for, if thou regard them not, in vain art thou esteemed the great god Zeus, though but a thing of naught. [Follows the Cyclops reluctantly.
Chorus
1.356: Ope wide the portal of thy gaping throat, Cyclops; for strangers’ limbs, both boiled and grilled, are ready from off the coals for thee to gnaw and tear and mince up small,
1.360:
reclining in thy shaggy goatskin coat.
Chorus
1.361: Relinquish not thy meal for me; keep that boat for thyself alone. Avaunt this cave! avaunt the burnt-offerings,
1.365:
which the godless Cyclops offers on Aetna’s altars, exulting in meals on strangers’ flesh!
Chorus
1.369:
Oh! the ruthless monster! to sacrifice his guests at his own hearth, the suppliants of his halls, cleaving and tearing and serving up to his loathsome teeth a feast of human flesh, hot from the coals.
Chorus
1.375:
(reappearing with a look of horror.) O Zeus! what can I say after the hideous sights I have seen inside the cave, things past belief, resembling more the tales men tell than aught they do?
Chorus
1.377:
What news, Odysseus? has the Cyclops, most godless monster, been feasting on thy dear comrades?
Odysseus
1.379: Aye, he singled out a pair, on whom the flesh was
1.380:
fattest and in best condition, and took them up in his hand to weigh.
Chorus
1.381:
How went it with you then, poor wretch?
Odysseus
1.382: When we had entered yonder rocky abode, he lighted first a fire, throwing logs of towering oak upon his spacious hearth,
1.385: enough for three waggons to carry as their load; next, close by the blazing flame, he placed his couch of pine-boughs laid upon the floor, and filled a bowl of some ten firkins, pouring white milk thereinto, after he had milked his kine;
1.390: and by his side he put a can of ivy-wood, whose breadth was three cubits and its depth four maybe; spits too he set beside him, fashioned of the branches of thorn, their points hardened in the fire and the rest of them trimmed with the hatchet,
1.395: and the blood-bowls of Aetna for the axe’s edge. Now when that hell-cook, god-detested, had everything quite ready, he caught up a pair of my companions and proceeded deliberately to cut the throat of one of them over the yawning brazen pot;
1.400: but the other he clutched by the tendon of his heel, and, striking him against a sharp point of rocky stone, dashed out his brains; then, after hacking the fleshy parts with glutton cleaver, he set to grilling them, but the limbs he threw into his cauldron to seethe.
1.405: And I, poor wretch, drew near with streaming eyes and waited on the Cyclops; but the others kept cowering like frightened birds in crannies of the rock, and the blood forsook their skin.
1.409: Anon, when he had gorged himself upon my comrades’ flesh and
1.410: had fallen on his back, breathing heavily, there came a sudden inspiration to me. I filled a cup of this Maronian wine and offered him a draught, saying, Cyclops, son of Ocean’s god, see here what heavenly drink the grapes of Hellas yield,
1.415: glad gift of Dionysus. He, glutted with his shameless meal, took and drained it at one draught, and, lifting up his hand, he thanked me thus, Dearest to me of all my guests! fair the drink thou givest me to crown so fair a feast.
1.420: Now when I saw his delight, I gave him another cup, knowing the wine would make him rue it, and he would soon be paying the penalty. Then he set to singing; but I kept filling bumper after bumper and heating him with drink.
1.425: So there he is singing discordantly amid the weeping of my fellow-sailors, and the cave re-echoes; but I have made my way out quietly and would fain save thee and myself, if thou wilt. Tell me then, is it your wish, or is it not, to fly from this unsocial wretch
1.430: and take up your abode with Naiad nymphs in the halls of the Bacchic god? Thy father within approves this scheme; but there! he is powerless, getting all he can out of his liquor; his wings are snared by the cup as if he had flown against bird-lime, and he is fuddled; but thou art young and lusty;
1.435:
so save thyself with my help and regain thy old friend Dionysus, so little like the Cyclops.
Chorus
1.437: Best of friends, would we might see that day, escaping the godless Cyclops!
1.441:
Hear then how I will requite this vile monster and rescue you from thraldom.
Chorus
1.443:
Tell me how; no note of Asiatic lyre would sound more sweetly in our ears than news of the Cyclops’ death.
Odysseus
1.445:
Delighted with this liquor of the Bacchic god, he fain would go a-revelling with his brethren.
Chorus
1.447:
I understand; thy purpose is to seize and slay him in the thickets when alone, or push him down a precipice.
Odysseus
1.449:
Not at ail; my plan is fraught with subtlety.
Chorus
1.450:
What then? Truly we have long heard of thy cleverness.
Odysseus
1.451: I mean to keep him from this revel, saying he must not give this drink to his brethren but keep it for himself alone and lead a happy life. Then when he falls asleep, o’ermastered by the Bacchic god,
1.455: I will put a point with this sword of mine to an olive-branch I saw lying in the cave, and will set it on fire; and when I see it well alight, I will lift the heated brand, and, thrusting it full in the Cyclops’ eye, melt out his sight with its blaze;
1.460:
and, as when a man in fitting the timbers of a ship makes his auger spin to and fro with a double strap, so will I make the brand revolve in the eye that gives the Cyclops light and will scorch up the pupil thereof.
Chorus
1.464:
Ho! ho! how glad I feel! wild with joy at the contrivance!
Odysseus
1.466:
That done, I will embark thee and those thou lovest with old Silenus in the deep hold of my black ship, my ship with double banks of oars, and carry you away from this land.
Chorus
1.469:
Well, can I too lay hold of the blinding brand, as though the god’s libation had been poured? for I would fain have a share in this offering of blood.
Odysseus
1.472:
Indeed thou must, for the brand is large, and thou must help hold it.
Chorus
1.473: How lightly would I lift the load of e’en a hundred wains, if that will help us to grub out
1.475:
the eye of the doomed Cyclops, like a wasp’s nest.
Odysseus
1.476: Hush! for now thou knowest my plot in fall, and when I bid you, obey the author of it; for I am not the man to desert my friends inside the cave and save myself alone.
1.480:
And yet I might escape; I am clear of the cavern’s depths already; but no! to desert the friends with whom I journeyed hither and only save myself is not a righteous course. [Re-enters the cave.
First Half-Chorus

Cyclops

Cyclops

Cyclops

Odysseus

1.629:
Silent we stand with ’bated breath.

1.630:

1.642:

Chorus
1.643: Because I feel for my back and spine, and express no wish to have my teeth

1.649: Long since I knew thou wert by nature such an one,

Chorus

the shepherd of Aetna; twirl the brand and drag it round and be careful lest in his agony he treat thee to some wantonness.
Cyclops
1.663:
(Bellowing in the cave.) Oh! oh! my once bright eye is burnt to cinders now.
Chorus
1.664:
Sweet indeed the triumph-song; pray sing it to us, Cyclops.
Cyclops

(from within.) Oh! oh! once more; what outrage on me and what ruin! But never shall ye escape this rocky cave unpunished, ye worthless creatures; for I will stand in the entrance of the cleft and fit my hands into it thus. [Staggering to the entrance.

Why dost thou cry out, Cyclops?

I am undone.
Chorus
1.670:
Thou art indeed a sorry sight.
Cyclops

Chorus
1.671:
Didst fall among the coals in a drunken fit?
Cyclops
1.672:
Noman has undone me.

Then there is no one hurting thee after all.
Cyclops

Noman is blinding me.

Then art thou not blind.
Cyclops
1.674:
As blind as thou, forsooth.
Chorus

Cyclops
1.675:

Nowhere, Cyclops.

1.676:

1.678:
Ah! wine is a terrible foe, hard to wrestle with.
Cyclops
1.679:

Cyclops

On thy right.

Where?

Cyclops
1.683:

Aye, and they are escaping thee.
Cyclops
1.685:

Cyclops

Cyclops
1.689:

Some way from thee

I am keeping careful guard over the person of Odysseus.
Cyclops

unless I had avenged on thee the slaughter of my comrades.

and crush thee, crew and all, beneath my throw. Blind though I be, I will climb the hill, mounting through yonder tunnel.

1.1: Halls of Admetus, wherein I steeled my heart to be content with a servant’s board, god though I was. Zeus was to blame; he slew my son Asclepius, piercing his bosom with a thunderbolt;

1.20: gasping out her life; for to-day is she doomed to die and pass from life to death. But I, for fear pollution overtake me in the house, am leaving the shelter of this roof I love so well, for already I see Death hard by,
1.25:
the priest of souls departed, who is on his way to lead her to the halls of Hades; true to time he comes, watching this day that calls her to her doom.

1.35:
hast thou armed thee with thy bow and art keeping guard o’er her, this daughter of Pelias, who undertook, of her free will, to die for her lord and set him free.
Apollo
1.38:
Never fear; I have, be sure, justice and fair pleas to urge.
Death
1.39:
What has that bow to do, if thou hast justice on thy side?
Apollo
1.40:
’Tis my habit ever to carry it.
Death
1.41:
Ay, and to help this house more than is right.
Apollo
1.42:

Death
1.43:

Apollo
1.44:
Come! I did not take the other from thee by violence.
Death
1.45:

Apollo
1.46:
He gave his wife instead, her whom now thou art come to fetch.
Death
1.47:
Yea, and I will bear her hence to the nether world.
Apollo
1.48:
Take her and go, for I do not suppose I can persuade thee.
Death
1.49:

Apollo
1.50:

Death
1.51:
I see thy drift, thy eager plea.
Apollo
1.52:

1.53:

Apollo
1.54:

Death
1.55:

Apollo
1.56:

1.57:

Apollo
1.58:

1.59:
Those who have wealth would buy the chance of their dying old.
Apollo
1.60:

1.61:

Apollo
1.62:

So wilt thou get no thanks from me but yet wilt do this all the same, and earn my hatred too.

Lo! I am going for her, that with the sword I may begin my rites, for he whose hair this sword doth hallow is sacred to the gods below.

Second Semichorus
1.106:

1.108:

Chorus

still is living or haply is no more.

Chorus

Maid
1.143:

Chorus
1.144:

Maid
1.145:

Chorus
1.146:

Maid
1.147:
None; the fated day comes on so fast.
Chorus
1.148:

Maid
1.149:
Death’s garniture is ready, wherewith her lord will bury her.
