Alcestis
1.245:
O scudding clouds that dance along the sky!
Admetus
1.246:
He sees us both with anguish bowed, albeit guiltless of any crime against the gods, for the which thy death is due.
Alcestis
1.248:
O earth, O sheltering roof, and ye my maiden chambers in my native land Iolcos!
Admetus
1.250:
Lift thyself, unhappy wife, forsake me not; entreat the mighty gods to pity us.
Alcestis
1.252: I see the two-oared skiff, I see it; and Charon, death’s ferryman, his hand upon the boatman’s pole,
1.255:
is calling me e’en now, Why lingerest thou? Hasten. Thou art keeping me. Thus in his eager haste he hurries me.
Admetus
1.257:
Ah me! bitter to me is this voyage thou speakest of. Unhappy wife, what woes are ours!
Alcestis
1.259: One draws me, draws me hence, seest thou not?
1.260:
to the courts of death, winged Hades glaring from beneath his dark brows. What wilt thou with me? Unhand me. On what a journey am I setting out, most wretched woman I!
Admetus
1.264: Bitter journey to thy friends, yet most of all to me
1.265:
and to thy babes, the partners in this sorrow.
Alcestis
1.266: Hands off! hands off at once! Lay me down, I cannot stand. Hades standeth near; and with its gloom steals night upon my eyes.
1.270:
O my children, my children, ye have no mother now. Fare ye well, my babes, live on beneath the light!
Admetus
1.273: Woe is me! this is a message of sorrow to me, worse than aught that death can do.
1.275:
Steel not thy heart to leave me, I implore, by heaven, by thy babes whom thou wilt make orphans; nay, raise thyself, have courage. For if thou die I can no longer live; my life, my death are in thy hands; thy love is what I worship.
Alcestis
1.280: Admetus, lo! thou seest how it is with me; to thee I fain would tell my wishes ere I die. Thee I set before myself, and instead of living have ensured thy life, and so I die, though I need not have died for thee,
1.285: but might have taken for my husband whom I would of the Thessalians, and have had a home blest with royal power; reft of thee, with my children orphans, I cared not to live, nor, though crowned with youth’s fair gifts, wherein I used to joy, did I grudge them.
1.290: Yet the father that begat thee, the mother that bare thee, gave thee up, though they had reached a time of life when to die were well, so saving thee their child, and winning noble death. For thou wert their only son, nor had they any hope, when thou wert dead, of other offspring.
1.295: And I should have lived and thou the remnant of our days, nor wouldst thou have wept thy wife’s loss, nor have had an orphan family. But some god hath caused these things to be even as they are. Enough! Remember thou the gratitude due to me for this;
1.300: yea, for I shall never ask thee for an adequate return, for naught is prized more highly than our life; but just is my request, as thou thyself must say, since thou no less than I dost love these children, if so be thou think’st aright. Be content to let them rule my house,
1.305: and do not marry a new wife to be a stepmother to these children, for she from jealousy, if so she be a woman worse than me, will stretch out her hand against the children of our union. Then do not this, I do beseech thee. For the stepmother that succeeds, hateth children
1.310: of a former match, cruel as the viper’s are her tender mercies. A son, ’tis true, hath in his sire a tower of strength,; but thou, my daughter, how shall thy maidenhood be passed in honour? What shall thy experience be of thy father’s wife?
1.315: She may fasten on thee some foul report in thy youthful bloom, and frustrate thy marriage. Never shall thy mother lead thee to the bridal bed, nor by her presence in thy travail hearten thee, my child, when a mother’s kindness triumphs over all.
1.320: No, for I must die; and lo! this evil cometh to me not to-morrow nor yet on the third day of the month, but in a moment shall I be counted among the souls that are no more. Fare ye well, be happy; and thou, husband, canst boast thou hadst a peerless wife,
1.325:
and you, children, that you had such an one for mother.
Chorus
1.326:
Take heart; I do not hesitate to answer for him; he will perform all this, unless his mind should go astray.
Admetus
1.328: It shall be so, fear not, it shall; alive thou wert the only wife I had, and dead shalt thou,
1.330: none else, be called mine; no Thessalian maid shall ever take thy place and call me lord; not though she spring from lineage high nor though besides she be the fairest of her sex. Of children I have enough; god grant I may in them
1.335: be blessed! for in thee has it been otherwise. No year-long mourning will I keep for thee, but all my life through, lady: loathing the mother that bare me, and hating my father, for they were friends in word but not in deed.
1.340: But thou didst give thy dearest for my life and save it. May I not then mourn to lose a wife like thee? And I will put an end to revelry, to social gatherings o’er the wine, forego the festal crown and music which once reigned in my halls.
1.345: For nevermore will I touch the lyre nor lift my soul in song to the Libyan flute, for thou hast taken with thee all my joy in life. But in my bed thy figure shall be laid full length, by cunning artists fashioned;
1.350: thereon will I throw myself and, folding my arms about thee, call upon thy name, and think I hold my dear wife in my embrace, although I do not; chill comfort this, no doubt, but still I shall relieve my soul of its sad weight; and thou wilt come
1.355: to me in dreams and gladden me. For sweet it is to see our friends, come they when they will, e’en by night. Had I the tongue, the tuneful voice of Orpheus to charm Demeter’s daughter or her husband by my lay and bring thee back from Hades,
1.360: I had gone down, nor Pluto’s hound, nor Charon, ferryman of souls, whose hand is on the oar, had held me back, till to the light I had restored thee alive. At least do thou await me there, against the hour I die, prepare a home for me to be my true wife still.
1.365:
For in this same cedar coffin I will bid these children lay me with thee and stretch my limbs by thine; for never even in death may I be severed from thee, alone found faithful of them all.
Chorus
1.369: Lo! I too will share with thee thy mourning for her, friend with friend;
1.370:
for this is but her due.
Alcestis
1.371:
My children, ye with your own ears have heard your father’s promise, that he will never wed another wife to set her over you, nor e’er dishonour me.
Admetus
1.374:
Yea, so I promise now, and accomplish it I will.
Alcestis
1.375:
On these conditions receive the children from my hand.
Admetus
1.376:
I receive them, dear pledges by a dear hapd given.
Alcestis
1.377:
Take thou my place and be a mother to these babes.
Admetus
1.378:
Sore will be their need when they are reft of thee.
Alcestis
1.379:
O my children, I am passing to that world below, when my life was needed most.
Admetus
1.380:
Ah me, what can I do bereft of thee?
Alcestis
1.381:
Thy sorrow Time will soothe; ’tis the dead who are as naught.
Admetus
1.382:
Take me, O take me, I beseech, with thee ’neath the earth.
Alcestis
1.383:
Enough that I in thy stead am dying.
Admetus
1.384:
O Destiny! of what a wife art thou despoiling me!
Alcestis
1.385:
Lo! the darkness deepens on my drooping eyes.
Admetus
1.386:
Lost indeed am I, if thou, dear wife, wilt really leave me.
Alcestis
1.387:
Thou mayst speak of me as naught, as one whose life is o’er.
Admetus
1.388:
Lift up thy face, leave not thy children.
Alcestis
1.389:
’Tis not my own free will; O my babes, farewell!
Admetus
1.390:
Look, look on them but once.
Alcestis
My end is come.
Admetus
1.391:
What mean’st thou? art leaving us?
Alcestis
Farewell!
Admetus
Lost! lost! woe is me!
Chorus
1.392:
She is gone, the wife of Admetus is no more.
Eumelus
1.393: O my hard fate! My mother has passed to the realms below; she lives no more,
1.395: dear father, ’neath the sun. Alas for her! she leaves us ere her time and to me bequeaths an orphan’s life. Behold that staring eye, those nerveless hands!
1.400:
Hear me, mother, hear me, I implore! ’tis I who call thee now, I thy tender chick, printing my kisses on thy lips.
Admetus
1.404: She cannot hear, she cannot see;
1.405:
a heavy blow hath fortune dealt us, you children and me.
Eumelus
1.406: O father, I am but a child to have my loving mother leave me here alone; O cruel my fate, alas!
1.410: and thine, my sister, sharer in my cup of woe. Woe to thee, father! in vain, in vain didst thou take a wife and hast not reached the goal of eld with her; for she is gone before, and now that thou art dead,
1.415:
my mother, our house is all undone.
Chorus
1.416:
Admetus, these misfortunes thou must bear. Thou art by no means the first nor yet shalt be the last of men to lose a wife of worth; know this, we all of us are debtors unto death.
Admetus
1.420: I understand; this is no sudden flight of ill hither; I was ware of it and long have pined. But since I am to. carry the dead forth to her burial, stay here with me and to that inexorable god in Hades raise your antiphone. While raise your antiphone.
1.425: While to all Thessalians in my realm I do proclaim a general mourning for this lady, with hair shorn off and robes of sable hue; all ye who harness steeds for cars, or single horses ride, cut off their manes with the sharp steel.
1.430:
Hush’d be every pipe, silent every lyre throughout the city till twelve full moons are past; for never again shall I bury one whom I love more, no! nor one more loyal to me; honour from me is her due, for she for me hath died, she and she alone. [Exeunt ADMETUS and EUMELUS, with the other children.
Chorus
1.435: Daughter of Pelias, be thine a happy life in that sunless home in Hades’ halls! Let Hades know, that swarthy god,
1.440:
and that old man who sits to row and steer alike at his death-ferry, that he hath carried o’er the lake of Acheron in his two-oared skiff a woman peerless amidst her sex.
Chorus
1.445: Oft of thee the Muses’ votaries shall sing on the seven-stringed mountain shell and in hymns that need no harp, glorifying thee, oft as the season in his cycle cometh round at Sparta in that Carnean month
1.450:
when all night long the moon sails high o’erhead, yea, and in splendid Athens, happy town. So glorious a theme has thy death bequeathed to tuneful bards.
Chorus
1.455: Would it were in my power and range to bring thee to the light from the chambers of Hades and the streams of Cocytus with the oar that sweeps yon nether flood!
1.460: For thou, and thou alone, most dear of women, hadst the courage to redeem thy husband from Hades in exchange for thy own life. Light lie the earth above thee, lady! And if ever thy lord take to him a new wife, I vow he will earn my hatred
1.466: His mother had no heart to plunge into the darkness of the tomb for her son, no! nor his aged sire. Their own child they had not the courage to rescue,
1.470: the wretches! albeit they were grey-headed. But thou in thy youth and beauty hast died for thy lord and gone thy way. O be it mine to have for partner such a loving wife! for this lot is rare in life. Surely she should be my help-meet all my life
1.475:
and never cause one tear.
Heracles
1.476:
Mine hosts, dwellers on this Phersean soil! say, shall I find Admetus in the house?
Chorus
1.478: The son of Pheres is within, Heracles. Tell me what need is bringing thee to the Thessalian land,
1.480:
to visit this city of the Pheraeans?
Heracles
1.481:
I am performing a labour for Tirynthian Eurystheus.
Chorus
1.482:
And whither art thou journeying? on what wandering art thou forced to go?
Heracles
1.483:
To fetch the chariot-steeds of Thracian Diomedes.
Chorus
1.484:
How canst thou? art a stranger to the ways of thy host?
Heracles
1.485:
I am; for never yet have I gone to the land of the Bistones.
Chorus
1.486:
Thou canst not master his horses without fighting.
Heracles
1.487:
Still I cannot refuse these labours.
Chorus
1.488:
Then shalt thou slay them and return, or thyself be slain and stay there.
Heracles
1.489:
It will not be the first hard course that I have run.
Chorus
1.490:
And what will be thy gain, suppose thou master their lord?
Heracles
1.491:
The steeds will I drive away to the Tirynthian king.
Chorus
1.492:
No easy task to bit their jaws.
Heracles
1.493:
Easy enough, unless their nostrils vomit fire.
Chorus
1.494:
With ravening jaws they rend the limbs of men.
Heracles
1.495:
Thou speakest of the food of mountain beasts, not of horses.
Chorus
1.496:
Their mangers blood-bedabbled thou shalt see.
Heracles
1.497:
Whose son doth he who feeds them boast to be?
Chorus
1.498:
Ares’ son, king of the golden targe of Thrace.
Heracles
1.499: This toil again is but a piece of my ill-luck;
1.500: hard it ever is and still is growing steeper, if I with Ares’ own-begotten sons must fight, first with Lycaon, next with Cycnus, while now I am bound on this third contest to engage the horses and their master.
1.505:
Yet shall no man ever see Alcmena’s son trembling at his foemen’s prowess.
Chorus
1.507:
See where Admetus, lord of this land, comes in person from the palace forth.
Admetus
1.509:
Hail! son of Zeus, from Perseus sprung.
Heracles
1.510:
Joy to thee also, Admetus, king of Thessaly.
Admetus
1.511:
Would there were! yet thy kindly heart I know full well.
Heracles
1.512:
Why dost thou appear with head shorn thus in mourning?
Admetus
1.513:
To-day I am to bury one who is dead.
Heracles
1.514:
Heaven avert calamity from thy children!
Admetus
1.515:
The children I have begotten are alive within my house.
Heracles
1.516:
Thy father maybe is gone; well, he was ripe to go.
Admetus
1.517:
No, Heracles, he lives; my mother too.
Heracles
1.518:
It cannot be thy wife is dead, thy Alcestis?
Admetus
1.519:
I can a twofold tale tell about her.
Heracles
1.520:
Dost mean that she is dead, or living still?
Admetus
1.521:
She lives, yet lives no more; that is my grief.
Heracles
1.522:
I am no wiser yet; thy words are riddles to me.
Admetus
1.523:
Knowest thou not the doom she must undergo?
Heracles
1.524:
I know she did submit to die in thy stead.
Admetus
1.525:
How then is she still alive, if so she promised?
Heracles
1.526:
Ah! weep not thy wife before the day, put that off till then.
Admetus
1.527:
The doomed is dead; the dead no more exists.
Heracles
1.528:
Men count to be and not to be something apart.
Admetus
1.529:
Thy verdict this, O Heracles, mine another.
Heracles
1.530:
Why weepest then? which of thy dear ones is the dead?
Admetus
1.531:
’Tis a woman; I spoke of a woman just now.
Heracles
1.532:
A stranger, or one of thine own kin?
Admetus
1.533:
A stranger, yet in another sense related to my house.
Heracles
1.534:
How then came she by her death in house of thine?
Admetus
1.535:
Her father dead, she lived here as an orphan.
Heracles
1.536:
Ah! would I had found thee free from grief, Admetus!
Admetus
1.537:
With what intent dost thou devise this speech?
Heracles
1.538:
I will seek some other friendly hearth.
Admetus
1.539:
Never, O prince! Heaven forefend such dire disgrace!
Heracles
1.540:
A guest is a burden to sorrowing friends, if come he should.
Admetus
1.541:
The dead are dead. Come in.
Heracles
1.542:
To feast in a friend’s house of sorrow is shameful.
Admetus
1.543:
The guest chambers lie apart, whereto we will conduct thee.
Heracles
1.544:
Let me go; ten thousandfold shall be my thanks to thee.
Admetus
1.545: Thou must not go to any other hearth. (To a Servant.) Go before, open the guest-rooms that face not these chambers, and bid my stewards see there is plenty of food; then shut the doors that lead into the courtyard; for ’tis not seemly that guests when at their meat
1.550:
should hear the voice of weeping or be made sad. [Exit HERACLES.
Chorus
1.551:
What doest thou? With such calamity before thee, hast thou the heart, Admetus, to welcome visitors? What means this folly?
Admetus
1.553: Well, and if I had driven him from my house and city when he came to be my guest, wouldst thou have praised me more?
1.555: No indeed! for my calamity would have been no whit less, while I should have been more churlish. And this would have been another woe to add to mine, that my house should be called no friend to guests. Yea, and I find him myself the best of hosts
1.560:
whene’er to Argos’ thirsty land I come.
Chorus
1.561:
Why then didst thou conceal thy present misfortune, if, as thy own lips declare, it was a friend that came?
Admetus
1.563: He would never have entered my house, had he known aught of my distress.
1.565:
Maybe there are who think me but a fool for acting thus, and these will blame me; but my halls have never learnt to drive away or treat with scorn my guests.
Chorus
1.569: O home of hospitality, thrown open by thy lord to all now and ever!
1.570: In thee it was that Pythian Apollo, the sweet harper, deigned to make his home, and in thy halls was content to lead a shepherd’s life,
1.575:
piping o’er the sloping downs shepherd’s madrigals to thy flocks.
Chorus
1.578: And spotted lynxes couched amid his sheep in joy to hear his melody,
1.580: and the lions’ tawny troop left the glen of Othrys and came; came too the dappled fawn on nimble foot from beyond the crested pines and frisked about thy lyre, O Phoebus,
1.585:
for very joy at thy gladsome minstrelsy.
Chorus
1.588: And so it is thy lord inhabits a home rich in countless flocks
1.590: by Boebe’s lovely mere, bounding his tilled corn-land and his level pastures with the clime of the Molossi near the sun’s dark stable,
1.595:
and holding sway as far as the harbourless strand of the Aegean ’neath Pelion’s shadow.
Chorus
1.597: Now too hath he opened wide his house and welcomed a guest although his eye is wet with tears in mourning for his wife so dear
1.600: but lately dead within his halls; yea, for noble birth to noble feeling is inclined. And in the good completest wisdom dwells; and at my heart sits the bold belief
1.605:
that heaven’s servant will be blessed.
Admetus
1.606: Men of Pherae, kindly gathered here, lo! even now my servants are bearing the corpse with all its trappings shoulder-high to the funeral pyre for burial; do ye, as custom bids,
1.610:
salute the dead on her last journey starting.
Chorus
1.611:
Look! I see thy father advancing with aged step, and servants too bearing in their arms adornment for thy wife, offerings for the dead.
Pheres
1.614: My son, I come to share thy sorrow,
1.615: for thou hast lost a noble, peerless wife; that no man will deny. Yet must thou needs bear this blow, hard though it be. Accept this garniture, and let it go beneath the earth, for rightly is her body honoured,
1.620: since she died to save thy life, my son, and gave me back my child, suffering me not to lose thee and pine away in an old age of sorrow. Thus by the generous deed she dared, hath she made her life a noble example for all her sex.
1.625:
Farewell to thee, who hast saved this son of mine and raised me up when falling; be thine a happy lot even in Hades’ halls! Such marriages I declare are gain to man, else to wed is not worth while.
Admetus
1.629: Thou hast come uncalled by me to this burial,
1.630: nor do I count thy presence as a friendly act. Never shall she be clad in any garniture of thine, nor in her burial will she need aught of thine. Thou shouldst have shewn thy sympathy at the time my doom was sealed. But thou didst stand aloof and let another die,
1.635: though thou wert old, the victim young; shalt thou then mourn the dead? Methinks thou wert no real sire of mine nor was she my true mother who calls herself and is called so, but I was sprung of slave’s blood and privily substituted at thy wife’s breast.
1.640: Brought to the test thou hast shewn thy nature; I cannot think I am thy child by birth. By heaven, thou art the very pattern of cowards, who at thy age, on the borderland of life, wouldst not, nay! couldst not find the heart to die
1.645: for thy own son; but ye, my parents, left to this stranger, whom I henceforth shall justly hold e’en as mother and as father too, and none but her. And yet ’twas a noble exploit to achieve, to die to save thy son, and in any case the
1.650: remnant of thy time to live was but short; and I and she would have lived the days that were to be, nor had I lost my wife and mourned my evil fate. Moreover thou hast had all treatment that a happy man should have; in princely pomp thy youth was spent,
1.655: thou hadst a son, myself, to be the heir of this thy home, so thou hadst no fear of dying childless and leaving thy house desolate, for strangers to pillage. Nor yet canst thou say I did dishonour thy old age and give thee up to die, seeing I have ever been
1.660: to thee most dutiful, and for this thou, my sire, and she, my mother, have made me this return. Go then, get other sons to tend thy closing years, prepare thy body for the grave, and lay out thy corpse.
1.665: For I will never bury thee with hand of mine; for I am dead for all thou didst for me; but if I found a saviour in another and still live, his son I say I am, and his fond nurse in old age will be. ’Tis vain, I see, the old man’s prayer for death,
1.670:
his plaints at age and life’s long weariness. For if death do but draw near, not one doth wish to die; old age no more they count so burdensome.
Chorus
1.674:
Peace! enough the present sorrow, O my son; goad not thy father’s soul to fury.
Pheres
1.675: Child, whom think’st thou art reviling? some Lydian or Phrygian bought with thy money? Art not aware I am a freebom Thessalian, son of a Thessalian sire? Thou art too insolent; yet from hence thou shalt not go as thou earnest,
1.680: after shooting out thy braggart tongue at me. To rule my house I begat and bred thee up; I own no debt of dying in thy stead; this is not the law that I received from my ancestors that fathers should die for children, nor is it a custom in Hellas.
1.685: For weal or woe, thy life must be thine own; whate’er was due from me to thee, thou hast. Dominion wide is thine, and acres broad I will leave to thee, for from my father did I inherit them. How, pray, have I wronged thee? of what am I robbing thee?
1.690: Die not thou for me, nor I for thee. Thy joy is in the light; think’st thou thy sire’s is not? By Heaven! ’tis a weary while, I trow, that time beneath the earth, and life, though short, is sweet. Thou at least didst struggle hard to ’scape thy death,
1.695: lost to shame, and by her death dost live beyond thy destined term. Dost thou then speak of cowardice in me, thou craven heart! no match for thy wife, who hath died for thee, her fine young lord? A clever scheme hast thou devised to stave off death for ever,
1.700: if thou canst persuade each new wife to die instead of thee; and dost thou then taunt thy friends, who will not do the like, coward as thou art thyself? Hold thy peace; reflect, if thou dost love thy life so well, this love by all is shared; yet if thou wilt speak ill of me,
1.705:
thyself shalt hear a full and truthful list of thy own crimes.
Chorus
1.706:
Too long that list both now and heretofore; cease, father, to revile thy son.
Admetus
1.708:
Say on, for I have said my say; but if it vexes thee to hear the truth, thou shouldst not have sinned against me.
Pheres
1.710:
My sin had been the deeper, had I died for thee.
Admetus
1.711:
What! is it all one for young or old to die?
Pheres
1.712:
To live one life, not twain, is all our due.
Admetus
1.714:
Dost curse thy parents, though unharmed by them?
Admetus
1.715:
Yea, for I see thy heart is set on length of days.
Pheres
1.716:
Is it not to save thyself thou art carrying to the tomb this corpse?
Admetus
1.717:
A proof of thy cowardice, thou craven heart!
Pheres
1.718:
At any rate her death was not due to me; this thou canst not say.
Admetus
1.719:
Ah! mayst thou some day come to need my aid!
Pheres
1.720:
Woo many wives, that there may be the more to die.
Admetus
1.721:
That is thy reproach, for thou didst refuse to die.
Pheres
1.722:
Dear is the light of the sun-god, dear to all.
Admetus
1.723:
A coward soul is thine, not to be reckoned among men.
Pheres
1.724:
No laughing now for thee at bearing forth my aged corpse.
Admetus
1.725:
Thy death will surely be a death of shame, come when it will.
Pheres
1.726:
Once dead I little reck of foul report.
Admetus
1.727:
Alas! how void of shame the old can be!
Pheres
1.728:
Hers was no want of shame; ’twas want of sense in her that thou didst find.
Admetus
1.729:
Begone! and leave me to bury my dead.
Pheres
1.730:
I go; bury thy victim, thyself her murderer. Her kinsmen yet will call for an account. Else surely has Acastus ceased to be a man, if he avenge not on thee his sister’s blood.
Admetus
1.734: Perdition seize thee and that wife of thine!
1.735: grow old, as ye deserve, childless, though your son yet lives, for ye shall never enter the same abode with me; nay! were it needful I should disown thy paternal hearth by heralds’ voice, I had disowned it. (Exit PHERES). Now, since we must bear our present woe,
1.740:
let us go and lay the dead upon the pyre. [Exit ADMETUS.
Chorus
1.741: Woe, woe for thee! Alas, for thy hardihood! Noble spirit, good beyond compare, farewell! May Hermes in the nether world, and Hades, too, give thee a kindly welcome! and if even in that other life
1.745:
the good are rewarded, mayst thou have thy share therein and take thy seat by Hades’ bride!
Attendant
1.747: Many the guests ere now from every comer of the world I have seen come to the halls of Admetus, for whom I have spread the board, but never yet
1.750: have I welcomed to this hearth a guest so shameless as this; a man who, in the first place, though he saw my master’s grief, yet entered and presumed to pass the gates, then took what cheer we had in no sober spirit, though he knew our sorrow;
1.755: no! was there aught we failed to bring? he called for it. Next in his hands he took a goblet of ivy-wood and drank the pure juice of the black grape, till the mounting fumes of wine heated him, and he crowned his head with myrtle-sprays,
1.760: howling discordantly, while two-fold strains were there to hear, for he would sing without a thought for the troubles in Admetus’ halls, while we servants mourned our mistress, though we did not let the stranger see our streaming eyes, for such was the bidding of Admetus.
1.765: So now here am I entertaining as a guest some miscreant thief maybe, or robber, while she is gone forth from the house, nor did I follow her nor stretch my hand towards her bier, in mourning for my lady, who, to me, and all her servants,
1.770:
was a mother, for she would save us from countless trouble, appeasing her husband’s angry mood. Have I not good cause then to loathe this guest who cometh in our hour of woe?
Heracles
1.773: Ho! sirrah, why that solemn, thoughtful look? ’Tis not the way for servants to scowl on guests,
1.775: but with courteous soul to welcome them. But thou, seeing a friend of thy master arrive, receivest him with sullen, lowering brow, though ’tis but a stranger that is the object of thy mourning. Come hither, that thou too mayst learn more wisdom.
1.780: Dost know the nature of this mortal state? I trow not; how shouldst thou? Well, lend an ear to me. Death is the common debt of man; no mortal really knows if he will live to see the morrow’s light;
1.785: for Fortune’s issues are not in our ken, beyond the teacher’s rule they lie, no art can master them. Hearken then to this and learn of me, be merry, drink thy cup, and count the present day thine own, the rest to Fortune yield.
1.790: And to Cypris too, sweetest of the gods by far to man, thy tribute pay, for kindly is her mood. Let be those other cares, and heed my counsel if thou think’st I speak aright; methinks I do. Come, banish this excessive grief,
1.795: and drink a cup with me when thou hast passed beyond these doors and wreathed thy brow; and I feel sure the plash of wine within the cup will bring thee to a better haven from this crabbed mood, this cabined state of mind. Mortals we are, and mortals’ thoughts should have;
1.800:
for all they who frown and scowl do miss,—leastways I think so,—the true life and get themselves misfortune.
Attendant
1.803:
I know all that, but our present state has little claim on revelry or laughter.
Heracles
1.805:
The dead was a stranger woman; grieve not to excess; for the rulers of thy house are living.
Attendant
1.807:
How, living? Thou knowest not the trouble in the house.
Heracles
1.808:
I do, unless thy master did in aught deceive me.
Attendant
1.810:
Was I to miss good cheer because a stranger had died?
Attendant
1.811:
A stranger surely! quite a stranger she!
Heracles
1.812:
Is there some trouble that he withheld from me?
Attendant
1.813:
Farewell, go thy way! my master’s troubles are my care.
Heracles
1.814:
This word of thine heralds not a grief for strangers felt.
Attendant
1.815:
Had it been, the sight of thy merriment had not grieved me so.
Heracles
1.816:
Can it be mine host hath strangely wronged me?
Attendant
1.817:
Thou earnest at no proper time for our house to welcome thee, for sorrow is come upon us; lo! thou seest our shorn heads and robes of sable hue.
Heracles
1.819: Who is it that is dead?
1.820:
Is it a child or his aged sire that hat hath passed away?
Attendant
1.821:
Nay, sir guest, ’tis Admetus’ wife that is no more.
Heracles
1.822:
What sayest thou? and did ye then in spite of that admit me to your cheer?
Attendant
1.823:
Yes, for his regard would not let him send thee from his door.
Heracles
1.824:
Unhappy husband, what a wife hast thou lost!
Attendant
1.825:
We are all undone, not she alone.
Heracles
1.826: I knew it when I saw his streaming eye, shorn head and downcast look, yet did he persuade me, saying it was a stranger he was bearing to burial. So I did constrain myself and passed his gates
1.830:
and sat drinking in his hospitable halls, when he was suffering thus. And have I wreathed my head and do I revel still? But—thou to hold thy peace when such a crushing sorrow lay upon the house! Where is he burying her? Whither shall I go to find her?
Attendant
1.835:
Beside the road that leadeth straight to Larissa, shalt thou see her carved tomb outside the suburb.
Heracles
1.837: O heart, O soul, both sufferers oft, now show the mettle of that son Tirynthian Alcmena, daughter of Electryon, bare to Zeus.
1.840: For I must save this woman, dead but now, setting Alcestis once again within this house, and to Admetus this kind service render. So I will go and watch for death the black-robed monarch of the dead, and him methinks I shall find
1.845: as he drinks of the blood-offering near the tomb. And if, from ambush rushing, once I catch and fold him in my arms’ embrace, none shall ever wrest him thence with smarting ribs, ere he give up the woman unto me.
1.850: But should I fail to find my prey and he come not to the clotted blood, I will go to the sunless home of those beneath the earth, to Persephone and her king, and make to them my prayer, sure that I shall bring Alcestis up again, to place her in the hands of him, my host,
1.855: who welcomed me to his house nor drove me thence, though fortune smote him hard, but this his noble spirit strove to hide out of regard for me. What host more kind than him in Thessaly? or in in the homes of Hellas? Wherefore shall he never say
1.860:
his generous deeds were lavished on a worthless wretch. [Exeunt HERACLES and Servant.
Admetus
1.861: Ah me! I loathe this entering in, and loathe to see my widowed home. Woe, woe is me! Whither shall I go? Where stand? what say? or what suppress? Would God that I were dead!
1.865: Surely in an evil hour my mother gave me birth. The dead I envy, and would fain be as they, and long to dwell within their courts. No joy to me to see the light, no joy to tread the earth;
1.870:
such a hostage death hath reft me of and handed o’er to Hades.
Chorus
1.872:
Move forward, go within the shelter of thy house.
Admetus
Woe is me!
Chorus
1.873:
Thy sufferings claim these cries of woe.
Admetus
Ah me!
Chorus
1.874:
Through anguish hast thou gone, full well I know.
Admetus
Alas! alas!
Chorus
1.875:
Thou wilt not help the dead one whit.
Admetus
O misery!
Chorus
1.876:
Nevermore to see thy dear wife face to face is grief indeed.
Admetus
1.878: Thy words have probed the sore place in my heart. What greater grief can come to man
1.880: than the loss of a faithful wife? Would I had never married or shared with her my home! I envy those ’mongst men who have nor wife nor child. Theirs is but one life; to grieve for that is no excessive burden;
1.885:
but to see children fall ill and bridal beds emptied by death’s ravages is too much to bear, when one might go through life without wife or child.
Chorus
1.889:
A fate we cannot cope with is come upon us.
Admetus
Woe is me!
Chorus
1.890:
But thou to sorrow settest no limit.
Admetus
Ah! ah!
Chorus
1.891:
’Tis hard to bear, but still—
Admetus
Woe is me!
Chorus
1.892:
Thou art not the first to lose—
Admetus
O! woe is me!
Chorus
1.893:
A wife; misfortune takes a different shape for every man she plagues.
Admetus
1.895: O the weary sorrow! O the grief for dear ones dead and gone! Why didst thou hinder me from plung-ing into the gaping grave, there to lay me down and die with her, my peerless bride?
1.900:
Then would Hades for that one have gotten these two faithful souls at once, crossing the nether lake together.
Chorus
1.903: I had a kinsman once, within whose home died
1.905: his only son, worthy of a father’s tears; yet in spite of that he bore his grief resignedly, childless though he was, his hair already turning grey, himself far on in years, upon
1.912: O house of mine, how can I enter thee? how can I live here, now that fortune turns against me? Ah me! How wide the gulf ’twixt then and now!
1.915: Then with torches cut from Pelion’s pines, with marriage hymns I entered in, holding my dear wife’s hand; and at our back a crowd of friends with cheerful cries, singing the happy lot of my dead wife and me,
1.920: calling us a noble pair made one, children both of highborn lineage; but now the voice of woe instead of wedding hymns, and robes of black instead of snowy white usher me
1.925:
into my house to my deserted couch.
Chorus
1.926: Hard upon prosperous fortune came this sorrow to thee, a stranger to adversity; yet hast thou saved thy soul alive.
1.930:
Thy wife is dead and gone; her love she leaves with thee. What new thing is here? Death ere now from many a man hath torn a wife.
Admetus
1.935: My friends, I count my dead wife’s lot more blest than mine, for all it seems not so; for nevermore can sorrow touch her for ever; all her toil is over, and glorious is her fame. While I, who had no right to live, have passed the bounds of fate
1.940: only to live a life of misery; I know it now. For how shall I endure to enter this my house? Whom shall I address, by whom be answered back, to find aught joyful in my entering in? Whither shall I turn? Within, the desolation will drive me forth,
1.945: whensoe’er I see my widowed couch, the seat whereon she sat, the floor ail dusty in the house, and my babes falling at my knees with piteous tears for their mother, while my servants mourn the good mistress their house hath lost.
1.950: These are the sorrows in my home, while abroad the marriages among Thessalians and the thronging crowds of women will drive me mad, for I can never bear to gaze upon the compeers of my wife. And whoso is my foe will taunt me thus,
1.955: Behold him living in his shame, a wretch who quailed at death himself, but of his coward heart gave up his wedded wife instead, and escaped from Hades; doth he deem himself a man after that? And he loathes his parents, though himself refused to die. Such ill report shall I to my evils add.
1.960:
What profit, then, my friends, for me to live, in fame and fortune ruined.
Chorus
1.962: Myself have traced the Muses’ path, have soared amid the stars, have laid my hold on many a theme,
1.965: and yet have found naught stronger than necessity, no spell inscribed on Thracian tablets written there by Orpheus, the sweet singer,
1.970:
no! nor aught among the simples culled by Phoebus for the toiling race of men, and given to Asclepius’ sons.
Chorus
1.973: The only goddess she, whose altar or whose image man cannot approach;
1.975: victims she heedeth not. O come not to me, dread goddess, in greater might than heretofore in my career. Even Zeus requires thy aid to bring to pass whatso he wills.
1.980:
Thou too it is that by sheer force dost bend the steel among the Chalybes; nor is there any pity in thy relentless nature.
Chorus
1.984: This is the goddess that hath gripped thee too in chains thou canst not ’scape;
1.985: yet steel thy heart, for all thy weeping ne’er will bring to light again the dead from the realms below. Even sons of gods perish in darkness
1.990:
in the hour of death. We loved her while she was with us, we love her still though dead; noblest of her sex was she, the wife thou tookest to thy bed.
Chorus
1.995: Her tomb let none regard as the graves of those who die and are no more, but let her have honours equal with the gods, revered by every traveller;
1.1000: and many a one will cross the road and read this verse aloud, This is she that died in days gone by to save her lord; now is she a spirit blest. Hail, lady revered; be kind to us!
1.1005:
Such glad greeting shall she have.
Chorus
1.1006:
But see, Admetus! yonder, I believe, comes Alcmena’s son toward thy hearth.
Heracles
1.1008: Admetus, to a friend we should speak freely, not hold our peace and harbour in our hearts complaints.
1.1010: I came to thee in thy hour of sorrow and claimed the right to prove myself thy friend, but thou wouldst not tell me that she, thy wife, lay stretched in death; but didst make me a welcome guest in thy halls, as though thy whole concern was centred on a stranger’s loss.
1.1015: So I crowned my head and poured drink-offerings to the gods in that thy house of sorrow. Wherefore I do blame thee for this treatment of me, yet would not grieve thee in thy trouble. So now the reason I have turned my steps and come hither again, I will tell.
1.1020: This lady take and keep for me until I come bringing hither the steeds of Thrace, after I have slain the lord of the Bistones. But should I fare as fare I fain would not, I give her to thee to serve within thy halls.
1.1025: With no small toil she came into my hands. ’Twas thus: I found folk just appointing an open contest for athletes, well worth a struggle, and there I won her as a prize and brought her thence; now those who were successful in the lighter contests had
1.1030: horses for their prize, but those who conquered in severer feats, in boxing and wrestling, won herds of oxen, and this woman was to be added thereto; with such a chance ’twere shame indeed to pass so fair a guerdon by.
1.1035:
So thou must take her in thy charge, as I said; for not by theft but honest toil I won the prize I bring; and maybe e’en thou in time wilt thank me.
Admetus
1.1037: ’Twas not because of any slight or unkind thought of thee that I concealed my wife’s sad fate; but this were adding grief to grief
1.1040: if thou hadst gone from hence to the halls of some other friend; and it sufficed that I should mourn my sorrow. But I do beseech thee, prince, if ’tis possible, bid some other Thessalian, one who hath not suffered as I have, keep the maiden for thee,—and thou hast many
1.1045: friends in Pherae; remind me not of my misfortune. For I could not see her in my house and stay my tears. Oh! add not new affliction to my stricken heart, for sure by sorrow am I bowed enough. And where within my halls could a tender maiden live?
1.1050: for such she is, as her dress and vesture show. Is she to dwell where men consort? Then how shall she retain her maiden purity, if ’mid our youths she come and go? O Heracles, it is no easy task to check a young man’s fancy, and I am anxious for thy sake.
1.1055: Or am I to take her to my dead wife’s bower and care for her? How can I bring her there to fill the other’s bed? Twofold reproach I fear; first, some fellow-townsman may taunt me with betraying my benefactress in eagerness to wed a new young bride;
1.1060: next, there is my dead wife, whom I should much regard, for she doth merit all my reverence. Thou too, lady, whosoe’er thou art, believe me, art the very counterfeit presentment of Alcestis, the picture of her form, ah me! O take this maiden, I conjure thee, from my sight;
1.1065:
slay me not already slain. For in her I seem once more to see my wife; and my heart is darkly troubled, and the fountains of my eyes are loosed. Ah, woe is me! Now do I taste the bitterness of this my grief.
Chorus
1.1070:
Indeed I cannot call thy fortune blest, yet heaven’s gift must thou endure, whoe’er the god that comes to bring it.
Heracles
1.1072:
Would I had the power to bring thy wife up to the light from the halls of death, and confer this kindness on thee!
Admetus
1.1075:
Right well I know thou wouldst. But what of that? The dead can never come to life again.
Heracles
1.1077:
Do not exceed the mark, but bear thy grief with moderation.
Admetus
1.1078:
’Tis easier to advise than to suffer and endure.
Heracles
1.1079:
Yet what thy gain, if thou for aye wilt mourn?
Admetus
1.1080:
I too know that myself, but some strange yearning leads me on.
Heracles
1.1081:
Love for the dead compels a tear.
Admetus
1.1082:
Her death was mine, more than any words of mine can tell.
Heracles
1.1083:
Thou hast lost a noble wife; who shall gainsay it?
Admetus
1.1084:
Life henceforth hath lost all charm for me.
Heracles
1.1085:
Time will soothe the smart; as yet thy grief is young.
Admetus
1.1086:
Time! use that word, if death and time are one.
Heracles
1.1087:
A new wife and a longing for a fresh marriage will stay thy sorrow.
Admetus
1.1088:
Peace! What words are thine? I ne’er of thee had thought it.
Heracles
1.1089:
What! wilt never wed, but preserve thy widowed state?
Admetus
1.1090:
There is no woman living that shall share my couch.
Heracles
1.1091:
Dost think that this will help the dead at all?
Admetus
1.1092:
My reverence she deserves, where’er she is.
Heracles
1.1093:
I praise thee, yes; but still thou bringest on thyself the charge of folly.
Admetus
1.1094:
So that thou never call’st me bridegroom, praise me if thou wilt.
Heracles
1.1095:
I praise thee for thy loyalty to thy wife.
Admetus
1.1096:
Come death! if ever I betray her, dead though she be.
Heracles
1.1097:
Well, take this maiden to the shelter of thy noble house.
Admetus
1.1098:
Spare me, I entreat thee by Zeus, thy sire.
Heracles
1.1099:
Be sure, if thou refuse, ’twill be a sad mistake.
Admetus
1.1100:
If I comply, remorse will gnaw my heart.
Heracles
1.1101:
Yield; for in god’s good time maybe thou wilt give me thanks.
Admetus
1.1102:
Ah! would thou hadst never won her in the games!
Heracles
1.1103:
Yet thou too sharest in my victory.
Admetus
1.1104:
True; still let this maiden go away.
Heracles
1.1105:
Go she shall, if go she must; but first see if this is needful.
Admetus
1.1106:
I needs must, else wilt thou be wroth with me.
Heracles
1.1107:
I have a reason good to press the matter thus.
Admetus
1.1108:
Have thy way then. Yet know well thy deed I disapprove.
Heracles
1.1109:
A day will come that thou wilt praise me; only yield.
Admetus
1.1110:
(to his servants). Take her in, if I needs must give her welcome in my house.
Heracles
1.1111:
To thy servants will I not hand her over.
Admetus
1.1112:
Conduct her then thyself within, if so thou thinkest good.
Heracles
1.1113:
Nay, but into thy hands shall mine consign her.
Admetus
1.1114:
I will not touch her, though she is free to go within my halls.
Heracles
1.1115:
To thy hand, and thine alone I her entrust.
Admetus
1.1116:
Prince, against my will thou dost constrain me to this deed.
Heracles
1.1117:
Boldly stretch out thy hand and touch the stranger maid.
Admetus
1.1118:
There, then, I stretch it out as toward the Gorgon’s severed head.
Heracles
1.1119:
Hast hold of her?
Admetus
I have.
Heracles
(removes the veil). So; keep her safely then, and
1.1120:
in days to come thou wilt confess the son of Zeus proved himself a noble guest. Look well at her, if haply to thy gaze she have a semblance of thy wife; and now that thou art blest, cease from sorrowing.
Admetus
1.1123: Great gods, what shall I say? a marvel past all hope is here! My wife, my own true wife I see,
1.1125:
or is some mocking rapture sent by heaven to drive me mad?
Heracles
1.1126:
No, no; ’tis thy own wife thou seest here.
Admetus
1.1127:
Beware it be not a phantom from that nether world.
Heracles
1.1128:
No necromancer was this guest whom thou didst welcome.
Admetus
1.1129:
Do I behold my wife, her whom I buried?
Heracles
1.1130:
Be well assured thereof; still I marvel not thou dost distrust thy luck.
Admetus
1.1131:
May I touch her, may I speak to her as my living wife?
Heracles
1.1132:
Speak to her. For thou hast all thy heart’s desire.
Admetus
1.1133:
O form and features of my well-loved wife! past all hope I hold thee, never expecting to see thee again.
Heracles
1.1135:
So thou dost; may no jealous god rise against thee!
Admetus
1.1136:
O noble son of almighty Zeus, good luck to thee! may the father that begat thee hold thee in his keeping; for thou and none else hast raised my fallen fortunes. How didst thou bring her from the world below to this light of day?
Heracles
1.1140:
By encountering the god who had her in his power.
Admetus
1.1141:
Where didst thou engage with Death? tell me this.
Heracles
1.1142:
Just by the tomb I from my ambush sprang and caught him in my grip.
Admetus
1.1143:
But why thus speechless stands my wife?
Heracles
1.1144: ’Tis not lawful yet for thee to hear her speak,
1.1145: ere she be purified from the gods below and the third day be come. So lead her in; and hereafter, e’en as now, be just and kind to guests, Admetus. Now farewell! for I must go to perform my appointed task
1.1150:
for the lordly son of Sthenelus.
Admetus
1.1151:
Abide with us and be our welcome guest.
Heracles
1.1152:
Another time; now must I use all haste.
Admetus
1.1153: Good luck to thee! and mayst thou come again! To the citizens and ail my realm
1.1155:
I make this proclamation, that they institute dances in honour of the glad event, and make the altars steam with sacrifice, and offer prayers; for now have I moored my bark of life in a happier haven than before, and so will own myself a happy man.
Chorus
1.1159: Many are the shapes that fortune takes,
1.1160: and oft the gods bring things to pass beyond our expectation. That which we deemed so sure is not fulfilled, while for that we never thought would be, God finds out a way. And such hath been the issue in the present case.

1.0: Scene.—Before the Palace of Creon at Corinth. Nurse
1.1: Ah! would to Heaven the good ship Argo ne’er had sped its course to the Colchian land through the misty blue Symplegades, nor ever in the glens of Pelion the pine been felled to furnish with oars the chieftain’s hands,
1.5: who went to fetch the golden fleece for Pelias; for then would my own mistress Medea never have sailed to the turrets of Iolcos, her soul with love for Jason smitten, nor would she have beguiled the daughters of Pelias
1.10: to slay their father and come to live here in the land of Corinth with her husband and children, where her exile found favour with the citizens to whose land she had come, and in all things of her own accord was she at one with Jason, the greatest safeguard this
1.15: when wife and husband do agree; but now their love is all turned to hate, and tenderest ties are weak. For Jason hath betrayed his own children and my mistress dear for the love of a royal bride, for he hath wedded the daughter of Creon, lord of this land.
1.20: While Medea his hapless wife, thus scorned, appeals to the oaths he swore, recalls the strong pledge his right hand gave, and bids heaven be witness what requital she is finding from Jason. And here she lies fasting, yielding her body to her grief,
1.25: wasting away in tears ever since she learnt that she was wronged by her husband, never lifting her eye nor raising her face from off the ground; and she lends as deaf an ear to her friend’s warning as if she were a rock or ocean billow, save when she turns her snow-white neck aside
1.30: and softly to herself bemoans her father dear, her country and her home, which she gave up to come hither with the man who now holds her in dishonour. She, poor lady, hath by sad experience learnt how good a thing it is
1.35: never to quit one’s native land. And she hates her children now and feels no joy at seeing them; I am afeard she may contrive some untoward scheme; for her mood is dangerous nor will she brook her cruel treatment; full well I know her, and I much do dread
1.40: that she will plunge the keen sword through their heart, stealing without a word into the chamber where their marriage couch is spread, or else that she will slay the prince and bridegroom too, and so find some calamity still more grievous than the present; for dreadful is her wrath;
1.45:
verily the man that doth incur her hate will have no easy task to raise o’er her a song of triumph. Lo! where her sons come hither from their childish sports; little they reck of their mother’s woes, for the soul of the young is no inend to sorrow.
Attendant
1.49: Why dost thou, so long my lady’s own handmaid,
1.50:
stand here at the gate alone, loudly lamenting to thyself the piteous tale? how comes it that Medea will have thee leave her to herself?
Nurse
1.53: Old man, attendant on the sons of Jason, our masters’ fortunes when they go awry make good slaves grieve
1.55:
and touch their hearts. Oh! I have come to such a pitch of grief that there stole a yearning wish upon me to come forth hither and proclaim to heaven and earth my mistress’s hard fate.
Attendant
1.59:
What! has not the poor lady ceased yet from her lamentation?
Nurse
1.60:
Would I were as thou art! the mischief is but now beginning; it has not reached its climax yet.
Attendant
1.61:
O foolish one, if I may call my mistress such a name; how little she recks of evils yet more recent!
Nurse
1.63:
What mean’st, old man? grudge not to tell me.
Attendant
1.64:
’Tis naught; I do repent me even of the words I have spoken.
Nurse
1.65:
Nay, by thy beard I conjure thee, hide it not from thy fellow-slave; I will be silent, if need be, on that text.
Attendant
1.67: I heard one say, pretending not to listen as I approached the place where our greybeards sit playing draughts near Pirene’s sacred spring,
1.70:
that Creon, the ruler of this land, is bent on driving these children and their mother from the boundaries of Corinth; but I know not whether the news is to be relied upon, and would fain it were not.
Nurse
1.74: What! will Jason brook such treatment of his sons,
1.75:
even though he be at variance with their mother?
Attendant
1.76:
Old ties give way to new; he bears no longer any love to this family.
Nurse
1.78:
Undone, it seems, are we, if to old woes fresh ones we add, ere we have drained the former to the dregs.
Attendant
1.80:
Hold thou thy peace, say not a word of this; ’tis no time for our mistress to learn hereof.
Nurse
1.82:
O children, do ye hear how your father feels towards you? Perdition catch him, but no! he is my master still; yet is he proved a veiy traitor to his nearest and dearest.
Attendant
1.85:

1.1190: and she starts from her seat in a blaze and seeks to fly, shaking her hair and head this way and that, to cast the crown therefrom; but the gold held firm to its fastenings, and the flame, as she shook her locks, blazed forth the more with double fury.
1.1195: Then to the earth she sinks, by the cruel blow o’ercome, past all recognition now save to a father’s eye; for her eyes had lost their tranquil gaze, her face no more its natural look preserved, and from the crown of her head blood and fire in mingled stream ran down;
1.1200: and from her bones the flesh kept peeling off beneath the gnawing of those secret drugs, e’en as when the pine-tree weeps its tears of pitch, a fearsome sight to see. And all were afraid to touch the corpse, for we were warned by what had chanced. Anon came her hapless father
1.1205: unto the house, all unwitting of her doom, and stumbles o’er the dead, and loud he cried, and folding his arms about her kissed her, with words like these the while, O my poor, poor child, which of the gods hath destroyed thee thus foully? Who is robbing me of thee, old as I am and
1.1210: ripe for death? O my child, alas! would I could die with thee! He ceased his sad lament, and would have raised his aged frame, but found himself held fast by the finespun robe as ivy that clings to the branches of the bay, and then ensued a fearful struggle.
1.1215: He strove to rise, but she still held him back; and if ever he pulled with all his might, from off his bones his aged flesh he tore. At last he gave it up, and breathed forth his soul in awful suffering; for he could no longer master the pain.
1.1220: So there they lie, daughter and aged sire, dead side by side, a grievous sight that calls for tears. And as for thee, I leave thee out of my consideration, for thyself must discover a means to escape punishment. Not now for the first time I think this human life a shadow;
1.1225: yea, and without shrinking I will say that they amongst men who pretend to wisdom and expend deep thought on words do incur a serious charge of folly; for amongst mortals no man is happy; wealth may pour in and make
1.1230:
one luckier than another, but none can happy be.
Chorus
1.1231: This day the deity, it seems, will mass on Jason, as he well deserves, a heavy load of evils. Woe is thee, daughter of Creon! We pity thy sad fate, gone as thou art to Hades’ halls
1.1235:
as the price of thy marriage with Jason.
Medea
1.1236: My friends, I am resolved upon the deed; at once will I slay my children and then leave this land, without delaying long enough to hand them over to some more savage hand to butcher.
1.1240: Needs must they die in any case; and since they must, I will slay them—I, the mother that bare them. O heart of mine, steel thyself! Why do I hesitate to do the awful deed that must be done? Come, take the sword, thou wretched hand of mine!
1.1245: Take it, and advance to the post whence starts thy life of sorrow! Away with cowardice! Give not one thought to thy babes, how dear they are or how thou art their mother This one brief day forget thy children dear, and after that lament; for though thou wilt slay them yet
1.1250:
they were thy darlings still, and am a lady of sorrows.
Chorus
1.1251: O earth, O sun whose beam illumines all, look, look upon this lost woman, ere she stretch forth, her murderous hand upon her sons for blood;
1.1255: for lo! these are scions of thy own golden seed, and the blood of gods is in danger of being shed by man. O light, from Zeus proceeding, stay her, hold her hand, forth from the house
1.1260:
chase this fell bloody fiend by demons led.
Chorus
1.1261: Vainly wasted were the throes thy children cost thee; vainly hast thou born, it seems, sweet babes, O thou who hast left behind thee that passage through the blue Symplegades, that strangers justly hate.
1.1265: Ah! hapless one, why doth fierce anger thy soul assail? Why in its place is fell murder growing up? For grievous unto mortal men are pollutions that come of kindred blood poured on the earth,
1.1270:
woes to suit each crime hurled from heaven on the murderer’s house.
Sons
within
Ah!
Chorus
1.1273:
Didst hear, didst hear the children’s cry? O lady, born to sorrow, victim of an evil fate!
1st Son
1.1271:
(within). Ah, me; what can I do? Whither fly to escape my mother’s blows?
2nd Son
1.1272:
(within). I know not, sweet brother mine; we are undone.
Chorus
1.1275:
Shall I enter the house? For the children’s sake I am resolved to ward off the murder.
1st Son
1.1277:
(within). Yea, by heaven I adjure you; help, your aid is needed.
2nd Son
1.1278:
(within). Even now the toils of the sword are closing round us.
Chorus
1.1279: O hapless mother, surely thou hast a heart of stone or steel
1.1280:
to slay the offspring of thy womb by such a murderous doom.
Chorus
1.1282: Of all the wives of yore I know but one who laid her hand upon her children dear, even Ino, whom the gods did madden in the day
1.1285: that the wife of Zeus drove her wandering from her home. But she, poor sufferer, flung herself into the sea because of the foul murder of her children, leaping o’er the wave-beat cliff, and in her death was she united to her children twain.
1.1290:
Can there be any deed of horror left to follow this? Woe for the wooing of women fraught with disaster! What sorrows hast thou caused for men ere now!
Jason
1.1293: Ladies, stationed near this house, pray tell me is the author of these hideous deeds,
1.1295: Medea, still within, or hath she fled from hence? For she must hide beneath the earth or soar on wings towards heaven’s vault, if she would avoid the vengeance of the royal house. Is she so sure she will escape herself unpunished from this house,
1.1300: when she hath slain the rulers of the land? But enough of this! I am forgetting her children. As for her, those whom she hath wronged will do the like by her; but I am come to save the children’s life, lest the victim’s kin visit their wrath on me, in vengeance for the murder foul,
1.1305:
wrought by my children’s mother.
Chorus
1.1306:
Unhappy man, thou knowest not the full extent of thy misery, else had thou never said those words.
Jason
1.1308:
How now? Can she want to kill me too?
Chorus
1.1309:
Thy sons are dead; slain by their own mother’s hand.
Jason
1.1310:
O God! what sayest thou? Woman, thou hast sealed my doom.
Chorus
1.1311:
Thy children are no more; be sure of this.
Jason
1.1312:
Where slew she them; within the palace or outside?
Chorus
1.1313:
Throw wide the doors and see thy children’s murdered corpses.
Jason
1.1314: Haste, ye slaves, loose the bolts,
1.1315:
undo the fastenings, that I may see the sight of twofold woe, my murdered sons and her, whose blood in vengeance I will shed. [Medea in mid air, on a chariot drawn by dragons; the children’s corpses by her.
Medea
1.1317: Why shake those doors and attempt to loose their bolts, in quest of the dead and me their murderess? From such toil desist. If thou wouldst aught with me,
1.1320:
say on, if so thou wilt; but never shalt thou lay hand on me, so swift the steeds the sun, my father’s sire, to me doth give to save me from the hand of my foes.
Jason
1.1323: Accursed woman! by gods, by me and all mankind abhorred as never woman was,
1.1325: who hadst the heart to stab thy babes, thou their mother, leaving me undone and childless; this hast thou done and still dost gaze upon the sun and earth after this deed most impious. Curses on thee! I now perceive what then I missed
1.1330: in the day I brought thee, fraught with doom, from thy home in a barbarian land to dwell in Hellas, traitress to thy sire and to the land that nurtured thee. On me the gods have hurled the curse that dogged thy steps, for thou didst slay thy brother at his hearth
1.1335: ere thou cam’st aboard our fair ship Argo. Such was the outset of thy life of crime; then didst thou wed with me, and having born me sons to glut thy passion’s lust, thou now hast slain them. Not one amongst the wives of Hellas e’er had dared
1.1340: this deed; yet before them all I chose thee for my wife, wedding a foe to be my doom, no woman, but a lioness fiercer than Tyrrhene Scylla in nature. But with reproaches heaped a thousandfold
1.1345: I cannot wound thee, so brazen is thy nature. Perish, vile sorceress, murderess of thy babes! Whilst I must mourn my luckless fate, for I shall ne’er enjoy my new-found bride, nor shall I have the children,
1.1350:
whom I bred and reared, alive to say the last farewell to me; nay, I have lost them.
Medea
1.1351: To this thy speech I could have made a long retort, but Father Zeus knows well all I have done for thee, and the treatment thou hast given me. Yet thou wert not ordained to scorn my love
1.1355: and lead a life of joy in mockery of me, nor was thy royal bride nor Creon, who gave thee a second wife, to thrust me from this land and rue it not. Wherefore, if thou wilt, call me e’en a lioness, and Scylla, whose home is in the Tyrrhene land;
1.1360:
for I in turn have wrung thy heart, as well I might.
Jason
1.1361:
Thou, too, art grieved thyself, and sharest in my sorrow.
Medea
1.1362:
Be well assured I am; but it relieves my pain to know thou canst not mock at me.
Jason
1.1363:
O my children, how vile a mother ye have found!
Medea
1.1364:
My sons, your father’s feeble lust has been your ruin!
Jason
1.1365:
’Twas not my hand, at any rate, that slew them.
Medea
1.1366:
No, but thy foul treatment of me, and thy new marriage.
Jason
1.1367:
Didst think that marriage cause enough to murder them?
Medea
1.1368:
Dost think a woman counts this a trifling injury?
Jason
1.1369:
So she be self-restrained; but in thy eyes all is evil.
Medea
1.1370:
Thy sons are dead and gone. That will stab thy heart.
Jason
1.1371:
They live, methinks, to bring a curse upon thy head.
Medea
1.1372:
The gods know, whoso of them began this troublous coil.
Jason
1.1373:
Indeed, they know that hateful heart of thine.
Medea
1.1374:
Thou art as hateful. I am aweary of thy bitter tongue.
Jason
1.1375:
And I likewise of thine. But parting is easy.
Medea
1.1376:
Say how; what am I to do? for I am fain as thou to go.
Jason
1.1377:
Give up to me those dead, to bury and lament
Medea
1.1378: No, never! I will bury them myself, bearing them to Hera’s sacred field, who watches o’er the Cape,
1.1380: that none of their foes may insult them by pulling down their tombs; and in this land of Sisyphus I will ordain hereafter a solemn feast and mystic rites to atone for this impious murder. Myself will now to the land of Erechtheus,
1.1385:
to dwell with Aegeus, Pandion’s son. But thou, as well thou mayest, shalt die a caitiff’s death, thy head crushed ’neath a shattered relic of Argo, when thou hast seen the bitter ending of my marriage.
Jason
1.1389: The curse of our sons’ avenging spirit and of Justice,
1.1390:
that calls for blood, be on thee!
Medea
1.1391:
What god or power divine hears thee, breaker of oaths and every law of hospitality?
Jason
1.1393:
Fie upon thee! cursed witch! child-murderess!
Medea
1.1394:
To thy house! go, bury thy wife.
Jason
1.1395:
I go, bereft of both my sons.
Medea
1.1396:
Thy grief is yet to come; wait till old age is with thee too.
Jason
1.1397:
O my dear, dear children!
Medea
Dear to their mother, not to thee.
Jason
1.1398:
And yet thou didst slay them?
Medea
Yea, to vex thy heart.
Jason
1.1399: One last fond kiss, ah me!
1.1400:
I fain would on their lips imprint.
Medea
1.1401:
Embraces now, and fond farewells for them; but then a cold repulse!
Jason
1.1402:
By heaven I do adjure thee, let me touch their tender skin.
Medea
1.1404:
No, no! in vain this word has sped its flight.
Jason
1.1405: O Zeus, dost hear how I am driven hence; dost mark the treatment I receive from this she-lion, fell murderess of her young? Yet so far as I may and can, I raise for them a dirge,
1.1410:
and do adjure the gods to witness how thou hast slain my sons, and wilt not suffer me to embrace or bury their dead bodies. Would I had never begotten them to see thee slay them after all!
Chorus
1.1415: Many a fate doth Zeus dispense, high on his Olympian throne; oft do the gods bring things to pass beyond man’s expectation; that, which we thought would be, is not fulfilled, while for the unlooked-for god finds out a way; and such hath been the issue of this matter.

1.0: Scene.—Before the altar of Zeus at Marathon. Iolaus
1.1: I hold this true, and long have held: Nature hath made one man upright for his neighbours’ good, while another hath a disposition wholly given over to gain, useless alike to the state and difficult to have dealings with,
1.5: but for himself the best of men; and this I know, not from mere hearsay. I, for instance, from pure regard and reverence for my kith and kin, though I might have lived at peace in Argos, alone of all my race shared with Heracles his labours, while he was yet with us, and now that he dwells in heaven,
1.10: I keep these his children safe beneath my wing, though myself I need protection. For when their father passed from earth away, Eurystheus would first of all have slain us, but we escaped. And though our home is lost, our life was saved. But in exile we wander from city to city,
1.15: ever forced to roam. For, added to our former wrongs, Eurystheus thought it fit to put this further outrage upon us: wheresoe’er he heard that we were settling, thither would he send heralds
1.20: demanding our surrender and driving us from thence, holding out this threat, that Argos is no mean city to make a friend or foe, and furthermore pointing to his own prosperity. So they, seeing how weak my means, and these little ones left without a father,
1.25: bow to his superior might and drive us from their land. And I share the exile of these children, and help them bear their evil lot by my sympathy, loth to betray them, lest someone say, Look you! now that the children’s sire is dead,
1.30: Iolaus no more protects them, kinsman though he is. Not one corner left us in the whole of Hellas, we are come to Marathon and its neighbouring land, and here we sit as suppliants at the altars of the gods, and pray their aid; for ’tis said
1.35: two sons of Theseus dwell upon these plains, the lot of their inheritance, scions of Pandion’s stock, related to these children; this the reason we have come on this our way to the borders of glorious Athens. To lead the flight two aged guides are we;
1.40: my care is centred on these boys, while she, I mean Alcmena, clasps her son’s daughter in her arms, and bears her for safety within this shrine, for we shrink from letting tender maidens come anigh the crowd or stand as suppliants at the altar.
1.45: Now Hyllus and the elder of his brethren are seeking some place for us to find a refuge, if we are driven by force from this land.
1.48: O children, children, come hither! hold unto my robe; for lo! I see a herald coming towards us from Eurystheus,
1.50:
by whom we are persecuted, wanderers excluded from every land. A curse on thee and him that sent thee, hateful wretch! for that same tongue of thine hath oft announced its master’s evil hests to these children’s noble sire as well.
Copreus
1.55: Doubtless thy folly lets thee think this is a good position to have taken up, and that thou art come to a city that will help thee. No! there is none that will prefer thy feeble arm to the might of Eurystheus. Begone! why take this trouble? Thou must arise and go
1.60:
to Argos, where awaits thee death by stoning.
Iolaus
1.61:
Not so, for the god’s altar will protect me, and this land of freedom, wherein we have set foot.
Copreus
1.63:
Wilt give me the trouble of laying hands on thee?
Iolaus
1.64:
By force at least shalt thou never drag these children hence.
Copreus
1.65:
That shalt thou soon learn; it seems thou wert a poor prophet, after all, in this. [Copreus here seizes the children.
Iolaus
1.66:
This shall never happen while I live.
Copreus
1.67:
Begone! for I will take them hence, for all thy refusals, for I hold that they belong to Eurystheus, as they do indeed.
Iolaus
1.69: Help, ye who long nave had your home in Athens!
1.70:
we suppliants at Zeus’ altar in your market-place are being haled by force away, our sacred wreaths defiled, shame to your city, to the gods dishonour.
Chorus
1.73:
Hark, hark! What cry is this that rises near the altar? At once explain the nature of the trouble.
Iolaus
1.75:
See this aged frame hurled in its feebleness upon the ground! Woe is me!
Chorus
1.77:
Who threw thee down thus pitiably?
Iolaus
1.78:
Behold the man who flouts your gods, kind sirs, and tries by force to drag me from my seat before the altar of Zeus.
Chorus
1.80:
From what land, old stranger, art thou come to this confederate state of four cities? or have ye left Euboea’s cliffs, and, with the oar that sweeps the sea, put in here from across the firth?
Iolaus
1.84: Sirs, no island life I lead,
1.85:
but from Mycenae to thy land I come.
Chorus
1.86:
What do they call thee, aged sir, those folk in Mycenae?
Iolaus
1.88:
Maybe ye have heard of Iolaus, the comrade of Heracles, for he was not unknown to fame.
Chorus
1.90:
Yea, I have heard of him in bygone days; but tell me, whose are the tender boys thou bearest in thine arms?
Iolaus
1.93:
These, sirs, are the sons of Heracles, come as suppliants to you and your city.
Chorus
1.95:
What is their quest? Are they anxious, tell me, to obtain an audience of the state?
Iolaus
1.97:
That so they may escape surrender, nor be tom with violence from thy altars, and brought to Argos.
Copreus
1.99: Nay, this will nowise satisfy thy masters,
1.100:
who o’er thee have a right, and so have tracked thee hither.
Chorus
1.101:
Stranger, ’tis but right we should reverence the gods’ suppliants, suffering none with violent hand to make them leave the altars, for that will dread Justice ne’er permit.
Copreus
1.105:
Do thou then drive these subjects of Eurystheus forth, and this hand of mine shall abstain from violence.
Chorus
1.107:
’Twere impious for the state to neglect the suppliant stranger’s prayer.
Copreus
1.109: Yet ’tis well to keep clear of troubles,
1.110:
by adopting that counsel, which is the wiser.
Chorus
1.111:
Thou then, shouldst have told the monarch of this land thy errand before being so bold, out of regard to his country’s freedom, instead of trying to drag strangers by force from the altars of the gods.
Copreus
1.114:
Who is monarch of this land and state?
Chorus
1.115:
Demophon, son of gallant Theseus.
Copreus
1.116:
Surely it were most to the purpose to discuss this matter somewhat with him; all else has been said in vain.
Chorus
1.118:
Lo! here he comes in person, in hot haste, and Acamas his brother, to hear what thou hast to say.
Demophon
1.120:
Since thou for all thy years hast outstripped younger men in coming to the rescue to this altar of Zeus, do thou tell me what hath chanced to bring this crowd together.
Chorus
1.123: There sit the sons of Heracles as suppliants, having wreathed the altar, as thou seest, O king,
1.125:
and with them is Iolaus, trusty comrade of their sire.
Demophon
1.126:
Why should this event have called for cries of pain?
Chorus
1.127:
(turning to Copreus). This fellow caused the uproar by trying to drag them forcibly from this altar, and he tripped up the old man, till my tears for pity flowed.
Demophon
1.130:
Hellenic dress and fashion in his robes doth he no doubt adopt, but deeds like these betray the barbarian. Thou, sirrah, tell me straight the country whence thou earnest thither.
Copreus
1.134: An Argive I; since that thou seek’st to know.
1.135: Who sent me, and the object of my coming, will I freely tell. Eurystheus, king of Mycenae, sends me hither to fetch these back; and I have come, sir stranger, with just grounds in plenty, alike for speech or action. An Argive myself, Argives I come to fetch,
1.140: taking with me these runaways from my native city, on whom the doom of death was passed by our laws there; and we have a right, since we rule our city independently, to ratify its sentences. And though they have come as suppliants to the altars of numerous others,
1.145: we have taken our stand on these same arguments, and no one has ventured to bring upon himself evils of his own getting. But they have come hither, either because they perceived some folly in thee, or, in their perplexity, staking all on one risky throw to win or lose;
1.150: for surely they do not suppose that thou, if so thou hast thy senses still, and only thou, in all the breadth of Hellas they have traversed, wilt pity their foolish troubles. Come now, put argument against argument: what will be thy gain, suppose thou admit them to thy land, or let us take them hence?
1.155: From us these benefits are thine to win: this city can secure as friends Argos, with its far-reaching arm, and Eurystheus’ might complete; whilst if thou lend an ear to their piteous pleading and grow soft, the matter
1.160: must result in trial of arms; for be sure we shall not yield this struggle without appealing to the sword. What pretext wilt thou urge? Of what domains art thou robbed that thou shouldst take and wage war with the Tirynthian Argives? What kind of allies art thou aiding? For whom
1.165: will they have fallen whom thou buriest? Surely thou wilt get an evil name from the citizens, if for the sake of an old man with one foot in the grave, a mere shadow I may say, and for these children, thou wilt plunge into troublous waters. The best thou canst say is, that thou wilt find in them a hope, and nothing more;
1.170: and yet this falls far short of the present need; for these would be but a poor match for Argives even when fully armed and in their prime, if haply that raises thy spirits; moreover, the time ’twixt now and then is long, wherein ye may be blotted out. Nay, hearken to me;
1.175:
give me naught, but let me take mine own, and so gain Mycenae; but forbear to act now, as is your Athenian way, and take the weaker side, when it is in thy power to choose the stronger as thy friends.
Chorus
1.179: Who can decide a cause or ascertain its merits,
1.180:
till from both sides he clearly learn what they would say?
Iolaus
1.181: O king, in thy land I start with this advantage, the right to hear and speak in turn, and none, ere that, will drive me hence as elsewhere they would. ’Twixt us and him is naught in common,
1.185: for we no longer have aught to do with Argos since that decree was passed, but we are exiles from our native land; how then can he justly drag us back as subjects of Mycenae, seeing that they have banished us? For we are strangers.
1.190: Or do ye claim that every exile from Argos is exiled from the bounds of Hellas? Not from Athens surely; for ne’er will she for fear of Argos drive the children of Heracles from her land. Here is no Trachis, not at all; no! nor that Achaean town, whence thou, defying justice,
1.195: but boasting of the might of Argos in the very words thou now art using, didst drive the suppliants from their station at the altar. If this shall be, and they thy words approve, why then I trow this is no more Athens, the home of freedom. Nay, but I know the temper and nature of these citizens;
1.200: they would rather die, for honour ranks before mere life with men of worth. Enough of Athens! for excessive praise is apt to breed disgust; and oft ere now I have myself felt vexed at praise that knows no bounds.
1.205: But to thee, as ruler of this land, I fain would show the reason why thou art bound to save these children. Pittheus was the son of Pelops; from him sprung Aethra, and from her Theseus thy sire was born. And now will I trace back these children’s lineage for thee.
1.210: Heracles was son of Zeus and Alcmena; Alcmena sprang from Pelops’ daughter; therefore thy father and their father would be the sons of first cousins. Thus then art thou to them related, O Demophon, but thy just debt to them beyond the ties of kinship
1.215: do I now declare to thee; for I assert, in days gone by, I was with Theseus on the ship, as their father’s squire, when they went to fetch that girdle fraught with death; yea, and from Hades’ murky dungeons did Heracles bring thy father up; as all Hellas doth attest.
1.220: Wherefore in return they crave this boon of thee, that they be not surrendered up nor torn by force from the altars of thy gods and cast forth from the land. For this were shame on thee, and hurtful likewise in thy state, should suppliants, exiles,
1.225: kith and kin of thine, be haled away by force. For pity’s sake! cast one glance at them. I do entreat thee, laying my suppliant bough upon thee, by thy hands and beard, slight not the sons of Heracles, now that thou hast them in thy power to help. Show thyself their kinsman and their friend;
1.230:
be to them father, brother, lord; for better each and all of these than to fall beneath the Argives’ hand.
Chorus
1.232: O king, I pity them, hearing their sad lot Now more than ever do I see noble birth o’ercome by fortune; for these, though sprung from a noble sire,
1.235:
are suffering what they ne’er deserved.
Demophon
1.236: Three aspects of the case constrain me, Iolaus, not to spurn the guests thou bringest; first and foremost, there is Zeus, at whose altar thou art seated with these tender children gathered round thee;
1.240: next come ties of kin, and the debt I owe to treat them kindly for their father’s sake; and last, mine honour, which before all I must regard; for if I permit this altar to be violently despoiled by stranger hands, men will think
1.245: the land I inhabit is free no more, and that through fear I have surrendered suppliants to Argives, and this comes nigh to make one hang oneself. Would that thou hadst come under a luckier star! yet, as it is, fear not that any man shall tear thee and these children from the altar by force.
1.250:
Get thee (to Copreus) to Argos and tell Eurystheus so; yea and more, if he have any charge against these strangers, he shall have justice; but never shalt thou drag them hence.
Copreus
1.253:
Not even if I have right upon my side and prove my case?
Demophon
1.254:
How can it be right to drag the suppliant away by force?
Copreus
1.255:
Well, mine is the disgrace; no harm will come to thee.
Demophon
1.256:
Tis harm to me, if I let them be haled away by thee.
Copreus
1.257:
Banish them thyself, and then will I take them from elsewhere.
Demophon
1.258:
Nature made thee a fool, to think thou knowest better than the god.
Copreus
1.259:
It seems then evildoers are to find a refuge here.
Demophon
1.260:
A temple of the gods is an asylum open to the world.
Copreus
1.261:
Maybe they will not take this view in Mycensa.
Demophon
1.262:
What! am I not lord of this domain?
Copreus
1.263:
So long as thou injure not the Argives, and if wise, thou wilt not.
Demophon
1.264:
Be injured for all I care, provided I sin not against the gods.
Copreus
1.265:
I would not have thee come to blows with Argos.
Demophon
1.266:
I am of like mind in this; but I will not dismiss these from my protection.
Copreus
1.267:
For all that, I shall take and drag my own away.
Demophon
1.268:
Why then perhaps thou wilt find a difficulty in returning to Argos.
Copreus
1.269:
That shall I soon find out by making the attempt.
Demophon
1.270:
Touch them and thou shalt rue it, and that without delay.
Chorus
1.271:
I conjure thee, never dare to strike a herald.
Demophon
1.272:
Strike I will, unless that herald learn discretion.
Chorus
1.273:
Depart; and thou, O king, touch him not.
Copreus
1.274: I go; for ’tis feeble fighting with a single arm.
1.275: But I will come again, bringing hither a host of Argive troops, spearmen clad in bronze; for countless warriors are awaiting my return, and king Eurystheus in person at their head; anxiously he waits the issue here on the borders of Alcathous’ realm.
1.280:
And when he hears thy haughty answer, he will burst upon thee, and thy citizens, on this land and all that grows therein; for all in vain should we possess such hosts of picked young troops in Argos, should we forbear to punish thee. [Exit Copreus.
Demophon
1.284: Perdition seize thee! I am not afraid of thy Argos.
1.285:
Be very sure thou shalt not drag these suppliants hence by force, to my shame; for I hold not this city subject unto Argos, but independently.
Chorus
1.288: ’Tis time to use our forethought, ere the host of Argos approach our frontier,
