1.1416:
I was worse than anyone as far as courage went.
Heracles
1.1417:
How then can you say of me, that I am abased by my troubles?
Theseus
1.1418:
Forward!
Heracles
Farewell, my aged father!
Amphitryon
Farewell to you, my son!
Heracles
1.1419:
Bury my children as I said.
Amphitryon
But who will bury me, my son?
Heracles
1.1420:
I will.
Amphitryon
When wil you come?
Heracles
After you have buried my children.
Amphitryon
1.1421:
How?
Heracles
I will fetch you from Thebes to Athens. But carry my children within, a grievous burden to the earth. And I, after ruining my house by deeds of shame, will follow as a little boat in the wake of Theseus, a total wreck.
1.1425:
Whoever prefers wealth or might to the possession of good friends, thinks wrongly.
Chorus
1.1427: With grief and many a bitter tear we go our way, robbed of all we prized most dearly.

1.0: Scene.—Before Apollo’s temple at Delphi. Hermes
1.1: Atlas, who bears upon his brazen back the pressure of the sky, ancient dwelling of the gods, begat Maia from a daughter of one of those gods, and she bare me Hermes to mighty Zeus, to be the servant of the powers divine.
1.5: Lo! I am come to this land of Delphi where sits Phoebus on the centre of the world and giveth oracles to men, ever chanting lays prophetic of things that are to be. Now there is a city in Hellas of no small note, called after Pallas, goddess of the golden lance;
1.10: there did Phoebus force his love on Creusa, daughter of Erechtheus, beneath the rock of Pallas, northward of Athens’ steep realm, called Macrae by the kings of Attica. And she without her father’s knowledge—for such was the god’s good pleasure,—
1.15: bore the burden in her womb unto the end, and when her time came, she brought forth a child in the house and carried him away to the selfsame cave wherein the god declared his love to her, and she cradled him in the hollow of a rounded ark and cast him forth to die,
1.20: observant of the custom of her ancestors and of earth-born Erichthonius, whom the daughter of Zeus gave into the charge of the daughters of Agraulus, after setting on either side, to keep him safe, a guard of serpents twain. Hence in that land among the Erechthidae ’tis a
1.25: custom to protect their babes with charms of golden snakes. But ere she left the babe to die, the young mother tied about him her own broidered robe. And this is the request that Phoebus craves of me, for he is my brother, Go, brother, to those children of the soil
1.30: that dwell in glorious Athens, for well thou knowest Athena’s city, and take a new-born babe from out the hollow rock, his cradle and his swaddling-clothes as well, and bear him to my prophetic shrine at Delphi, and set him at the entering-in of my temple.
1.35: What else remains shall be my care, for that child is mine, that thou mayst know it. So I, to do my brother Loxias a service, took up the woven ark and bore it off, and at the threshold of the shrine I have laid the babe,
1.40: after opening the lid of the wicker cradle that the child might be seen.
1.41: But just as the sun-god was starting forth to run his course, a priestess chanced to enter the god’s shrine; and when her eyes lit upon the tender babe she thought it strange that any Delphian maid
1.45: should dare to cast her child of shame down at the temple of the god; wherefore her purpose was to remove him beyond the altar, but from pity she renounced her cruel thought, and the god to help his child did second her pity to save the babe from being cast out. So she took and brought him up,
1.50: but she knew not that Phoebus was his sire nor of the mother that bare him, nor yet did the child know his parents. While yet he was a child, around the altar that fed him he would ramble at his play, but when he came to man’s estate, the Delphians made him treasurer of the god
1.55: and steward of all his store, and found him true, and so until the present day he leads a holy life in the god’s temple. Meantime Creusa, mother of this youth, is wedded to Xuthus; and thus it came to pass; a war broke out ’twixt Athens and the folk of Chalcodon
1.60: who dwell in the land of Euboea; and Xuthus took part therein and helped to end it, for which he received the hand of Creusa as his guerdon, albeit he was no native, but an Achaean, sprung from Aeolus, the son of Zeus; and after many years of wedded life
1.65: he and Creusa still are childless; wherefore they are come to this oracle of Apollo in their desire for offspring. To this end is Loxias guiding their destiny nor hath it escaped his ken, as some suppose. For when Xuthus enters this shrine,
1.70: the god will give him his own son and declare that Xuthus is the sire, that so the boy may come to his mother’s home and be acknowledged by Creusa, while the marriage of Loxias remains a secret and the child obtains his rights; and he shall cause him to be called Ion, founder of a realm in Asia,
1.75: through all the breadth of Hellas. But now will I get me to yon grotto ’neath the laurel’s shade that I may learn what is decreed about the child. For I see the son of Loxias now coming forth to cleanse the gateway in front of the temple
1.80:
with boughs of laurel. I greet him first of all the gods by his name Ion which he soon shall bear.
Ion
1.82: Lo! the sun-god is e’en now turning towards the earth his chariot-car resplendent; before yon fire the stars retire
1.85: to night’s mysterious gloom from forth the firmament; the peaks of Parnassus, where no man may set foot, are all ablaze and hail the car of day for mortal’s service. Up mounts the smoke of myrrh, offering of the desert;
1.90: to Phoebus’ roof; there on the holy tripod sits the Delphian priestess, chanting to the ears of Hellas in numbers loud, whate’er Apollo doth proclaim. Ye Delphians, votaries of Phoebus, away!
1.95: to Castalia’s gushing fount as silver clear, and, when ye have bathed you in its waters pure, enter the shrine; and keep your lips in holy silence that it may be well, careful to utter words of good omen amongst yourselves
1.100: to those who wish to consult the oracle; while I with laurel-sprays and sacred wreaths and drops of water sprinkled o’er the floor will purify the entrance to the shrine of Phoebus,
1.105: my task each day from childhood’s hour; and with my bow will I put to flight the flocks of feathered fowls that harm his sacred offerings;
1.110:
for here in Phoebus’ shrine, which nurtured me, I minister, an orphan, fatherless and motherless.
Ion
1.112: Come, thou tender laurel-shoot, gathered from gardens divine to wait upon the glorious god,
1.115: thou that sweepest clean the altar of Phoebus hard by his shrine, where holy founts, that ever gush with ceaseless flow,
1.120: bedew the myrtle’s hallowed spray wherewith I cleanse the temple-floor the livelong day, so soon as the swift sun-god wings his flight on high, in my daily ministration.
1.125:
Hail Paean, prince of healing! blest, ah! doubly blest be thou, child of Latona!
Ion
1.128: Fair the service that I render to thee, Phoebus, before thy house,
1.130: honouring thy seat of prophecy; a glorious task I count it, to serve not mortal man but deathless gods; wherefore I never weary
1.135: of performing holy services. Phoebus is to me as the father that begot me, for as such I praise the god that gives me food. Whom I call by that helpful name of father,
1.140:
Tis Phoebus, who dwelleth in the temple, Hail Paean, healing god, good luck to thee and blessing, child of Latona!
Ion
1.145: of sweeping with the laurel broom, so now from a golden ewer will I sprinkle o’er the ground water from Castalia’s gushing spring, scattering the liquid dew
1.150: with hands from all defilement free. Oh may I never cease thus to serve Phoebus, or, if I do, may fortune smile upon me!
1.154: Ha! they come, the feathered tribes,
1.155: leaving their nests on Parnassus. I forbid ye to settle on the coping or enter the gilded dome. Thou herald of Zeus, that masterest the might of other birds with those talons of thine,
1.160: once more shall my arrow o’ertake thee.
1.161: Lo! another comes sailing towards the altar, a swan this time; take thy bright plumes elsewhere; the lyre that Phoebus tuneth to thy song shall never
1.165: save thee from the bow; so fly away, and settle at the Delian mere, for if thou wilt not hearken, thy blood shall choke the utterance of thy fair melody.
1.170: Ha! what new bird comes now? Does it mean to lodge a nest of dry straw for its brood beneath the gables? Soon shall my twanging bow drive thee away. Dost not hear me?
1.175: Away and rear thy young amid the streams of swirling Alpheus, or get thee to the woody Isthmian glen, that Phoebus’ offerings and his shrine may take no hurt. I am loth to slay ye,
1.180:
ye messengers to mortal man of messages from heaven; still must I serve Phoebus, to whose tasks I am devoted, nor will I cease to minister to those that give me food.
(First) Chorus
1.184: It is not in holy Athens
1.185:
only that there are courts of the gods with fine colonnades, and the worship of Apollo, guardian of highways; but here, too, at the shrine of Loxias, son of Latona, shines the lovely eye of day on faces twain.
(Second) Chorus
1.190:
Just look at this! here is the son of Zeus killing with his scimitar of gold the watersnake of Lerna. Do look at him, my friend!
(First) Chorus
1.194: Yes, I see. And close to him stands another
1.195: with a blazing torch uplifted; who is he? Can this be the warrior Iolaus whose story is told on my broidery, who shares with
1.200:
the son of Zeus his labours and helps him in the moil?
(Third) Chorus
1.201:
Oh! but look at this! a man mounted on a winged horse, killing a fire-breathing monster with three bodies.
(First) Chorus
1.205:
I am turning my eyes in every direction. Behold the rout of the giants carved on these walls of stone.
(Fourth) Chorus
1.208:
Yes, yes, good friends, I am looking.
(Fifth) Chorus
1.210:
Dost see her standing over Enceladus brandishing her shield with the Gorgon’s head?
(Sixth) Chorus
1.211:
I see Pallas, my own goddess.
(Seventh) Chorus
1.212:
Again, dost see the massy thunderbolt all aflame in the far-darting hands of Zeus?
(Eighth) Chorus
1.215:
I do; ’tis blasting with its flame Mimas, that deadly foe.
(Ninth) Chorus
1.217:
Bromius too, the god of revelry, is slaying another of the sons of Earth with his thyrsus of ivy, never meant for battle.
(First) Chorus
1.219: Thou that art stationed by this fane, to thee I do address me,
1.220:
may we pass the threshold of these vaults, with our fair white feet?
Ion
1.222:
Nay, ye must not, stranger ladies.
(Tenth) Chorus
May I ask thee about something I have heard?
Ion
1.223:
What wouldst thou ask?
(Eleventh) Chorus
Is it really true that the temple of Phoebus stands upon the centre of the world?
Ion
1.224:
Aye, there it stands with garlands decked and gorgeous all around.
(Twelfth) Chorus
1.225:
E'en so the legend saith.
Ion
1.226:
If ye have offered a sacrificial cake before the shrine and have aught ye wish to ask Phoebus, approach the altar; but enter not the inmost sanctuary, save ye have sacrificed sheep.
(Thirteenth) Chorus
1.230:
I understand; but we have ho mind to trespass against the god’s law; the pictures here without will amuse us.
Ion
1.233:
Feast your eyes on all ye may.
(Fourteenth) Chorus
My mistress gave me leave to see these vaulted chambers.
Ion
1.234:
Whose handmaids do ye avow yourselves?
(Fifteenth) Chorus
1.235:
The temple, where Pallas dwells, is the nursing-home of my lords. But lo! here is she of whom thou askest.
Ion
1.237: Lady, whosoe’er thou art, I see thou art of noble birth, and thy bearing proves thy gentle breeding. For from his bearing one may mostly judge
1.240: whether a man is nobly born. Yet am I much amazed to see thee close thine eyes in grief and with tears bedew thy noble face, when thou standest face to face with the holy oracle of Loxias. Why, lady, art thou thus disquieted?
1.245:
Here, where all others show their joy at sight of Phoebus’ sanctuary, thine eye is wet with tears.
Creusa
1.247: Most courteously, sir stranger, dost thou express surprise at these my tears; the sight of this temple of Apollo
1.250:
recalled to me a memory of long ago, and somehow my thoughts went wandering home, though I am here myself. Ah, hapless race of women! ah, ye reckless gods! What shall I say? to what standard shall we refer justice if through the injustice of our lords and masters we are brought to ruin?
Ion
1.255:
Why, lady, art thou thus cast down, past all finding out?
Creusa
1.256:
’Tis naught; I have shot my bolt; for what remains, I say no more, nor seek thou further to inquire.
Ion
1.258:
Who art thou and whence? who is the father that begat thee? by what name are we to call thee?
Creusa
1.260:
Creusa is my name, the daughter of Erechtheus I; my native land is Athens.
Ion
1.262:
A glorious city thine, lady, a noble line of ancestry! with what reverence I behold thee!
Creusa
1.264:
Thus far, no further goes my luck, good sir.
Ion
1.265:
Pray, is the current legend true—
Creusa
1.266:
What is thy question? I fain would learn.
Ion
1.267:
Was thy father’s grandsire really sprung from Earth?
Creusa
1.268:
Yes, Erichthonius was; but my high birth avails me not
Ion
1.269:
Is it true Athena reared him from the ground?
Creusa
1.270:
Aye, and into maidens’ hands, though not his mother’s—
Ion
1.271:
Consigned him, did she? as ’tis wont to be set forth in painting.
Creusa
1.272:
Yes, to the daughters of Cecrops, to keep him safe unseen.
Ion
1.273:
I have heard the maidens opened the ark wherein the goddess laid him.
Creusa
1.274:
And so they died, dabbling with their blood the rocky cliff.
Ion
1.275:
Even so. But what of this next story? Is it true or groundless?
Creusa
1.276:
What is thy question? Ask on, I have no calls upon my leisure.
Ion
1.277:
Did thy sire Erechtheus offer thy sisters as a sacrifice?
Creusa
1.278:
For his country’s sake he did endure to slay the maids as victims.
Ion
1.279:
And how didst thou, alone of al thy sisters, escape?
Creusa
1.280:
I was still a tender babe in my mother’s arms.
Ion
1.281:
Did the earth really open its mouth and swallow thy father?
Creusa
1.282:
The sea-god smote and slew him with his trident.
Ion
1.283:
Is there a spot there called Macrae?
Creusa
1.284:
Why ask that? what memories thou recallest!
Ion
1.285:
Doth the Pythian god with his flashing fire do honour to the place?
Creusa
1.286:
Honour, yes! Honour, indeed! would I had never seen the spot!
Ion
1.287:
How now? dost thou abhor that which the god holds dear?
Creusa
1.288:
No, no; but I and that cave are witnesses of a deed of shame.
Ion
1.289:
Lady, who is the Athenian lord that calls thee wife?
Creusa
1.290:
No citizen of Athens, but a stranger from another land.
Ion
1.291:
Who is he? he must have been one of noble birth.
Creusa
1.292:
Xuthus, son of Aeolus, sprung from Zeus.
Ion
1.293:
And how did he, a stranger, win thee a native born?
Creusa
1.294:
Hard by Athens lies a neighbouring township, Euboea.
Ion
1.295:
With a bounding line of waters in between, so I have heard.
Creusa
1.296:
This did he sack, making common cause with Cecrops’ sons.
Ion
1.297:
Coming as an ally, maybe; he won thy hand for this?
Creusa
1.298:
Yes, this was his dower of battle, the prize of his prowess.
Ion
1.299:
Art thou come to the oracle alone, or with thy lord?
Creusa
1.300:
With him. But he is now visiting the cavern of Trophonius.
Ion
1.301:
As a spectator merely, or to consult the oracle?
Creusa
1.302:
’Tis his wish to hear the self-same answer from Trophonius and Phoebus too.
Ion
1.303:
Is it to seek earth’s produce or fruit of offspring that ye come?
Creusa
1.304:
We are childless, though wedded these many years.
Ion
1.305:
Hast thou never been a mother? art thou wholly childless?
Creusa
1.306:
Phoebus knows whether I am childless.
Ion
1.307:
Unhappy wife! how this doth mar thy fortune else so happy!
Creusa
1.308:
But who art thou? how blest I count thy mother!
Ion
1.309:
Lady, I am called the servant of Apollo, and so I am.
Creusa
1.310:
An offering of thy city, or sold to him by some master?
Ion
1.311:
Naught know I but this, that I am called the slave of Loxias.
Creusa
1.312:
Then do i in my turn pity thee, sir stranger.
Ion
1.313:
Because I know not her that bare me, or him that begat me.
Creusa
1.314:
Is thy home here in the temple, or hast thou a house to dwell in?
Ion
1.315:
The god’s whole temple is my house, wherever sleep o’ertakes me.
Creusa
1.316:
Was it as a child or young man that thou earnest to the temple?
Ion
1.317:
Those who seem to know the truth, say I was but a babe.
Creusa
1.318:
What Delphian maid, then, weaned thee?
Ion
1.319:
I never knew a mother’s breast. But she who brought me up—
Creusa
1.320:
Who was she, unhappy youth? I see thy sufferings in my own.
Ion
1.321:
The priestess of Phoebus; I look oh her as my mother.
Creusa
1.322:
Until thou earnest unto man’s estate, what nurture hadst thou?
Ion
1.323:
The altar fed me, and the bounty of each casual guest.
Creusa
1.324:
Woe is thy mother, then, whoe’er she was!
Ion
1.325:
Maybe my birth was some poor woman’s wrong.
Creusa
1.326:
Hast thou any store, for thy dress is costly enough?
Ion
1.327:
The god I serve gives me these robes to wear.
Creusa
1.328:
Wert thou never eager to inquire into thy birth?
Ion
1.329:
Ah! yes, lady! but I have no clue at all to guide me.
Creusa
1.330:
Alas! I know another woman who hath suffered as thy mother did.
Ion
1.331:
Who is she? If she would but help me in the task, how happy should I be!
Creusa
1.332:
’Tis she on whose account I have preceded my husband hither.
Ion
1.333:
What are thy wishes? be sure I will serve thee, lady.
Creusa
1.334:
I would fain obtain a secret answer from Apollo’s oracle.
Ion
1.335:
Name it, then; the rest will I undertake for thee.
Creusa
1.336:
Hear, then, this story. Yet am I ashamed.
Ion
1.337:
Thus wilt thou accomplish naught, for shame is a goddess slow to act.
Creusa
1.338:
A friend of mine asserts that Phoebus lay with her.
Ion
1.339:
Phoebus with a mortal woman? Stranger lady, say not so.
Creusa
1.340:
Yea, and she bare the god a child without her father’s knowledge.
Ion
1.341:
It cannot be; some man did wrong her, and she is ashamed of it.
Creusa
1.342:
This she denieis herself; and she hath suffered further woe.
Ion
1.343:
How so, if she was wedded to a god?
Creusa
1.344:
The babe she bare she did expose.
Ion
1.345:
Where is the child who was thus cast forth? is he yet alive?
Creusa
1.346:
No man knoweth. That is the very thing I would ask the oracle.
Ion
1.347:
But if he be no more, how did he perish?
Creusa
1.348:
She supposes that beasts devoured the hapless babe.
Ion
1.349:
What proof led her to form this opinion?
Creusa
1.350:
She came to the place where she exposed him, but found him no longer there.
Ion
1.351:
Were any drops of blood upon the path?
Creusa
1.352:
None, she says; and yet she ranged the ground to and fro.
Ion
1.353:
How long is it since the babe was destroyed?
Creusa
1.354:
Thy age and his would measure out the self-same span, were he alive.
Ion
1.355:
Hath she given birth to no other child since then?
Creusa
1.356:
The god doth wrong her, and wretched is she in having no child.
Ion
1.357:
But what if Phoebus privily removed her child, and is rearing it?
Creusa
1.358:
Then is he acting unfairly in keeping to himself alone a joy he ought to share.
Ion
1.359:
Ah me! this misfortune sounds so like my own.
Creusa
1.360:
Thee too, fair sir, thy poor mother misses, I am sure.
Ion
1.361:
Oh! call me not back to piteous thoughts I had forgotten.
Creusa
1.362:
I am dumb; proceed with that which touches my inquiry.
Ion
1.363:
Dost know the one weak point in this thy story?
Creusa
1.364:
’Tis all weak in that poor lady’s case.
Ion
1.365:
How should the god declare that which he wishes hidden?
Creusa
1.366:
He must, if here upon the tripod he sits for all Hellas to seek to.
Ion
1.367:
He is ashamed of the deed; do not question him.
Creusa
1.368:
Aye, but his victim has her sorrows too.
Ion
1.369: There is none who will act as thy medium in this.
1.370: For were Phoebus in his own temple proved a villain, he would justly wreak his vengeance on the man who expounded to thee his oracles; desist then, lady; we must not prophesy against the god’s will,
1.375: for it would be the height of folly in us, were we to try and make the gods against their will declare reluctant truths either by sacrifice of sheep at their altars, or by omens from birds. For those answers we strive to extort from heaven, lady, are goods that bring no blessing on our getting;
1.380:
but what they freely offer, thereby we profit.
Chorus
1.381:
Many are the chances that befall the many tribes of men, and diverse are their forms. But scarce one happy scene canst thou find in all the life of man.
Creusa
1.384: Ah! Phoebus, here as there, art thou unjust
1.385: to that absent sufferer, whose cause I now am pleading. Thou didst not preserve thy child, as in duty bound, nor wilt thou, for all thy prophetic skill, answer his mother’s questioning, that, if he be no more, a mound may be raised o’er him, or, if he live, he may some day be restored to his mother’s eyes.
1.390: In vain is this the home of oracles if the god prevents me from learning what I wish to ask. But lo! I see my noble lord, Xuthus, nigh at hand, returning 278 from the lair of Trophonius; say nothing,
1.395: sir, to my husband of what I have told thee, lest I incur reproach for troubling about secrets, and the matter take a different turn to that which I sought to give it. For women stand towards men in a difficult position, and the virtuous from being mingled with the wicked amongst us are hated;
1.400:
such is our unhappy destiny.
Xuthus
1.401:
First to the god all hail! for he must receive the first-fruits of my salutation, and next all hail to thee, my wife! Has my delay in arriving caused thee alarm?
Creusa
1.404: By no means; but thou art come at an anxious time.
1.405:
Tell me what response thou bringest from Trophonius, touching our future hopes of mutual offspring.
Xuthus
1.407:
He deigned not to forestal the prophecies of Phoebus. This only did he say, that neither thou nor I should return unto our house childless from the shrine.
Creusa
1.410:
Majestic mother of Phoebus, to our journey grant success, and may our previous dealings with thy son now find a better issue!
Xuthus
1.413:
It will be so; but who acts as the god’s spokesman here?
Ion
1.414: I serve outside the shrine, others within,
1.415:
who stand near the tripod, even the noblest of the Delphians chosen by lot, sir stranger.
Xuthus
1.417: ’Tis well; I have attained the utmost of my wishes. I will go within; for I am told that a victim has been slain in public before the temple for strangers,
1.420:
and to-day,—for it is a lucky day,—I would fain receive the god’s oracle. Do thou, my wife, take branches of laurel, and seated at the altars pray to the gods that I may carry home from Apollo’s shrine an answer that bodeth well for offspring.
Creusa
1.425:
All this shall be. Now, at any rate, if Loxias would retrieve his former sins, e’en though he cannot be my friend entirely, yet will I accept whate’er he deigns to give, because he is a god.
[Exeunt Xuthus and Creusa.
Ion
1.429: Why doth this stranger lady hint dark reproaches against the god
1.430: unceasingly, either out of affection for her on whose behalf she seeks the oracle, or maybe because she is hiding something needing secrecy? Yet what have I to do with the daughter of Erectheus? She is naught to me.
1.435: No, I will go to the laver, and from golden ewers sprinkle the holy water. Yet must I warn Phoebus of what is happening to him; he ravishes a maid and proves unfaithful to her, and after secretly begetting a son leaves him to die. O! Phoebus, do not so, but as thou art supreme,
1.440: follow in virtue’s track; for whosoever of mortal men transgresses, him the gods punish. How, then, can it be just that you should enact your laws for men, and yourselves incur the charge of breaking them? Now I will put this case, though it will never happen.
1.445: Wert thou, wert Poseidon, and Zeus, the lord of heaven, to make atonement to mankind for every act of lawless love, ye would empty your temples in paying the fines for your misdeeds. For when ye pursue pleasure in preference to the claims of prudence, ye act unjustly; no longer is it fair
1.450:
to call men wicked, if we are imitating the evil deeds of gods, but rather those who give us such examples. [Exit Ion
Chorus
1.452: On thee I call, Athena mine, at whose birth-throes no kindly goddess lent her aid,
1.455: delivered as thou wert by Titan Prometheus from the forehead of Zeus. Come, O lady Victory, come to the Pythian shrine, winging thy way from the gilded chambers of Olympus
1.460: to the city’s streets, where Phoebus at his altar on the centre of the world brings his oracles to pass beside the dance-encircled tripod;
1.465: come, too, thou daughter of Latona, together come, ye virgin goddesses, fair sisters of Phoebus! And be this your prayer, fair maidens, that the ancient house of Erechtheus
1.470:
may obtain by clear oracles the blessing of children, though late it come.
Chorus
1.472: For this brings to man a settled source of all-surpassing bliss,
1.475: even to such as see in their ancestral halls a splendid race of strong young parents blest with offspring, to inherit from their sires
1.480: their wealth in due succession after other children; yea, for they are a defence in time of trouble, and add a charm to weal, affording to their fatherland a saving help in battle.
1.485: Give me before the pomp of wealth or royal marriages the careful nurture of noble children. The childless life I do abhor, and him who thinks it good I blame;
1.490:
to a happy life amongst my children, blest with moderate wealth, may I hold fast.
Chorus
1.492: Ye haunts of Pan, and rocks hard by the grots of Macrae,
1.495: where Agraulos’ daughters three trip it lightly o’er the green grass-lawns before the shrine of Pallas, to the music of the piper’s varied note,
1.500: what time thou, Pan, art piping in those caves of thine, where a maiden once that had a child by Phoebus, unhappy mother! exposed her babe, forced issue of her woful wooing,
1.505:
for birds to tear and beasts to rend, a bloody banquet! Never have I seen it told in woven tale or legend that children born to gods by daughters of earth have any share in bliss.
Ion
1.510:
Attendant maids, that watch and wait your mistress here at the steps of the temple fragrant with incense, say, hath Xuthus already left the holy tripod and the sanctuary, or doth he still abide within to ask yet further of his childlessness?
Chorus
1.514: He is still in the temple, sir, nor hath he passed this threshold yet.
1.515:
But hark! I hear a footstep at the outlet of the door, and lo! thou mayst see my master this moment coming out.
Xuthus
1.517:
All hail! my son; that word suits well as my first greeting to thee.
Ion
1.518:
’Tis well with me; do but restrain thyself, and then both of us will be happy.
Xuthus
1.519:
Give me thy hand to grasp, thy body to embrace.
Ion
1.520:
Art thou in thy senses, sir, or hath some spiteful god reft thee of them?
Xuthus
1.521:
I am in my senses, for I have found what I hold most dear, and am eager to show my love.
Ion
1.522:
Cease! touch me not, nor tear these garlands of the god!
Xuthus
1.523:
I will embrace thee, for I am not seizing what is not my own, but only finding my own that I love full well.
Ion
1.524:
Hands off! or thou shalt feel an arrow pierce thy ribs.
Xuthus
1.525:
Why dost thou shun me, now that thou findest in me thy nearest and dearest?
Ion
1.526:
I am not fond of schooling boors and crazy strangers.
Xuthus
1.527:
Kill me, burn me, if thou wilt; for, if thou dost, thou wilt be thy father’s murderer.
Ion
1.528:
Thou my father, indeed i Oh! is not news like this enough to make me laugh?
Xuthus
1.529:
Not so; my tale, as it proceeds, will prove to thee what I assert.
Ion
1.530:
Pray, what hast thou to tell me?
Xuthus
That I am thy own father, and thou my very child.
Ion
1.531:
Who says so?
Xuthus
Loxias, who gave thee nurture, though thou wert my son.
Ion
1.532:
Thou art thy own witness.
Xuthus
Nay, I have learnt the answer of the god.
Ion
1.533:
Thou art mistaken in the dark riddle thou hast heard.
Xuthus
It seems then I do not hear aright.
Ion
1.534:
What said Phoebus?
Xuthus
That the man who met me—
Ion
1.535:
When and where?
Xuthus
As I came forth from the god’s temple—
Ion
1.536:
Well! what should happen to him?
Xuthus
Should be my own true son.
Ion
1.537:
Thy own true son, or a gift from others?
Xuthus
A gift, but mine for all that.
Ion
1.538:
Am I the first that thou didst meet?
Xuthus
I have met no other, my son.
Ion
1.539:
Whence came this piece of luck?
Xuthus
To both of us alike it causes surprise.
Ion
1.540:
Ah I but who was my mother?
Xuthus
I cannot tell.
Ion
1.541:
Did not Phoebus tell thee that?
Xuthus
I was so pleased with this, I did not ask him that.
Ion
1.542:
I must have sprung from mother earth.
Xuthus
The ground brings forth no children.
Ion
1.543:
How can I be thine?
Xuthus
I know not; I refer it to the god.
Ion
1.544:
Come, let us try another theme.
Xuthus
Better hold to this, my son.
Ion
1.545:
Didst thou e’er indulge in illicit amours?
Xuthus
Yes, in the folly of youth.
Ion
1.546:
Ere thou didst win Erechtheus’ daughter?
Xuthus
Never since.
Ion
1.547:
Could it be, then, thou didst beget me?
Xuthus
The time coincides therewith.
Ion
1.548:
In that case, how came I hither?
Xuthus
That puzzles me.
Ion
1.549:
After that long journey too?
Xuthus
That, too, perplexes me.
Ion
1.550:
Didst thou in days gone by come to the Pythian rock?
Xuthus
Yes, to join in the mystic rites of Bacchus.
Ion
1.551:
Didst thou lodge with one of the public hosts?
Xuthus
With one who at Delphi—
Ion
1.552:
Initiated thee? or what is it thou sayest?
Xuthus
Among the frantic votaries of Bacchus.
Ion
1.553:
Wert thou sober, or in thy cups?
Xuthus
I had indulged in the pleasures of the wine-cup.
Ion
1.554:
That is just the history of my birth.
Xuthus
Fate hath discovered thee, my son.
Ion
1.555:
How came I to the temple?
Xuthus
Maybe the maid exposed thee.
Ion
1.556:
I have escaped the shame of slavish birth.
Xuthus
Acknowledge then thy father, my son.
Ion
1.557:
It is not right that I should mistrust the god.
Xuthus
Thou art right there.
Ion
1.558:
What more can I desire—
Xuthus
Thine eyes now open to the sights they should.
Ion
1.559:
Than from a son of Zeus to spring?
Xuthus
Which is indeed thy lot.
Ion
1.560:
May I embrace the author of my being?
Xuthus
Aye, put thy trust in the god.
Ion
1.561:
Hail to thee, father mine.
Xuthus
With joy that title I accept.
Ion
1.562:
This day—
Xuthus
Hath made me blest.
Ion
1.563: Ah, mother dear! shall I ever see thee too? Now more than ever do I long to gaze upon thee, whoe’er thou art.
1.565:
But thou perhaps art dead, and I shall never have the chance.
Chorus
1.566:
We share the good luck of thy house; but still I could have wished my mistress too, and Erechtheus’ line, had been blest with children.
Xuthus
1.569: My son, albeit the god hath for thy discovery brought his oracle
1.570: to a true issue, and united thee to me, while thou, too, hast found what most thou dost desire, till now unconscious of it; still, as touching this anxiety so proper in thee, I feel an equal yearning that thou, my child, mayst find thy mother, and I the wife that bare thee unto me.
1.575: Maybe we shall discover this, if we leave it to time. But now leave the courts of the god, and this homeless life of thine, and come to Athens, in accordance with thy fathers wishes, for there his happy realm and bounteous wealth await thee; nor shalt thou
1.580:
be taunted with base origin and poverty to boot, because in one of these respects thou something lackest, but thou shalt be renowned alike for birth and wealth. Art silent? why dost fix thy eyes upon the ground? Thou art lost in thought, and by this sudden change from thy former cheerfulness, thou strikest thy father with dismay.
Ion
1.585: Things assume a different form according as we see them before us, or far off. I am glad at what has happened, since I have found in thee a father; but hear me on some points which I am now deciding.
1.590: Athens, I am told,—that glorious city of a native race,—owns no aliens; in which case I shall force my entrance there under a twofold disadvantage, as an alien’s son and base-born as I am. Branded with this reproach, while as yet I am unsupported, I shall get the name of a mere nobody, a son of nobodies;
1.595: and if I win my way to the highest place in the state, and seek to be some one, I shall be hated by those who have no influence, for superiority is galling; while ’mongst men of worth who could show their wisdom, but are silent, and take no interest in politics,
1.600: I shall incur ridicule and be thought a fool for not keeping quiet in such a fault-finding city. Again, if I win a name amongst the men of mark who are engaged in politics, still more will jealous votes bar my progress; for thus, father, is it ever wont to be;
1.605: they who have the city’s ear, and have already made their mark, are most bitter against all rivals.
1.607: Again, if I, a stranger, come to a home that knows me not, and to that childless wife who before had thee as partner in her sorrow, but now
1.610: will feel the bitterness of having to bear her fortune all alone,—how, I ask, shall I not fairly earn her hatred, when I take my stand beside thee; while she, still childless, sees thy dear pledge with bitter eyes; and then thou have to choose between deserting me and regarding her,
1.615: or honouring me and utterly confounding thy home? How many a murder, and death by deadly drugs have wives devised for husbands! Besides, I pity that wife of thine, father, with her childless old age beginning; she little deserves
1.620: to pine in barrenness, a daughter of a noble race. That princely state we fondly praise is pleasant to the eye; but yet in its mansions sorrow lurks; for who is happy, or by fortune blest, that has to live his life in fear of violence with many a sidelong glance?
1.625: Rather would I live among the common folk, and taste their bliss, than be a tyrant who delights in making evil men his friends, and hates the good, in terror of his life. Perchance thou wilt tell me, Gold outweighs all these evils,
1.630: and wealth is sweet. I have no wish to be abused for holding tightly to my pelf, nor yet to have the trouble of it. Be mine a moderate fortune free from annoyance! Now hear the blessings, father, that here were mine; first, leisure, man’s chiefest joy,
1.635: with but moderate trouble; no villain ever drove me from my path, and that is a grievance hard to bear, to make room and give way to sorry knaves. My duty was to pray unto the gods, or with mortal men converse, a minister to their joys, not to their Sorrows.
1.640: And I was ever dismissing one batch of guests, while another took their place, so that I was always welcome from the charm of novelty. That honesty which men must pray for, even against their will, custom and nature did conspire to plant in me in the sight of Phoebus. Now when I think on this,
1.645:
I deem that I am better here than there, father. So let me live on here, for ’tis an equal charm to joy in high estate, or in a humble fortune find a pleasure.
Chorus
1.648:
Well said! if only those I love find their happiness in thy statement of the case.
Xuthus
1.650: Cease such idle talk, and learn to be happy; for on that spot where I discovered thee, my son, will I begin the rites, since I have chanced on the general banquet, open to all comers, and I will offer thy birth sacrifice which aforetime I left undone. And now will I bring thee to the banquet as my guest and rejoice thy heart,
1.655: and take thee to the Athenian land as a visitor forsooth, not as my own son. For I will not grieve my wife in her childless sorrow by my good fortune. But in time will I seize a happy moment
1.660: and prevail on her to let thee wield my sceptre o’er the realm. Thy name shall be Ion, in accordance with what happened, for that thou wert the first to cross my path as I came forth from Apollo’s sanctuary. Go, gather every friend thou hast, and with them make merry o’er the flesh of sacrifice,
1.665:
on the eve of thy departure from the town of Delphi. On you, ye handmaids, silence I enjoin, for, if ye say one word to my wife, death awaits you.
[Exit Xuthus.
Ion
1.668: Well, I will go; one thing my fortune lacks, for if I find not her that gave me birth, life is no life to me, my father;
1.670: and, if I may make the prayer, Oh may that mother be a daughter of Athens! that from-her I may inherit freedom of speech. For if a stranger settle in a city free from aliens, e’en though in name he be a citizen,
1.675:
yet doth he find him-setf tongue-tied and debarred from open utterance.
[Exit Ion.
Chorus
1.676: Weeping and lamentation and the beginning of mourning I foresee, when my mistress shall see her lord blest with a son,
1.680: while she is childless and forlorn. What was this oracle thou didst vouchsafe, prophetic son of Latona? Whence came this boy, thy foster-child who lingers in thy temple? who was his mother?
1.685: I like not thy oracle; I fear there is some treachery. In terror I await the issue of this chance;
1.690:
for strange are these tidings and strange it is that the god declares them to me. There is guile connected with this waif’s fortune. All must allow that.
Chorus
1.695: Shall we, good friends, throw off disguise and tell our mistress this story about her husband in whom her all was centred and whose hopes, poor lady, she once shared? But now in misery is she plunged, while he enjoys the smiles of fortune;
1.700: to hoary eld she drifteth fast, while he, her lord, pays no regard to his loved ones,—the wretch, who came an alien to her house to share great wealth and failed to guard her fortunes! Perdition catch this traitor to my lady!
1.705: never may he succeed in offering to the gods upon their blazing altar a hallowed cake with flames that augur well! He shall know to his cost my regard
1.710:
for my mistress. Now are sire and new-found son bent on the approaching feast.
Chorus
1.715: that rear your rocky heads to heaven, where Bacchus with uplifted torch of blazing pine bounds nimbly amid his bacchanals, that range by night! Never to my city come this boy!
1.720:
let him die and leave his young life as it dawns! For should our city fall on evil days, this bringing-in of strangers would supply it with a reason. Enough, enough for us Erechtheus’ line that erst held sway!
Creusa
1.725: Aged retainer of my father Erechtheus while yet he lived and saw the light of day, mount to the god’s prophetic shrine that thou mayst share my gladness, if haply Loxias, great king, vouchsafe an answer touching my hopes of offspring;
1.730:
for sweet it is to share with friends prosperity, and sweet likewise to see a friendly face if any ill betide,—which God forbid! As thou of yore didst tend my sire, so now, thy mistress though I am, I take his place in tending thee.
Old Servant
1.735: Daughter, thy manners bear good witness still to thy noble lineage; thou hast never brought shame upon those ancestors of thine, the children of the soil. A hand, I prithee, to the shrine! a hand to lean upon!’Tis a steep path thither, truly;
1.740:
but lend thy aid to guide my steps and make me young again.
Creusa
1.741:
Come follow then, and look where thou art treading.
Old Servant
1.742:
Behold! though my steps loiter, my thoughts take wings.
Creusa
1.743:
Lean on thy staff as thou climbest this winding path.
Old Servant
1.744:
Even this staff is a blind guide when I myself can scarcely see.
Creusa
1.745:
True, but do not yield through fatigue.
Old Servant
1.746:
Never willingly, but I am not master of that which is mine no more.
Creusa
1.747: Maidens mine, my trusty servants at the loom and web, declare to me how my lord hath fared as touching the question of offspring which brought us hither:
1.750:
for if ye give me good news, ye will cause joy to a mistress who will not prove faithless to her word.
Chorus
1.753:
This prelude to your speech is unlucky.
Chorus
1.755:
Can it be that the oracles delivered to my master wound me at all?
Chorus
1.756:
Enough! why have aught to do with that which brings down death?
Creusa
1.757:
What means this piteous strain? wherefore this alarm?
Chorus
1.758:
Are we to speak or keep silence? What shall we do?
Creusa
1.759:
Speak; for thou hast somewhat to tell that touches me.
Chorus
1.760:
Then speak I will, though twice to die were mine. O mistress mine! never shalt thou hold a babe within thy arms or clasp him to thy breast.
Creusa
1.762:
Ah me! would I were dead!
Old Servant
1.763:
My daughter!
Creusa
O woe is me for my calamity! Mine is a heritage of suffering and woe that poisons life, good friends.
Old Servant
1.765:
Ah, my child, ’tis death to us!
Creusa
Ah me! ah me! grief drives its weapon through this heart of mine.
Old Servant
1.769:
Stay thy lamentations.
Creusa
Nay, but sorrow lodges here.
Old Servant
1.770:
Till we learn—
Creusa
Ah, what further news is there for me?
Old Servant
1.771:
Whether our master is in the same plight and shares thy misfortune, or thou art alone in thy misery.
Chorus
1.774: On him, old sir, Loxias hath bestowed a son,
1.775:
and he is enjoying his good fortune apart from her.
Creusa
1.776:
Herein hast thou declared a further evil crowning all, a grief for me to mourn.
Old Servant
1.778:
The child of whom thou speakest—is he some woman’s destined babe, or did the god declare the fate of one already born?
Chorus
1.780:
A youth already born and grown to man’s estate doth Phoebus give to him; for I was there myself.
Creusa
1.782:
What sayest thou? nor tongue nor lip should speak the word thou tellest me.
Old Servant
1.785:
And me. But declare more clearly how this oracle is finding its fulfilment, and say who is the child.
Chorus
1.787:
Whomso thy husband first should meet as he issued from the shrine, him the god gave him for his son.
Creusa
1.789: Ah me! my fate, it seems, has doomed me to a childless
1.790:
life, and all forlorn am I to dwell in ray halls, without an heir.
Old Servant
1.792:
To whom did the oracle refer? whom did our poor lady’s husband meet? how and where did he see him?
Chorus
1.794: Dear mistress mine, dost know that youth
1.795:
that was sweeping yonder shrine? He is that son.
Creusa
1.796:
Oh! for wings to cleave the liquid air beyond the land of Hellas, away to the western stars, so keen the anguish of my soul, my friends!
Old Servant
1.800:
Dost know the name his father gave to him, or is that left as yet unsettled and unsaid?
Chorus
1.802:
He called him Ion, because he was the first to cross his path.
Old Servant
1.803:
Who is his mother?
Chorus
That I cannot say. But,—to tell thee all I know, old sir,—
1.805:
her lord is gone, with furtive step, into the hallowed tent, there to offer on this child’s behalf such gifts and victims as are offered for a birth, and with his new-found son to celebrate the feast.
Old Servant
1.808: Mistress mine, we are betrayed by thy husband, fellow-sufferers thou and I; ’tis a deep-laid plot to outrage us
1.810: and drive us from Erechtheus’ halls. And this I say not from any hatred of thy lord but because I bear thee more love than him; for he, after coming as a stranger to thy city and thy home, and wedding thee, and of thy heritage taking full possession,
1.815: has been detected in a secret marriage with another woman, by whom he hath children. His secret will I now disclose; when he found thee barren, he was not content to share with thee thy hard lot, but took to himself a slave to be his stealthy paramour
1.820: and thus begat a son, whom he sent abroad, giving him to some Delphian maid to nurse; and, to escape detection, the child was dedicated to the god and reared in his temple. But when he heard his boy was grown to manhood, he persuaded thee to come hither to inquire about thy childless state.
1.825: And after this, ’twas not the god that lied, but thy husband, who long had been rearing the child, and he it was that wove this tissue of falsehood, intending, if he were detected, to refer it to the god, whereas if he escaped exposure, to repel all odium, he meant to vest the sovereignty in this son of his.
1.830:
Likewise he devised anew his name, coined to suit the circumstances, Ion, because, as he asserts, he met him on his way.
Chorus
1.832: Ah! how I ever hate the wicked
1.835:
who plot unrighteousness and then cunningly trick it out. Far rather would I have a virtuous friend of no great intellect than a knave of subtler wit.
Old Servant
1.836: Of all thy wretched fate this will be the crowning sorrow, the bringing to thy house to be its lord some slave-girl’s child, whose mother is unknown, himself of no account. For this evil had been to itself confined,
1.840: had he persuaded thee, pleading thy childlessness, to let him establish in the house some high-born mother’s son; or if this had displeased thee, he ought to have sought a daughter of Aeolus in marriage. Wherefore must thou now put thy woman’s wit to work; either take the dagger, or by guile
1.845: or poison slay thy husband and his son, ere they deal out death to thee; since if thou spare him, thou wilt lose thy own life; for when two foes meet beneath one roof, one or the other must rue it.
1.850: Myself too am ready to share this labour with thee, and to help destroy the child when I have made my way into the chamber where he is furnishing the feast, and so repaying my masters for my maintenance I am willing either to die or still behold the light of life. ’Tis but a single thing that brands the slave with shame—
1.855:
his name; in all else no upright slave is a whit worse than freeborn men.
Chorus
1.857:
I too, beloved mistress, am ready to share thy fate, be it death or victory.
Creusa
1.859: Ah! my suffering soul! how am I to keep silence?
1.860: Am I to disclose the secrets of my love and lose all claim to modesty? What is there to keep me back any longer? With whom have I to pit myself in virtue’s lists? Hath not my husband proved untrue?
1.865: Home and children, both are torn from me; all hope is dead; I have not realized my wish to set the matter straight, by hushing up my former union and saying naught about my son of sorrow.
1.870: No! by the starry seat of Zeus, by her whose home is on my rocks, and by the hallowed strand of Triton’s mere with brimming flood, I will no more conceal my love; for if
1.875: I can lift that burden from my breast I shall rest easier. With tears my eyes are streaming and my heart is wrung with anguish for the treacherous counsels both of men and gods,—traitors they! as I will show,
1.881: O! thou who dost awake that tuneful lyre with seven strings till to its sweet note of music the lifeless pegs of wild ox-hom resound again,
1.885: thou child of Latona, to yon 293 bright orb of thine will I publish thy reproach. Yes, I saw thee come, the glint of gold upon thy locks, as I was gathering in my folded robe the saffron blooms
1.890: that blazed like flowers of gold; and by my lily wrist didst thou catch me and ledst me to the cavern’s bed, what time I cried aloud upon my mother’s name,—thou a god
1.895: to mate with me in shameless wise to pleasure lady Cypris! Then to my sorrow I bore thee a son, whom, though anguish thrilled my mother’s breast, I cast upon that bed of thine,
1.900: where thou didst join in woful wedlock this unhappy maid. Ah! woe is me! that poor babe I bare thee is now no more; winged fowls have tom and devoured him,
1.905: but thou art gaily carolling unto thy lyre some song of joy.
1.907: Hark! thou son of Latona, to thee I call, for that thou dispensest warnings; there at thy golden throne
1.910: on earth’s centre planted will I proclaim a word into thy ear. O! thou wicked bridegroom who art bringing to my husband’s house an heir, though from him thou hast received no boon;
1.916: while that child of thine and mine hath died unrecognized, a prey to carrion birds, his mother’s swaddling-clothes all lost. Delos hates thee now, thy bay-tree loves thee not,
1.920:
whose branches sprout beside the tufted palm, where in holy throes Latona, big with child by Zeus, gave birth to thee.
Chorus
1.923:
Ah me! what store of sorrows is here disclosed, enough to draw a tear from every eye!
Old Servant
1.925: Daughter, with pity am I filled as a gaze upon thy face; my reason leaves me; for just as I am striving to lighten my spirit of its sea of troubles, comes another wave astern and catches me by reason of thy words; for no sooner hadst thou uttered this tale of present troubles
1.930:
than thou didst turn aside into a fresh a track of other woes. What is it thou sayest? What charge against Apollo dost thou bring? What child is this thou dost assert that thou didst bear? Where was it in the city that thou didst expose him, for beasts to rejoice o’er his burial? Tell me once again.
Creusa
1.934:
Old friend, although to meet thine eye, I am ashamed, yet will I tell thee.
Old Servant
1.935:
Full well I know how to lend my friends a generous sympathy.
Creusa
1.936:
Then hearken; dost know a cave toward the north of Cecrops’ rock, that we call Macrae?
Old Servant
1.938:
I know it; there is the shrine of Pan, and his altar hard by.
Creusa
1.939:
That was the scene of my dire conflict.
Old Servant
1.940:
What conflict? see how my tears start forth to meet thy words.
Creusa
1.941:
Phoebus forced me to a woful marriage.
Old Servant
1.942:
Was it then this, my daughter, that I noticed myself?
Creusa
1.943:
I know not; but I will tell thee if thou speak the truth.
Old Servant
1.944:
At the time thou wert mourning in secret some hidden complaint?
Creusa
1.945:
Yes, ’twas then this trouble happened, which now I am declaring to thee.
Old Servant
1.946:
How then didst conceal thy union with Apollo?
Creusa
1.947:
I bore a child; hear me patiently, old friend.
Old Servant
1.948:
Where? and who helped thy travail? or didst thou labour all alone?
Creusa
1.949:
All alone, in the cave where I became a wife.
Old Servant
1.950:
Where is the child? that thou mayst cease thy childless state.
Creusa
1.951:
Dead, old friend, to beasts exposed.
Old Servant
1.952:
Dead? did Apollo, evil god, no help afford?
Creusa
1.953:
None; my boy is in the halls of Hades.
Old Servant
1.954:
Who then exposed him? surely not thyself.
Creusa
1.955:
Myself, when ’neath the gloom of night I had wrapped him in my robe.
Old Servant
1.956:

1.1409:

1.1417:

Ion

1.1419:

1.1425:

1.1427:

1.1428:

1.1429:
Yes, to copy our ancestor Erichthonius.

1.1431:

1.1432:

Mother, dearest mother, with what rapture I behold thee, as on thy cheeks, that share my joy, I press my lips!

1.1443:

1.1445:

1.1450:

Creusa
1.1452:

Ion

1.1458: In tears wert thou brought forth, my child,

1.1462:

1.1472:

1.1475:

Be witness she who slew the Gorgon,

makes the olive-clad hill her seat.

1.1565: fearing that thou wouldst be slain by thy mother’s wiles and she by thine. to take compassion on the town now that it is burnt to ashes?
