Hecuba
1.275:
whose hair is white with age, who need to hold a staff to be to me a third foot, whose servant am I to be?
Talthybius
1.277:
Odysseus, king of Ithaca, has taken you to be his slave.
Hecuba
1.278: Oh, oh! Now smite the close-shorn head!
1.280: tear your cheeks with your nails! Ah me! I have fallen as a slave to a treacherous foe I hate, a monster of lawlessness,
1.285: one that by his double tongue has turned against us all that once was friendly in his camp, changing this for that and that for this again. Oh weep for me, you Trojan women! Lost and ill-fated!
1.290:
Ah woe! a victim to a most unhappy lot!
Chorus Leader
1.292:
Your fate, royal mistress, now you know; but for me, what Helene or Achaean is master of my destiny?
Talthybius
1.294: Go, servants, and bring Cassandra forth to me here
1.295: at once, that I may place her in our captain’s hands, and then conduct to the rest of the chiefs the captives each has had assigned. Ha! what is the blaze of torches there within? What are they doing? Are they firing the chambers,
1.300: because they must leave this land and be carried away to Argos? Are they setting themselves aflame in their longing for death? Truly the free bear their troubles in cases like this with a stiff neck. Open up! lest their deed, which suits them well
1.305:
but finds small favor with the Achaeans, bring blame on me.
Hecuba
1.306:
It is not that they are setting anything ablaze, but my child Cassandra, frenzied maid, comes rushing wildly here.
Cassandra
1.308: Bring the light, uplift and show its flame! I am doing the god’s service, see! see! making his shrine to glow with tapers bright.
1.310: O Hymen, lord of marriage! blessed is the bridegroom; blessed am I also, soon to wed a princely lord in Argos. Hail Hymen, lord of marriage!
1.315: Since you, my mother, are busied with tears and lamentations in your mourning for my father’s death and for our country dear, I at my own nuptials
1.320: am making this torch to blaze and show its light, giving to you, O Hymen, giving, O Hecate, a light, at the maiden’s wedding, as the custom is.
1.325: Nimbly lift the foot; lead the dance on high, with cries of joy, as if to greet my father’s happy fate. The dance is sacred. Come, Phoebus, now, for it is in your temple
1.330: among your bay-trees that I minister. Hail Hymen, god of marriage! Hymen, hail! Dance, mother, and laugh! link your steps with me, and circle in the delightful measure, now here, now there.
1.335: Salute the bride on her wedding-day with hymns and cries of joy. Come, you maids of Phrygia in fair raiment, sing my marriage
1.340:
with the husband fate ordains that I should wed.
Chorus Leader
1.341:
Hold the frantic maiden, royal mistress, lest with nimble foot she rush to the Argive army.
Hecuba
1.343: You god of fire, it is yours to light the bridal torch for men, but piteous is the flame you kindle here,
1.345: beyond my blackest expectation. Ah, my child! how little did I ever dream that such would be your marriage, a captive, and of Argos too! Give up the torch to me; you do not bear its blaze aright in your wild frantic course, nor have your afflictions left you in your sober senses,
1.350:
but still you are as frantic as before. Take in those torches, Trojan friends, and for her wedding madrigals weep your tears instead.
Cassandra
1.353: O mother, crown my head with victor’s wreaths; rejoice in my royal match; lead me
1.355: and if you find me unwilling at all, thrust me there by force; for if Loxias is indeed a prophet, Agamemnon, that famous king of the Achaeans, will find in me a bride more vexatious than Helen. For I will slay him and lay waste his home
1.360: to avenge my father’s and my brothers’ death. But let that go; I will not tell of that axe which shall sever my neck and the necks of others, or of the conflict ending in a mother’s death, which my marriage shall cause, nor of the overthrow of Atreus’ house.
1.365: But I, for all my frenzy, will so far rise above my frantic fit, that I will prove this city happier far than those Achaeans, who for the sake of one woman and one passion have lost a countless army in hunting Helen.
1.370: Their captain too, whom men call wise, has lost for what he hated most what most he prized, yielding to his brother for a woman’s sake—and she was willing and not taken by force—the joy he had of his own children in his home. For from the day that they landed upon Scamander’s strand, their doom began,
1.375: not for loss of stolen frontier nor yet for fatherland with high towers; whomever Ares took, those never saw their children again, nor were they shrouded for the tomb by hand of wife, but in a foreign land they lie. At home the case was still the same;
1.380: wives were dying widows, parents were left childless in their homes, having reared their sons for others, and none is left to make libations of blood upon the ground before their tombs. Truly to such praise as this their army can make an ample claim. It is better to pass by their shame in silence, nor may mine be the Muse
1.386: But the Trojans were dying, first for their fatherland, fairest fame to win; whomever the sword took, all these found friends to bear their bodies home and were laid to rest in the embrace of their native land,
1.390: their funeral rites all duly paid by duteous hands. And all such Phrygians as escaped the warrior’s death lived always day by day with wife and children by them, joys the Achaeans had left behind. As for Hector and his griefs, hear how the case stands;
1.395: he is dead and gone, but still his fame remains as bravest of the brave, and this was a result of the Achaeans’ coming; for had they remained at home, his worth would have gone unnoticed. And Paris married the daughter of Zeus, whereas, had he never done so, the alliance he made in his family would have been forgotten.
1.400: Whoever is wise should fly from making war; but if he come to this, a noble death will crown his city with glory, a coward’s end with shame. Therefore, mother, you should not pity your country or my bed, for this my marriage
1.405:
will destroy those whom you and I most hate.
Chorus Leader
1.406:
How sweetly at your own sad lot you smile, chanting a strain, which, in spite of you, may prove you wrong!
Talthybius
1.408: Had not Apollo turned your wits to maenad revelry, you would not for nothing have sent my chiefs
1.410: with such ominous predictions forth on their way. But, after all, these lofty minds, reputed wise, are nothing better than those that are held as nothing. For that mighty king of all Hellas, dear son of Atreus, has yielded to a passion
1.415: for this mad maiden of all others; though I am poor enough, yet would I never have chosen such a wife as this. As for you, since your senses are not whole, I give your taunts against Argos and your praise of Troy to the winds to carry away. Follow me now
1.420:
to the ships to grace the wedding of our chief. And you too follow, whenever the son of Laertes demands your presence, for you will serve a mistress most discreet, as all declare who came to Ilium.
Cassandra
1.424: A clever fellow, this servant! Why is it heralds hold
1.425: the name they do? All men unite in hating with one common hate the attendants of kings or governments. You say my mother shall come to the halls of Odysseus? Where then are Apollo’s words, so clear to me in their interpretation, which declare
1.430: that she shall die here? What else remains, I will not taunt her with. Unhappy Odysseus, he does not know the sufferings that await him; or how these ills I and my Phrygians endure shall one day seem to him precious as gold. For beyond the ten long years spent at Troy he shall drag out other ten and then come to his country all alone...
1.435: where dreadful Charybdis lurks in a narrow channel between the rocks; past Cyclops the savage shepherd, and Ligurian Circe who turns men to swine; shipwrecked often upon the salt sea-wave; longing to eat the lotus, and the sacred cattle of the sun,
1.440:
whose flesh shall utter in the days to come a human voice, bitter to Odysseus. In brief, he shall descend alive to Hades, and, though he shall escape the waters’ flood, yet shall he find a thousand troubles in his country when he arrives.
Cassandra
1.444: Enough! why do I recount the troubles of Odysseus?
1.445: Lead on at once, that I may wed my husband for his home in Hades’ halls. Base you are, and basely shall you be buried, in the dead of night when day is done, you captain of that army of Danaids, who think so proudly of your fortune! Yes, and the rocky chasm with its flood of wintry waters shall give my corpse cast forth in nakedness to wild beasts to make their meal upon,
1.450: near my husband’s tomb, I, Apollo’s servant. O garlands of that god most dear to me! farewell, you mystic symbols! I here resign your feasts, my joy in days gone by. Go, I tear you from my body, that, while yet mine honor is intact, I may give them to the rushing winds to waft to you, my prince of prophecy!
1.455: Where is that general’s ship? Where must I go to take my place there? Lose no further time in watching for a favoring breeze to fill your sails, doomed as you are to carry from this land one of the three avenging spirits. Fare you well, mother! dry your tears. O dear country! my brothers below the earth and my own father,
1.460:
it will not be long before you shall welcome me; victory shall crown my advent among the dead, when I have overthrown the home of our destroyers, the house of the sons of Atreus.
Chorus Leader
1.462: You guardians of the grey-haired Hecuba, see how your mistress is sinking speechless to the ground! Take hold of her! will you let her fall,
1.465:
you worthless slaves? lift up again, from where it lies, her withered body.
Hecuba
1.466: Leave me, my maidens—unwelcome service does not grow welcome—lying where I fell; my sufferings now, my troubles past, afflictions yet to come, all claim this lowly posture. Gods of heaven! small help I find in calling such allies,
1.470: yet is there something in the form of invoking heaven, whenever we fall on evil days. First I will sing of my former blessings; so shall I inspire the greater pity for my present woes. Born to royal estate and wedded to a royal lord,
1.475: I was the mother of a race of gallant sons; no mere ciphers they, but Phrygia’s chiefest pride, children such as no Trojan or Hellenic or barbarian mother ever had to boast. All these have I seen slain by the spear of Hellas,
1.480: and at their tombs have I shorn off my hair; with these my eyes I saw their father, Priam, butchered on his own hearth, and my city captured, nor did others bring this bitter news to me. The maidens I brought up
1.485: to see chosen for some marriage high, for strangers have I reared them, and seen them snatched away. Nevermore can I hope to be seen by them, nor shall my eyes behold them ever in the days to come. And last, to crown my misery,
1.490: I shall be brought to Hellas, a slave in my old age. And there the tasks that least befit the evening of my life will they impose on me, Hector’s mother, to watch their gates and keep the keys, or bake their bread, and on the ground instead of my royal bed
1.495: lay down my shrunken limbs, with tattered rags about my wasted frame, a shameful garb for those who once were prosperous. Ah, woe is me! and this is what I bear and am to bear for one woman’s marriage!
1.500: O my daughter, O Cassandra! whom gods have summoned to their frenzied train, how cruel the lot that ends your virgin days! And you, Polyxena! my child of sorrow, where, oh! where are you? None of all the many sons and daughters I have born comes to aid a wretched mother.
1.505: Why then raise me up? What hope is left us? Guide me, who before trod so daintily the streets of Troy, but now am a slave, to a bed upon the ground, near some rocky ridge, that from there I may cast myself down and perish, after I have wasted my body with weeping.
1.510:
Of all the prosperous crowd, count none a happy man before he die.
Chorus
1.512: Sing me, Muse, a tale of Troy, a funeral dirge in strains unheard as yet, with tears;
1.515: for now I will uplift for Troy a piteous chant, telling how I met my doom and fell a wretched captive to the Argives by reason of a four-footed beast that moved on wheels, when Achaea’s sons left at our.gates that horse,
1.520: loud rumbling to the sky, with its trappings of gold and its freight of warriors; and our people cried out as they stood upon the rocky citadel, Up now, you whose toil is over,
1.525: and drag this sacred image to the shrine of the Zeus-born maiden, goddess of our Ilium! Forth from his house came every youth and every grey-head too; and with songs of joy
1.530:
they took the fatal snare within.
Chorus
1.531: Then hastened all the race of Phrygia to the gates, to make the goddess a present of an Argive band ambushed in the polished mountain-pine,
1.535: Dardania’s ruin, a welcome gift to be to her, the virgin queen of deathless steeds; and with nooses of cord they dragged it, as it had been a ship’s dark hull, to the stone-built
1.540: temple of the goddess Pallas, and set it on that floor so soon to drink our country’s blood. But, as they labored and made merry, came on the pitchy night; loud the Libyan flute was sounding,
1.545: and Phrygian songs awoke, while maidens beat the ground with airy foot, uplifting their glad song; and in the halls a blaze of torchlight shed its flickering shadows
1.551: In that hour around the house I was singing as I danced to that maiden of the hills, the child of Zeus;
1.555: when there rang along the town a cry of death which filled the homes of Troy, and babies in terror clung about their mothers’ skirts,
1.560: as forth from their ambush came the warrior-band, the handiwork of maiden Pallas. Soon the altars ran with Phrygian blood, and desolation reigned over every bed where young men lay beheaded,
1.565:
a glorious crown for Hellas won, for her, the nurse of youth, but for our Phrygian fatherland a bitter grief.
Chorus Leader
1.568: Hecuba, do you see Andromache advancing here on a foreign chariot?
1.570: and with her, clasped to her throbbing breast, is her dear Astyanax, Hector’s child. Where are you being carried, unhappy wife, mounted on that chariot, side by side with Hector’s brazen arms and Phrygian spoils of war,
1.575:
with which Achilles’ son will deck the shrines of Phthia on his return from Troy?
Andromache
1.577:
My Achaean masters are leading me away.
Hecuba
1.578:
Ah me!
Andromache
Why do you in note of woe utter the dirge that is mine?
Hecuba
1.579:
Alas—
Andromache
For these sorrows—
Hecuba
1.580:
O Zeus—
Andromache
And for this calamity.
Hecuba
1.581:
O my children!
Andromache
Our day is past.
Hecuba
1.582:
Joy is gone, Troy is gone.
Andromache
1.583:
Unhappy!
Hecuba
For my gallant sons
Andromache
1.584:
Alas!
Hecuba
Alas indeed, for my
Andromache
1.585:
Misery!
Hecuba
Piteous the fate
Andromache
1.586:
Of our city,
Hecuba
Smouldering in the smoke.
Andromache
1.587:
Come to me, my husband, come to me!
Hecuba
1.588:
Ah, hapless wife! you call on my son who lies in the tomb.
Andromache
1.591:
Oh, you, who before made the Achaeans grieve, eldest of the sons I bore to Priam, take me to your rest in Hades’ halls!
Andromache
1.595:
These great griefs—
Hecuba
Unhappy one, bitter these woes to bear.
Andromache
1.596:
Our city ruined—
Hecuba
And sorrow to sorrow added.
Andromache
1.597: Through the will of angry heaven, since the day that son of yours escaped death, he that for a hated bride brought destruction on the Trojan citadel. There lie the gory corpses of the slain by the shrine of Pallas for vultures to carry off;
1.600:
and Troy has come to slavery’s yoke.
Hecuba
1.601:
O my country, O unhappy land—
Andromache
I weep for you now left behind.
Hecuba
1.602:
Now do you behold your piteous end.
Andromache
And you, my house, where I gave birth.
Hecuba
1.603: O my children! bereft of her city as your mother is, she now is losing you. Oh, what mourning and what sorrow!...
1.605:
oh, what endless streams of tears in our houses! The dead alone forget their griefs.
Chorus Leader
1.608:
What sweet relief to sufferers it is to weep, to mourn, lament, and chant the dirge that tells of grief!
Andromache
1.610:
Do you see this, mother of that man, Hector, who once laid low in battle many a son of Argos?
Hecuba
1.612:
I see that it is heaven’s way to exalt what men accounted nothing, and ruin what they most esteemed.
Andromache
1.614: Hence with my child as booty am I borne; the noble
1.615:
are brought to slavery—a bitter change.
Hecuba
1.616:
This is necessity’s grim law; it was just now that Cassandra was torn with brutal violence from my arms.
Andromache
1.618:
Alas, alas! it seems a second Aias has appeared to wrong your daughter; but there are other ills for you.
Hecuba
1.620:
Yes, beyond all count or measure are my sorrows; evil vies with evil in the struggle to be first.
Andromache
1.622:
Your daughter Polyxena is dead, slain at Achilles’ tomb, an offering to his lifeless corpse.
Hecuba
1.624: O woe is me! This is that riddle Talthybius
1.625:
long ago told me, a truth obscurely uttered.
Andromache
1.626:
I saw her myself; so I alighted from the chariot, and covered her corpse with a mantle, and struck upon my breast.
Hecuba
1.628:
Alas! my child, for your unhallowed sacrifice! and yet again, alas! for your shameful death!
Andromache
1.630:
Her death was even as it was, and yet that death of hers was after all a happier fate than my life.
Hecuba
1.632:
Death and life are not the same, my child; the one is annihilation, the other keeps a place for hope.
Andromache
1.634: Hear, O mother of children! give ear to what I urge so well,
1.635: that I may cheer my drooping spirit. It is all one, I say, never to have been born and to be dead, and better far is death than life with misery. For the dead feel no sorrow any more and know no grief; but he who has known prosperity and has fallen on evil days
1.640: feels his spirit straying from the scene of former joys. Now that child of yours is dead as though she never had seen the light, and little she knows of her calamity; whereas I, who aimed at a fair repute, though I won a higher lot than most, yet missed my luck in life.
1.645: For all that stamps the wife a woman chaste, I strove to do in Hector’s home. In the first place, whether there is a slur upon a woman, or whether there is not, the very fact of her not staying at home brings in its train an evil name;
1.650: therefore I gave up any longing to do so, and stayed within my house; nor would I admit indoors the clever gossip women love, but conscious of a heart that told an honest tale I was content. And ever would I keep a silent tongue and modest eye before my husband;
1.655: and well I knew where I might rule him, and where it was best to yield.
1.657: Report of this has reached the Achaean army, and proved my ruin; for when I was taken captive, Achilles’ son would have me
1.660: as his wife, and I must serve in the house of murderers. And if I set aside my love for Hector, and open my heart to this new lord, I shall appear a traitress to the dead, while, if I hate him, I shall incur my master’s displeasure.
1.665: And yet they say a single night removes a woman’s dislike for her husband; I despise the woman who, when she has lost her former husband, transfers her love by marrying another. Not even the horse, if parted from her stablemate,
1.670: will cheerfully draw the yoke; and animals have neither speech nor sense to help them, and are by nature man’s inferiors.
1.673: O my dear Hector, in you I found a husband amply dowered with wisdom, noble birth and fortune, a brave man and a mighty;
1.675: while you took from my father’s house a spotless bride, yourself the first to make this maiden wife. But now death has claimed you, and I am soon to sail to Hellas, a captive doomed to wear the yoke of slavery. Has not then the dead Polyxena,
1.680:
for whom you wail, less evil to bear than I? I have not so much as hope, the last resource of every human heart, nor do I beguile myself with dreams of future bliss, the very thought of which is sweet.
Chorus Leader
1.684: You are in the same plight as I; your lamentations
1.685:
for yourself remind me of my own sad case.
Hecuba
1.686: I never yet have set foot on a ship’s deck, though I have seen such things in pictures and know of them from hearsay. Now sailors, if there comes a storm of moderate force, are all eagerness to save themselves by toil;
1.690: one stands at the tiller, another sets himself to work the sheets, a third meanwhile is baling out the ship; but if tempestuous waves arise to overwhelm them, they yield to fortune and commit themselves to the driving billows. Even so I, by reason of my countless troubles,
1.695: am speechless and forbear to say a word; for this surge of misery from the gods is too strong for me. Cease, my darling child, to speak of Hector’s fate; no tears of yours can save him; honor your present master,
1.700: offering your sweet nature as the bait to win him. If you do this, you will cheer your friends as well as yourself and you shalt rear my Hector’s child to lend stout aid to Ilium, that so your children in the aftertime
1.705:
may build her up again, and our city yet be established. But our talk must take a different turn; who is this Achaean servant I see coming here again, sent to tell us of some new design?
Talthybius
1.709: You that once were the wife of Hector, bravest of the Phrygians,
1.710:
do not hate me, for I am not a willing messenger. The Danaids and sons of Pelops both command—
Andromache
1.712:
What is it? your prelude bodes evil news.
Talthybius
1.713:
It is decreed your son is—how can I tell my news?
Andromache
1.714:
Surely not to have a different master from me?
Talthybius
1.715:
None of all Achaea’s chiefs shall ever lord it over him.
Andromache
1.716:
Is it their will to leave him here, a remnant of Phrygia’s race?
Talthybius
1.717:
I know no words to break the sorrow lightly to you.
Andromache
1.718:
I thank you for your consideration, unless indeed you have good news to tell.
Talthybius
1.719:
They mean to slay your son; there is my hateful message to you.
Andromache
1.720:
Oh me! this is worse tidings than my forced marriage.
Talthybius
1.721:
So spoke Odysseus to the assembled Hellenes, and his word prevails.
Andromache
1.722:
Oh, once again alas! there is no measure in the woes I bear.
Talthybius
1.723:
He said they should not rear so brave a father’s son.
Andromache
1.724:
May such counsels prevail about children of his!
Talthybius
1.725: He must be thrown from Troy’s battlements. Let it be so, and you will show more wisdom; do not cling to him, but bear your sorrows with heroic heart, nor in your weakness think that you are strong. For nowhere do you have any help; consider this you must;
1.730: your husband and your city are no more, so you are in our power, and I alone am match enough for one woman; therefore I would not see you bent on strife, or any course to bring you shame or hate, nor would I hear you rashly curse the Achaeans.
1.735:
For if you say anything to anger the army, this child will find no burial nor pity either. But if you hold your peace and with composure take your fate, you will not leave his corpse unburied, and you yourself will find more favor with the Achaeans.
Andromache
1.740: My dearest! my own sweet child and priceless treasure! your death the foe demands, and you must leave your wretched mother. That which saves the lives of others, proves your destruction—your father’s nobility; to you your father’s valiancy has proved no gift.
1.745: O my unlucky bed and marriage, that brought me once to Hector’s home, hoping to be the mother of a son that should rule over Asia’s fruitful fields instead of serving as a victim to the Danaids! Do you weep, my child? do you know your hapless fate?
1.750: Why clutch me with your hands and to my garment cling, nestling like a tender chick beneath my wing? Hector will not rise from the earth and come gripping his famous spear to bring you salvation; no kinsman of your father appears, nor might of Phrygian hosts;
1.755: one dreadful headlong leap from the dizzy height and you will dash out your life with none to pity you! Oh to clasp your tender limbs, a mother’s fondest joy! Oh to breathe your fragrant breath! In vain it seems these breasts did suckle you, wrapped in your swaddling-clothes;
1.760: all for nothing I used to toil and wear myself away! Kiss your mother now for the last time, nestle to her that bore you, twine your arms about my neck and join your lips to mine! O you Hellenes, cunning to devise new forms of cruelty,
1.765: why slay this child who never wronged any? You daughter of Tyndareus, you are no child of Zeus, but I say you were born of many a father, first of some evil demon, next of Envy, then of Murder and of Death, and every horror that the earth breeds.
1.770: That Zeus was never father of yours I boldly do assert, bane as you have been to many a Hellene and barbarian too. Destruction catch you! Those fair eyes of yours have brought a shameful ruin on the fields of glorious Troy. Take the child and bear him hence, hurl him down if you wish,
1.775:
then feast upon his flesh! It is the gods’ will we perish, and I cannot ward the deadly stroke from my child. Hide me and my misery; cast me into the ship’s hold; for it is to a fair wedding I am going, now that I have lost my child!
Chorus Leader
1.780:
Unhappy Troy! you have lost countless men for the sake of one woman and her hateful bed.
Talthybius
1.782: Come, child, leave fond embracing of your woeful mother, and mount the high coronal of your ancestral towers,
1.785:
there to draw your parting breath, as is ordained. Take him away. His should the duty be to do such herald’s work, whose heart knows no pity and who loves ruthlessness more than my soul does. Exeunt Andromache and Talthybius with Astyanax.
Hecuba
1.790: O child, son of my hapless boy, an unjust fate robs me and your mother of your life. How is it with me? What can I do for you, luckless one? For you I strike upon my head and beat my breast, my only gift;
1.795:
for that is in my power. Woe for my city! woe for you! What sorrow do we not have? What is wanting now to our utter and immediate ruin?
Chorus
1.799: O Telamon, King of Salamis, the feeding-ground of bees,
1.800: who have your home in a seagirt isle that lies near the holy hills where first Athena made the grey olive branch to appear, a crown for heavenly heads and a glory to happy Athens, you came, you came in knightly brotherhood
1.805:
with that great archer, Alcmena’s son, to sack our city Ilium, in days gone by,;
Chorus
1.809: When he led the chosen flower of Hellas, vexed
1.810: for the steeds, and at the fair stream of Simois he stayed his sea-borne ship and fastened cables to the stern, and forth from the ship he took the bow his hand could deftly shoot, to be the doom of Laomedon; and with the ruddy breath of fire
1.815:
he wasted the masonry squared by Phoebus’ line and chisel, and sacked the land of Troy; so twice in two attacks has the blood-stained spear destroyed Dardania’s walls.
Chorus
1.820: In vain, it seems, you Phrygian boy pacing with dainty step among your golden chalices, do you fill high the cup of Zeus, a lovely service;
1.825: the land of your birth is being consumed by fire. The shore re-echoes to our cries; and, as a bird bewails its young,
1.830: so we bewail our husbands or our children, or our old mothers. The dew-fed springs where you bathed, the course where you trained,
1.835:
are now no more; but you beside the throne of Zeus are sitting with a calm, sweet smile upon your fair young face, while the spear of Hellas has destroyed the land of Priam.
Chorus
1.840: Ah! Love, Love, who once sought these Dardanian halls, deep-seated in the hearts of heavenly gods, how high you made Troy to tower in those days,
1.845: allying her with deities! But I will cease to urge reproaches against Zeus; for white-winged dawn, whose light is dear to man,
1.850: turned a baleful eye upon our land and watched the ruin of our citadel, though she had within her bridal bower a husband to give her children, from this land,
1.855:
whom once a chariot of gold spangled stars caught up and carried there, great source of hope to his native country; but all the love the gods once had for Troy is passed away.
Menelaus
1.860: Hail! you radiant flare of the sun, by whose fair light I now shall capture her that was my wife, Helen; for I am that Menelaus, who has toiled so hard, I and Achaea’s army. I came to Troy, not so much as men suppose
1.865: for, the sake of a woman, but to punish the man who from my house stole my wife, traitor to my hospitality. But he, by the gods’ will, has paid the penalty, ruined, and his country too, by the spear of Hellas. And I have come to bear that wretched woman away—wife I have no mind
1.870: to call her, though she once was mine—for now she is one among the other Trojan women who share these tents as captives. For they, the very men who who toiled to take her with the spear, have granted to me to slay her,
1.875: or, if I will, to spare and carry back with me to Argos. Now my purpose is not to put her to death in Troy, but to carry her to Hellas in my sea-borne ship, and then surrender her to death, a recompense to all whose friends were slain in Ilium.
1.880:
Ho! my servants, enter the tent, and drag her out to me by her hair foul with murder; and when a favoring breeze shall blow, to Hellas will we convey her.
Hecuba
1.884: O you that do support the earth and rest thereupon,
1.885:
whoever you are, a riddle past our knowledge! Zeus, owhether you are natural necessity, or man’s intellect, to you I pray; for, though you tread over a noiseless path, all your dealings with mankind are guided by justice.
Menelaus
1.889:
What is this? Strange the prayer you offer to the gods!
Hecuba
1.890:
I thank you, Menelaus, if you will slay that wife of yours. Yet shun the sight of her, lest she strike you with longing. For she ensnares the eyes of men, overthrows their towns, and burns their houses, so potent are her witcheries! Well I know her; so do you and those her victims too.
Helen
1.895: Menelaus! this prelude well may fill me with alarm; for I am taken with violence by your servants’ hands and brought before these tents. Still, though I am sure you hate me, yet I want to inquire
1.900:
what you and Hellas have decided about my life.
Menelaus
1.901:
To judge your case required no great exactness; the army with one consent, that army whom you wronged, handed you over to me to die.
Helen
1.903:
May I answer this decision, proving that my death, if I am to die, will be unjust?
Menelaus
1.905:
I came not to argue, but to slay you.
Hecuba
1.906: Hear her, Menelaus; let her not die for want of that, and let me answer her again, for you know nothing of her villainies in Troy; and the whole case, if summed up,
1.910:
will insure her death against all chance of an escape.
Menelaus
1.911:
This gift needs leisure; still, if she wishes to speak, she may. Yet I will grant her this because of your words, that she may hear them, and not for her own sake.
Helen
1.913: Perhaps you will not answer me, from counting me a foe,
1.915: whether my words seem good or ill. Yet I will put my charges and yours over against each other, and then reply to the accusations I suppose you will advance against me. First, then, that woman was the author of these troubles
1.920: by giving birth to Paris; next, old Priam ruined Troy and me, because he did not slay his child Alexander, baleful semblance of a fire-brand, long ago. Hear what followed. This man was to judge the claims of three rival goddesses;
1.925: so Pallas offered him command of all the Phrygians, and the destruction of Hellas; Hera promised he should spread his dominion over Asia, and the utmost bounds of Europe, if he would decide for her; but Cypris spoke in rapture of my loveliness,
1.930: and promised him this gift, if she should have the preference over those two for beauty. Now mark the inference I deduce from this; Cypris won the day over the goddesses, and thus far has my marriage proved of benefit to Hellas, that you are not subject to barbarian rule, neither vanquished in the strife, nor yet by tyrants crushed.
1.935: What Hellas gained, was ruin to me, sold for my beauty, and now I am reproached for that which should have set a crown upon my head. But you will say I am silent on the real matter at hand, how it was I started forth and left your house by stealth.
1.940: With no small goddess at his side he came, my evil genius, call him Alexander or Paris, as you will; and you, villain, left him behind in your house, and sailed away from Sparta to the land of Crete.
1.945: Enough of this! For all that followed I must question myself, not you; what thought led me to follow the stranger from your house, traitress to my country and my home? Punish the goddess, show yourself more mighty even than Zeus, who, though he lords it over the other gods,
1.950: is her slave; therefore I may well be pardoned. Still, from this you might draw a specious argument against me; when Paris died, and earth concealed his corpse, I should have left his house and sought the Argive fleet, since my marriage was no longer in the hands of gods.
1.955: That was what I was eager to do; and the warders on the towers and watchmen on the walls can bear me witness, for often they found me seeking to let myself down stealthily by cords from the battlements
1.960: . How then, my lord, could I be justly put to death... by you, with any show of right, seeing that he wedded me against my will, and those my other natural gifts have served a bitter slavery, instead of leading on to triumph? If it is your will indeed
1.965:
to master gods, that very wish displays your folly.
Chorus Leader
1.966:
O my royal mistress, defend your children’s and your country’s cause, bringing to nothing her persuasive arguments, for she pleads well in spite of all her villainy; this is monstrous!
Hecuba
1.969: First I will take up the cause of those goddesses,
1.970: and prove how she perverts the truth. For I can never believe that Hera or the maiden Pallas would have been guilty of such folly, the one to sell her Argos to barbarians, or that Pallas ever would make her Athens subject to the Phrygians,
1.975: coming as they did in mere wanton sport to Ida to contest the palm of beauty. For why should goddess Hera set her heart so much on such a prize? Was it to win a nobler lord than Zeus? or was Athena hunting down among the gods a husband,
1.980: she who in her dislike of marriage won from her father the gift of remaining unwed? Do not seek to impute folly to the goddesses, in the attempt to adorn your own sin; never will you persuade the wise. Next you have said—what well may make men jeer—that Cypris came with my son to the house of Menelaus.
1.985: Could she not have stayed quietly in heaven and brought you and Amyclae as well to Ilium?
1.987: No! my son was exceedingly handsome, and when you saw him your mind straight became your Aphrodite; for every folly that men commit, they lay upon this goddess,
1.990: and rightly does her name begin the word for senselessness; so when you caught sight of him in gorgeous foreign clothes, ablaze with gold, your senses utterly forsook you. Yes, for in Argos you had moved in simple state, but, once free of Sparta,
1.995: it was your hope to deluge by your lavish outlay Phrygia’s town, that flowed with gold; nor was the palace of Menelaus rich enough for your luxury to riot in.
1.998: Enough of this! My son carried you off by force, so you say; what Spartan saw this? what cry for help
1.1000: did you ever raise, though Castor was still alive, a vigorous youth, and his brother also, not yet among the stars? Then when you had come to Troy, and the Argives were on your track, and the mortal combat had begun, whenever tidings came to you of
1.1005: Menelaus’ prowess, you would praise him, to grieve my son, because he had so powerful a rival in his love; but if the Trojans prospered, Menelaus was nothing to you. Your eye was fixed on Fortune, and by such practice you were careful to follow in her steps, careless of virtue’s cause.
1.1010: And then you assert that you tried to let yourself down from the towers by stealth with twisted cords, as if unwilling to stay? Where were you ever found fastening the noose about your neck, or whetting the knife, as a noble wife would have done in regret for her former husband?
1.1015: And yet often I advised you saying, Get away, daughter; my sons will take other brides, and I will belp you to steal away, and convey you to the Achaean fleet; oh, end the strife between us and Hellas! But this was bitter to you.
1.1020: For you were wantoning in Alexander’s house, wishing to have obeisance done you by barbarians. Yes, it was a proud time for you; and now after all this you have adorned yourself, and come forth and have dared to appear under the same sky as your husband, revolting wretch!
1.1025: Better if you had come in tattered raiment, cowering humbly in terror, with hair cut short, and if your feeling for your past sins were one of shame rather than effrontery. Menelaus, hear the conclusion of my argument;
1.1030:
crown Hellas by slaying her as she deserves, and establish this law for all other women: death to every one who betrays her husband.

1.1033: Avenge yourself, Menelaus, on your wife, as is worthy of your home and ancestors,
1.1035:
clear yourself from the reproach of effeminacy at the lips of Hellas, and let your foes see your spirit.

Oh, by your knees, I implore you, do not impute that heaven-sent affliction to me, or slay me; forgive me!

1.1045:
on their behalf, and for my children’s sake, I entreat you.
Menelaus
1.1046:
Peace, revered lady; to her I pay no heed. I bid my servants take her away, aboard the ship, in which she is to sail.
Hecuba

Oh never let her set foot within the same ship as you.
Menelaus
1.1050:
Why is that? is she heavier than before?
Hecuba
1.1051:
The one who loves once, must love always.
Menelaus
1.1052: Why, that depends how those we love are minded. But your wish shall be granted; she shall not set foot upon the same ship with me; for your advice is surely sound;

1.1060: So then you have delivered into Achaea’s hand, O Zeus, your shrine in Ilium and your fragrant altar, the offerings of burnt sacrifice with smoke of myrrh to heaven uprising,
1.1065: and holy Pergamos, and glens of Ida tangled with the ivy’s growth, where rills of melting snow pour down their flood, a holy sun-lit land that bounds the world
1.1070:
and takes the god’s first rays!
Chorus
1.1071: Gone are your sacrifices! gone the dancer’s cheerful shout! gone the vigils of the gods as night closed in! your images of carven gold are now no more;
1.1075: and Phrygia’s holy festivals, twelve times a year, at each full moon, are ended now. It is this, it is this that fills me with anxious thought whether you, lord, seated on the sky, your heavenly throne, care at all that my city is destroyed,
1.1080:
a prey to the furious fiery blast.
Chorus
1.1081: Ah! my loved husband, you are a wandering spectre;
1.1085: unwashed, unburied lies your corpse, while over the sea the ship sped by wings will carry me to Argos, land of steeds, where stand Cyclopian walls of stone reaching to heaven. There in the gate the children gather,
1.1090: and weep their piteous lamentation; they cry, they cry: Mother, alas! torn from your sight, the Achaeans bear me away from you to their dark ship
1.1095:
to row me over the deep to sacred Salamis or to the hill on the Isthmus, that overlooks two seas, the seat that holds the gates of Pelops.
Chorus
1.1100: Oh may the sacred blazing thunderbolt of the Aegean, hurled in might, smite the ship of Menelaus full in the middle, on its way in mid-sea,
1.1105: since he is carrying me away in bitter sorrow from the shores of Ilium to be a slave in Hellas, while the daughter of Zeus still keeps her golden mirrors, delight of maidens’ hearts.
1.1110: Never may he reach his home in Laconia or his father’s hearth and home, nor come to the town of Pitane or the temple of the goddess with the gates of bronze, having taken as his captive the one whose marriage brought disgrace on Hellas through its length and breadth and woful anguish
1.1115:
on the streams of Simois!
Enter Talthybius and attendants, bearing the corpse of Astyanax on Hector’s shield. Chorus Leader
1.1118: All me! ah me! new troubles fall on my country, to take the place of those that still are fresh! Behold,
1.1120:
you hapless wives of Troy, the corpse of Astyanax, whom the Danaids have cruelly slain by hurling him from the battlements.
Talthybius
1.1123: Hecuba, one ship alone delays its plashing oars,
1.1125: and it is soon to sail to the shores of Phthia freighted with the remnant of the spoils of Achilles’ son; for Neoptolemus is already out at sea, having heard that new calamities have befallen Peleus, for Acastus, son of Pelias, has banished him from the realm. Therefore he is gone, too quick to indulge in any delay,
1.1130: and with him goes Andromache, who drew many tears from me when she set out from the land, wailing her country and crying her farewell to Hector’s tomb. And she begged her master leave to bury this poor dead child of Hector
1.1135: who breathed his last when hurled from the turrets; entreating too that he would not carry this shield, the terror of the Achaeans—this shield with plates of brass with which his father would gird himself—to the home of Peleus or to the same bridal bower where she, Andromache,
1.1140: the mother of this corpse, would be wed, a bitter sight to her, but let her bury the child in it instead of in a coffin of cedar or a tomb of stone, and to your hands commit the corpse that you may deck it with robes and garlands as best you can with your present means;
1.1145: for she is far away and her master’s haste prevented her from burying the child herself. So we, when you have decked the corpse, will heap the earth above and set upon it a spear; but do you with your best speed perform your allotted task;
1.1150: one toil however I have already spared you, for I crossed Scamander’s stream and bathed the corpse and cleansed its wounds. But now I will go to dig a grave for hiin, that our united efforts
1.1155:
shortening our task may speed our ship towards home. Exit Talthybius.
Hecuba
1.1156: Place the shield upon the ground, Hector’s shield so deftly rounded, a piteous sight, a bitter grief for me to see. O you Achaeans, more reason have you to boast of your prowess than your wisdom. Why have you in terror of this child
1.1160: been guilty of a murder never matched before? Did you fear that some day he would rear again the fallen walls of Troy? It seems then you were nothing after all, when, though Hector’s fortunes in the war were prosperous and he had ten thousand other arms to back him, we still were daily overmatched; and yet, now that our city is taken and every Phrygian slain,
1.1165: you fear a tender child like this! I do not commend the fear of one who fears but never yet has reasoned out the cause.
1.1168: Ah! my beloved, yours is a piteous death indeed! If you had died for your city, when you had tasted of the sweets of manhood, of marriage, and of godlike power over others,
1.1170: then were you blessed, if anything here is blessed. But now after one glimpse, one dream of them, you know them no more, my child, and have no joy of them, though heir to all. Ah, poor child! how sadly have your own father’s walls, those towers that Loxias reared, shorn from your head
1.1175: the locks your mother fondled, and so often caressed, from which through fractured bones the face of murder grins—briefly to dismiss my shocking theme. O hands, how sweet the likeness you retain of his father, and yet you lie Iimp in your sockets before me!
1.1180: Dear mouth, so often full of words of pride, death has closed you, and you have not kept the promise you made, when nestling in my robe, Ah, mother, many a lock of my hair I will cut off for you, and to your tomb will lead my troops of friends, taking a fond farewell of you.
1.1185: But now I am not to be buried by you, but you, the younger one, a wretched corpse, are buried by me, on whom old age has come with loss of home and children. Ah me, those kisses numberless, the nurture that I gave to you, those sleepless nights—they all are lost! What shall the bard inscribe upon your tomb about you?
1.1190: Argives once for fear of him slew this child? Foul shame should that inscription be to Hellas. O child, though you have no part in all your father’s wealth, yet shall you have his brazen shield in which to find a tomb. Ah! shield that kept safe the comely arm of Hector,
1.1195: now have you lost your valiant keeper! How fair upon your handle lies his imprint, and on the rim that circles around are marks of sweat, that trickled often from Hector’s brow as he pressed it against his beard in battle’s stress.
1.1200: Come, bring forth, from such store as you have, adornment for the hapless dead, for fortune gives no chance now for lovely offerings; yet of such as I possess, you shall receive these gifts. He is a foolish mortal who thinks his luck secure and so rejoices; for fortune, like a madman in her moods,
1.1205:
springs towards this man, then towards that; and no one ever experiences the same unchanging luck.
Chorus Leader
1.1207:
Look! all is ready and they are bringing at your bidding from the spoils of Troy adornment to put upon the dead.
Hecuba
1.1209: Ah! my child, it is not as victor over your comrades
1.1210: with horse or bow—customs Troy esteems, without pursuing them to excess—that Hector’s mother decks you now with ornaments from the store that once was yours, though now Helen, whom the gods abhor, has bereft you of your own, yes, and robbed you
1.1215:
of your life and caused your house to perish root and branch.
Chorus
1.1216:
Woe! thrice woe! my heart is touched, and you the cause, my mighty prince in days now passed!
Hecuba
1.1218: About your body now I swathe this Phrygian robe of honor, which should have clad you on your marriage-day,
1.1220: wedded to the noblest of Asia’s daughters. You too, dear shield of Hector, victorious parent of countless triumphs past, accept your crown, for though you share the dead child’s tomb, death cannot touch you; for you merit honors far beyond those arms
1.1225:
that the crafty villain Odysseus won.
Chorus
1.1226:
Alas! alas! you, O child, shall earth take to her breast, a cause for bitter weeping. Mourn, you mother!
Hecuba
1.1230:
Wail for the dead.
Hecuba
Woe is me!
Chorus
1.1231:
Woe indeed for your unending sorrow!
Hecuba
1.1232:
Your wounds in part I will bind up with bandages, a wretched healer in name alone, without reality; but for the rest your father must look to that among the dead.
Chorus
1.1235:
Smite, oh smite upon your head with frequent blow of hand. Woe is me!
Hecuba
1.1239:
Speak out, Hecuba, the word that was on your lips.
Hecuba
1.1240: It seems the only things that heaven concerns itself about are my troubles and Troy hateful in their eyes above all other cities. In vain did we sacrifice to them. But if the god had not caught us in his grip and plunged us headlong beneath the earth, we should have been unheard of, and not ever sung in Muses’ songs,
1.1245: furnishing to bards of after-days a subject for their minstrelsy. Go, bury now in his poor tomb the dead, wreathed all duly as befits a corpse. And yet I think it makes little difference to the dead, if they get a gorgeous funeral;
1.1250:
but this is a cause of idle pride to the living. The corpse is carried off to burial.
Chorus Leader
1.1251: Alas! for your unhappy mother, who over your corpse has closed the high hopes of her life! Born of a noble stock, counted most happy in your lot,
1.1255:
ah! what a tragic death is yours! Ha! who are those I see on yonder pinnacles darting to and fro with flaming torches in their hands? Some new calamity wiII soon alight on Troy.
Soldiers are seen on the battlements of Troy, torch in hand.
Talthybius
1.1260: You captains whose allotted task it is to fire this town of Priam, to you I speak. No longer keep the fire-brand idle in your hands, but launch the flame, that when we have destroyed the city of Ilium we may set forth in gladness on our homeward voyage from Troy.
1.1265: And you, you sons of Troy, to let my orders take at once a double form—start for the Achaean ships for your departure from the land, as soon as the leaders of the army blow loud and clear upon the trumpet. And you, unhappy grey-haired lady,
1.1270:
follow; for here come servants from Odysseus to fetch you, for to him you are assigned by lot to be a slave far from your country.

1.1272: Ah, woe is me! This surely is the last, the utmost limit, of all my sorrows; I go forth from my land; my city is ablaze with flame.

1.1280:
to slavery. O gods! Yet why do I call on the gods? They did not hearken ever before to our call. Come, let us rush into the flames, for to die with my country in its blazing ruin would be a noble death for me.

1.1284: Your sorrows drive you frantic, poor lady.
1.1285:
Go, lead her away, make no delay, for you must deliver her into the hand of Odysseus, conveying to him his prize.

1.1287: Woe! oh woe! Son of Cronos, prince of Phrygia, father of our race,

Chorus

1.0: On the borders of Argolis. Peasant
1.1: O ancient plain of land, the streams of Inachus, from which king Agamemnon once mounted war on a thousand ships and sailed to the land of Troy. After he had slain Priam, the ruler of Ilium,
1.5: and captured the famous city of Dardanus, he came here to Argos and set up on the high temples many spoils of the barbarians. And in Troy he was successful; but at home he died by the guile of his wife Clytemnestra
1.10: and the hand of Aegisthus, son of Thyestes. And he left behind the ancient scepter of Tantalus, and is dead; but Aegisthus rules the land, possessing Agamemnon’s wife, the daughter of Tyndareus. Now as for those whom he left in his house when he sailed to Troy,
1.15: his son Orestes and his young daughter Electra: when Orestes was about to die at the hand of Aegisthus, his father’s old servant stole him away and gave him to Strophius to bring up in the land of the Phocians. Electra stayed in her father’s house,
1.20: and when she came to the blooming season of youth, the foremost suitors of the land of Hellas asked for her in marriage. But Aegisthus feared she might bear to some chieftain a son who would avenge Agamemnon, and so he kept her at home and did not betroth her to any bridegroom.
1.25: When even this filled him with great fear, that she might secretly bear children to some noble lord, Aegisthus planned to kill her, but her mother, although cruel at heart, rescued her from his hand. For she had a pretext for having slain her husband,
1.30: but she feared that she would be despised for the murder of her children. So then, for these reasons, Aegisthus devised such a scheme: he promised gold to anyone who should kill Agamemnon’s son, who had left the country as an exile, while Electra he gave
1.35: in marriage to me. My ancestors were Mycenaeans; in that respect at least I am not to blame. My family was noble in race but poor in money—which is the ruin of good birth. He gave her to a powerless man so that his fear might lose its power.
1.40: For if some man of high position got her, he would have roused the sleeping blood of Agamemnon and judgment would have come at some time to Aegisthus. But I have never (Cypris knows this too) dishonored her in bed; she is still a virgin indeed.
1.45: I am ashamed to have the daughter of a wealthy man and violate her, when I was not born of equal rank. And I groan for the wretched Orestes, called my kinsman, if he shall ever return to Argos and see the unfortunate marriage of his sister.
1.50:
And whoever says I am a fool if I do not touch a young girl when I have her in my house, let him know that he measures soundness of mind by worthless standards of judgment, and he himself is a fool.
Electra
1.54: O black night, nurse of the golden stars,
1.55: in which I go to the river’s streams, bearing this pitcher resting on my head—not because I have come to such a point of necessity, but so that I may show to the gods Aegisthus’ insolence—and send forth laments into the wide sky, to my father.
1.60:
For the deadly daughter of Tyndareus, my mother, has cast me out of the house to please her husband; since she has borne other children in her union with Aegisthus, she considers Orestes and me secondary in the home.
Peasant
1.64: Why, unhappy one, do you do this work, laboring for my sake,
1.65:
though you were well brought up before, and do not stop, even when I tell you this?
Electra
1.67: I hold you equal to the gods in kindness, for in my distress you have not insulted me. It is a great allotment for mortals
1.70: to find a healer for ill fortune, such as I have in you. And so, even though unbidden, I ought to share your labors, relieving you of work as far as I have strength, so that you may bear it more easily. You have enough to do outside; I must keep the house
1.75:
in order. It is pleasant for the worker coming in from outside to find things within right.
Peasant
1.77: Go, then, if you wish; and in fact the springs are not far from my house. When it is day, I will drive the oxen to my lands and sow the fields.
1.80:
For no idler, though he has the gods’ names always on his lips, can gather a livelihood without hard work. Exeunt Peasant and Electra. Enter Orestes and Pylades.
Orestes
1.82: Pylades, I hold you first among men as a kind and trusted friend to me. You alone of my friends have honored me, Orestes,
1.85: being as I am in dreadful suffering from Aegisthus, who killed my father, he and my most deadly mother. I have come from the mystic shrine of the god to Argive land, and no one knows it, to repay my father’s murderers with murder.
1.90: During this past night, going to my father’s tomb, I wept and cut off a lock of my hair as an offering and sacrificed over the altar the blood of a slaughtered sheep, unnoticed by the tyrants who rule this land. And now I do not set foot within the walls,
1.95: but I have come to the borders of this land combining two desires: I may escape to another country if anyone on the watch should recognize me; and, looking for my sister (for they say that she lives here, joined in marriage, and is no longer a virgin),
1.100: I may meet with her and, having her as an accomplice for murder, I may learn clearly what is happening within the walls. And now, since dawn is lifting up her bright eye, let us step aside from this path. For either some plowman or serving maid
1.105: will come in our sight, from whom we may ask if my sister lives in this place. But now that I see this maidservant, bearing a weight of water on her shorn head, let us sit down, and inquire
1.110:
of this slave girl, if we may receive some word about the matter, Pylades, for which we have come to this land. They retire a little.
Electra
1.112: Hasten your step, it is time; go onward, onward, weeping! Ah me!
1.115: I am Agamemnon’s child, and Clytemnestra, hated daughter of Tyndareus, bore me; the citizens call me unhappy Electra.
1.120:
Alas for my cruel pain and hateful life! O father, Agamemnon, you lie in Hades, by the butchery of your wife and Aegisthus.
Electra
1.125:
Come, waken the same lament, take up the enjoyment of long weeping.
Electra
1.127: Hasten your step, it is time; go onward, onward, weeping. Ah me!
1.130: In what city and what household do you wander about, my wretched brother, leaving your pitiable sister in our ancestral home, to great pain?
1.135:
Come to me, the unhappy one, as a deliverer from this pain, oh Zeus, Zeus, and as a defender for my father against his most hateful bloodshed; bring the wanderer to shore in Argos.
Electra
1.140: Take this pitcher from my head and put it down, so that I may cry aloud the night-time laments for my father. A wail, a song of death, of death, for you, father, under the earth, I speak the laments
1.145:
in which I am always engaged, day by day, tearing my skin with my nails, and striking my cropped head with my hand, for your death.
Electra
1.150: Oh, oh, tear my face; as a clear-sounding swan beside the river’s streams calls to its dearest father, dying in the crafty snares of the
1.155:
net, so I lament you, my unhappy father,
Electra
1.157: washed by the very last bath, in the most piteous bed of death. Oh, me,
1.160: your bitter cleaving by the axe, father, the bitter plans of the way from Troy! Your wife welcomed you with no victor’s garlands or crowns, but with a two-edged sword,
1.165:
making you the mournful victim of Aigisthus, she got a treacherous bed-fellow.
Chorus
1.167: O Electra, daughter of Agamemnon, I have come to your rustic courtyard. A milk-drinker from Mycenae has come, he has come,
1.170:
a mountain walker; he reports that the Argives are proclaiming a sacrifice for the third day from now, and that all maidens are to go to Hera’s temple.
Electra
1.175: My unhappy heart beats fast, friends, but not at adornment or gold; nor will I set up choruses with the maidens of Argos
1.180: and beat my foot in the mazes of the dance. By tears I pass the night; tears are my unhappy care day by day. See if my filthy hair,
1.185:
and the rags of my dress, will be fit for a princess, a daughter of Agamemnon, or for Troy, once taken, which remembers my father.
Chorus
1.190: Mighty is the goddess; come then, and borrow from me thick-woven clothes to wear, and gold—as a favor to me—accessories to adornment. Do you think to rule over your enemies by tears, if you do not revere the gods?
1.195:
Honoring the gods not by lamentation but by prayers, you will have good fortune, child.
Electra
1.198: No god attends to the voice of the ill-fated one,
1.200: or to the slaying of my father long ago. Alas for the dead, and for the living vagabond, who dwells in another land somewhere,
1.205: miserably wandering to a slave’s hearth, yet born of that renowned father. I myself live in a poor man’s house, wasting my life away, an exile from my father’s house,
1.210:
on the mountain crags. But my mother, with a new husband, makes her home in a bed stained by blood.
Chorus Leader
1.213:
Helen, your mother’s sister, is the cause of many evils to the Hellenes and to your house.
Electra
Catching sight of Orestes and Pylades
1.215:
Ah! Women, I have broken off my lament; strangers, who had their lair at the altar, are rising from ambush towards the household. Let us escape the villains by flight, you along the path and I to the house.
Orestes
1.220:
Stay, poor girl; do not fear my hand.
Electra
1.221:
O Phoebus Apollo! I beseech you to spare my life.
Orestes
1.222:
May I kill others more hated than you!
Electra
1.223:
Go away! Do not touch one whom you must not touch.
Orestes
1.224:
There is no one I have a better right to touch.
Electra
1.225:
Then why are you in ambush, with drawn sword, near my house?
Orestes
1.226:
Wait and hear, and you will soon say the same.
Electra
1.227:
I am still; in any case, I am yours, since you are the stronger.
Orestes
1.228:
I have come to bring you word from your brother.
Electra
1.229:
Oh best of friends! Is he alive or dead?
Orestes
1.230:
Alive; for I want to tell you the good news first.
Electra
1.231:
May you be happy, as a reward for your most welcome tidings.
Orestes
1.232:
I give that blessing for us two to have in common.
Electra
1.233:
Where does the unhappy one live, in his unhappy exile?
Orestes
1.234:
He goes miserably about, not following the customs of any one city.
Electra
1.235:
Surely he does not want for a living, day by day?
Orestes
1.236:
He has that, but an exile is a helpless man at best.
Electra
1.237:
What is this message you have come bringing from him?
Orestes
1.238:
If you are alive, and if so, how you are.
Electra
1.239:
Well then, you see first of all how withered my body is.
Orestes
1.240:
Yes, so wasted with sorrow that I sigh for it.
Electra
1.241:
And my head and hair, close shaven as if by a Scythian’s razor.
Orestes
1.242:
Your brother and your dead father perhaps gnaw at your heart.
Electra
1.243:
Alas! For what is dearer to me than they?
Orestes
1.244:
Ah! What are you to your brother, do you think?
Electra
1.245:
He is far away, not here to be my friend.
Orestes
1.246:
Why are you living here, far from the city?
Electra
1.247:
I am married, stranger; a deadly match.
Orestes
1.248:
I pity your brother. Is your husband a Mycenaean?
Electra
1.249:
Not one to whom my father ever hoped to give me.
Orestes
1.250:
Tell me so that I may hear and inform your brother.
Electra
1.251:
I live in his house, at a distance from the city.
Orestes
1.252:
A ditch-digger or a herdsman is worthy of the house.
Electra
1.253:
He is a man poor but noble, and respectful to me.
Orestes
1.254:
What is this respect that your husband has?
Electra
1.255:
He has never dared to touch me in bed.
Orestes
1.256:
Does he hold some form of religious chastity, or does he think you unworthy?
Electra
1.257:
He did not think himself worthy to insult my family.
Orestes
1.258:
And how was he not delighted to make such a marriage?
Electra
1.259:
He thinks the person who gave me did not have that right, stranger.
Orestes
1.260:
I understand; he fears that he may someday be punished by Orestes.
Electra
1.261:
He does fear that, but he is also a virtuous man.
Orestes
1.262:
Ah! You have described a noble man, and he must be treated well.
Electra
1.263:
Yes, if ever the one now absent comes home.
Orestes
1.264:
But did your mother, who gave you birth, endure this?
Electra
1.265:
Women love their husbands, stranger, not their children.
Orestes
1.266:
Why did Aegisthus insult you in this way?
Electra
1.267:
He planned for me to bear powerless children, when he gave me to such a man.
Orestes
1.268:
So that you might not bear sons to punish him, of course?
Electra
1.269:
That was his plan; may he make amends to me for it!
Orestes
1.270:
Does your mother’s husband know that you are a virgin?
Electra
1.271:
He does not know; we steal that from him by our silence.
Orestes
1.272:
Are these women who hear our talk friends of yours?
Electra
1.273:
They will keep both your words and mine well hidden.
Orestes
1.274:
What then could Orestes do in this matter if he comes to Argos?
Electra
1.275:
Do you ask this? You have said a shameful word; isn’t it the critical time now?
Orestes
1.276:
But if he does come, how might he kill his father’s murderers?
Electra
1.277:
By daring such things as his enemies dared against my father.
Orestes
1.278:
And would you dare, with him, to kill your mother?
Electra
1.279:
Yes, with that same axe by which my father died.
Orestes
1.280:
Am I to tell him this, and that your purpose is steadfast?
Electra
1.281:
Once I had shed my mother’s blood, I might die!
Orestes
1.282:
Ah! Would that Orestes were near by, to hear that!
Electra
1.283:
But, stranger, I would not know him if I saw him.
Orestes
1.284:
No wonder, for you were both young when you were parted.
Electra
1.285:
There is only one of my friends who would recognize him.
Orestes
1.286:
The man who is said to have stolen him away from murder?
Electra
1.287:
Yes, the old man, my father’s old servant.
Orestes
1.288:
Did the dead man, your father, find burial?
Electra
1.289:
He found what he could, cast out of the house.
Orestes
1.290: Alas, the things you have said! For perception of suffering, even another’s, gnaws at mortals. Speak, so that when I know, I may tell your brother the story, unpleasant, but necessary to hear. Pity is not present at all in clownishness,
1.295:
but in wise men. And indeed it is not without mischief for the wise to have overly profound thoughts.
Chorus Leader
1.297:
And I have the same desire in my heart as this man. Being far from the town, I do not know the city’s scandals, and now I want to learn them.
Electra
1.300: I will speak, if I must—and one must speak to a friend—about my own and my father’s heavy misfortunes. Since you are setting the tale in motion, I entreat you, stranger, tell Orestes of our sorrows, mine and his. First of all, in what clothes I live like a beast in a stall,
1.305: with what filth I am weighted down, under what roof I dwell, having lived in a royal home; I myself working hard on my clothes at the loom, or else I shall go barely clad and do without; always carrying water from the springs myself,
1.310: with no share in the festival rites, no part in the dance. I turn away from married women, as a virgin; and I turn away from Castor, who sought me in marriage before he joined the gods, for I was his relative. But my mother, in the spoils of Troy,
1.315: is seated on her throne, and at her chair stand slaves from Asia, my father’s plunder, fastening their Trojan robes with golden brooches. And still my father’s blood has rotted black on the wall, while the one who killed him
1.320: mounts the same chariot and goes forth; and is proud to hold in his blood-stained hands the scepter with which my father used to command the Hellenes. Agamemnon’s grave, dishonoured, has not yet ever received any libations, or branch of myrtle,
1.325: but his altar is barren of ornament. That famous one, my mother’s husband, leaps on the grave, they say, when soaked in drink, and pelts my father’s marble monument with stones, and dares to say this to us:
1.330: Where is your son Orestes? Is he here to defend the tomb for you nobly? Orestes is insulted in this way while absent. But, stranger, I beg you, report these things. There are many calling him to come—I am their interpreter—these hands, this tongue, my broken heart,
1.335:
my shorn head, and his own father. For it is shameful, if his father exterminated the Trojans but Orestes is unable to kill a man, one against one, being young and born from a more noble father.
Chorus Leader
1.339: And look, I see him, I mean your husband,
1.340:
on his way home, his day’s work done.
Peasant
Entering and catching sight of strangers talking to Electra.
1.341:
Oh! who are these strangers I see at my door? Why have they come here to my rustic gate? Do they want something from me? For it is shameful for a woman to be standing with young men.
Electra
1.345:
Dearest, do not be suspicious of me; you shall hear the truth; for these strangers have come to me as messengers of news from Orestes. But, strangers, pardon him for what he said.
Peasant
1.349:
What do they say? The man is alive and sees the light of day?
Electra
1.350:
He is, at least in their report, and I believe them.
Peasant
1.351:
Surely then he remembers something of your father’s wrongs and your own?
Electra
1.352:
These are things to hope for; a man in exile is powerless.
Peasant
1.353:
What message from Orestes have they come to declare?
Electra
1.354:
He sent them as spies of my wrongs.
Peasant
1.355:
Then they see a part of it, and perhaps you are telling them the rest.
Electra
1.356:
They know; they have all these things in abundance.
Peasant
1.357: Then shouldn’t you have opened the doors to them long before? Go into the house; for in return for your good tidings, you shall find as much hospitality as my house holds in store.
1.360:
Servants, take their baggage within the house. Do not contradict me, since you are friends coming from a friend; for, even if I am poor, I will not display manners that are ill-bred.
Orestes
1.364: By the gods! Is this the man who makes a fraud of your marriage,
1.365:
because he does not want to shame Orestes?
Electra
1.366:
This is the one who is called my husband, unhappy as I am.
Orestes
1.367: Ah! There is no exact way to test a man’s worth; for human nature has confusion in it. For instance, I have seen before now the son of a noble father
1.370: worth nothing, and good children from evil parents; famine in a rich man’s spirit, and a mighty soul in a poor man’s body. How then does one rightly distinguish and judge these things? By wealth? A sorry test to use.
1.375: Or by those who have nothing? But poverty has a disease, it teaches a man to be wicked in his need. But shall I turn to warfare? Who, facing the enemy’s spear, could be a witness as to who is brave? It is best to leave these matters alone, at random.
1.380: For this man, neither important in Argos, nor puffed up by the good reputation of his family, but one of the many, has been found to be the best. Do not be foolish, you who wander about full of empty notions, but judge those noble among men by their company
1.385: and by their habits. For such men rule well both states and homes; while those bodies that are empty of mind are only ornaments in the market-place. For the strong arm does not await the battle any better than the weak;
1.390: this depends on natural courage. But, since Agamemnon’s son, both present and not present, for whose sake we have come, is worthy of it, let us accept a lodging in this house. Calling to his servants. We must go within this house, slaves. May a man poor
1.395: but eager be a better host for me than a rich man! And so I am content with the reception into this man’s house, though I would have wanted your brother, in good fortune, to lead me to his fortunate home. Perhaps he may come; the oracles of Loxias are
1.400:
sure, but human prophecy I dismiss. Exeunt Orestes and Pylades.
Chorus Leader
1.401:
Now more than before, Electra, I feel the warmth of joy at my heart; for perhaps good fortune, advancing with difficulty, might come to a good resting-place.
Electra
1.404: O reckless man, why, knowing the poverty of your house,
1.405:
did you welcome these strangers, greater than you?
Peasant
1.406:
What? If they are really as noble as they seem, won’t they be equally content among great and small?
Electra
1.408: Since you, one of the small, have now made this error, go to my father’s dear old servant,
1.410: who tends his flocks, an outcast from the city, by the river Tanaus which cuts a boundary between Argive land and the land of Sparta; bid him come, since these men have arrived at my house, and provide something for the guests’ meal.
1.415:
He will be glad, and will offer prayers to the gods, when he hears that the child, whom he once saved, is alive. I cannot get anything from my mother or from my father’s house; for we would bring bitter news, if she, the hard-hearted, were to learn that Orestes is still alive.
Peasant
1.420: I will take this message to the old man, if you wish; but go inside the house at once and make things ready there. Surely a woman, if she wants to, can find many additions to a meal. Really there is still enough in the house
1.425: to cram them with food for one day at least. It is in such cases, whenever I fail in my intentions, that I see how wealth has great power, to give to strangers, and to expend in curing the body when it falls sick; but money for our daily food
1.430:
comes to little; for every man when full, rich or poor, gets an equal amount. Exeunt Electra and Peasant.
Chorus
1.432: O famous ships, you that once with countless oars went to Troy, conducting dances with the Nereids,
1.435: where the music-loving dolphin leapt and rolled at your dark-blue prows, bringing Achilles, the son of Thetis, light in the leap of his foot,
1.440:
with Agamemnon to the banks of Trojan Simois.
Chorus
1.442: The Nereids, leaving Euboea’s headlands, brought from Hephaestus’ anvil his shield-work of golden armor,
1.445: up to Pelion and the glens at the foot of holy Ossa, the Nymphs’ watch-tower... where his father, the horseman, was training the son of Thetis as a light for Hellas,
1.450:
sea-born, swift-footed for the sons of Atreus.
Chorus
1.452: I heard, from someone who had arrived at the harbor of Nauplia from Ilium, that
1.455: on the circle of your famous shield, O son of Thetis, were wrought these signs, a terror to the Phrygians: on the surrounding base of the shield’s rim, Perseus the throat-cutter, over
1.460:
the sea with winged sandals, was holding the Gorgon’s body, with Hermes, Zeus’ messenger, the rustic son of Maia.
Chorus
1.464: In the center of the shield the sun’s bright circle
1.465: was shining on winged horses, and the heavenly chorus of stars, Pleiades, Hyades, bringing defeat to the eyes of Hector;
1.470: and upon his gold-forged helmet were sphinxes, bearing in their talons prey from singing. On his breast-plate a lioness, breathing flame, was eager in flight, with her claws,
1.475:
seeing the colt of Pirene.
Chorus
1.476: On the bloody hilt four-footed horses were prancing, while over their backs black dust rose up. But your adultery killed the lord of such mighty warriors,
1.480: evil-minded daughter of Tyndareus! For this the gods of heaven will one day send you to death;
1.485:
truly the day will come when I shall see, under your red throat, blood gushing forth at the sword.
Old man
1.487: Where, where is my young queen and mistress, Agamemnon’s child, whom I once brought up? How steep is the approach to her house,
1.490: for a wrinkled old man to ascend with this foot! Still, for these friends, I must drag along my back bent double and sinking knees. Oh, daughter—for I see you now before the house—I have come, bringing you from my own sheep
1.495: this newborn nursling of the flock, having drawn it away from its mother, and garlands, and cheeses I have taken from the press, and this old treasure of Dionysus, furnished with fragrance, small, but sweet to pour a cup of it into a weaker drink.
1.500:
Let some one carry these gifts into the house for the guests. I have moistened my eyes with tears, and wish to wipe them off on this shred of my robe.
Electra
1.503: Why are your eyes wet, old man? Have my troubles stirred your memory, after an interval of time?
1.505:
Or are you groaning over the sad exile of Orestes, and over my father, whom you once held in your arms and brought up, in vain for you and for your friends?
Old man
1.508: In vain; but still I could not endure this: for I came to his grave, an addition to my journey,
1.510: and falling on it I wept for its desolation; then I opened the wine-skin which I am bringing to the guests, and poured a libation, and set myrtle-sprigs round the tomb. On the alter itself I saw a black-fleeced ram as an offering, and there was blood, not long poured out,
1.515: and severed locks of yellow hair. And I wondered, child, who ever dared come to the the tomb; for it was no Argive at least. But perhaps your brother has somehow come secretly and on his return has done honor to his father’s wretched grave.
1.520:
Go look to see if the color of the cut lock is the same as yours, putting it to your own hair; it is usual for those who have the same paternal blood to have a close bodily resemblance in most points.
Electra
1.524: Old man, your words are unworthy of a wise man,
1.525: if you think my own brave brother would come to this land secretly for fear of Aegisthus. Then, how will a lock of hair correspond, the one made to grow in the wrestling schools of a well-bred man, the other, a woman’s lock, by combing? No, it is impossible.
1.530:
But you could find in many people hair very similar, although they are not of the same blood, old man.
Old man
1.532:
Then stand in the footprint and see if the tread of the boot will measure with your own foot, child.
Electra
1.534: How could there be an imprint of feet on a stony plot of ground?
1.535:
And if there is, the foot of brother and sister would not be the same in size, for the male conquers.
Old man
1.538: There is not, even if your brother, coming to this land... by which you might know your loom’s weaving,
1.540:
in which I once stole him away from death?
Electra
1.541: Don’t you know that I was still young when Orestes was driven out of the land? And even if I had woven him a robe, how could he, a child then, have the same one now, unless his clothes grew together with his body?
1.545:
But either a stranger, taking pity on his grave...
Old man
1.547:
Where are the guests? I want to see them and question them about your brother.
Electra
1.549:
There they are, coming quickly out of the house.
Old man
1.550:
They are well-born, but that may ring false; for many of the well-born are base. However; I give the guests welcome.
Orestes
1.553:
Welcome, old man! To which of your friends, Electra, does this ancient remnant of a man belong?
Electra
1.555:
This is the one who brought up my father, stranger.
Orestes
1.556:
What are you saying? Is this the one who stole away your brother?
Electra
1.557:
This is the one who saved him, if indeed he is still alive.
Orestes
1.558:
Oh! Why does he look at me, as if he were examining the clear mark impressed on a silver coin? Is he comparing me to someone?
Electra
1.560:
Perhaps he is glad to see in you a companion of Orestes.
Orestes
1.561:
A beloved man, yes. But why is he circling all around me?
Electra
1.562:
I too am amazed, looking at this, stranger.
Old man
1.563:
O mistress, daughter Electra, pray to the gods.
Electra
1.564:
For what thing, present or absent?
Old man
1.565:
To have a beloved treasure, which the god is revealing.
Electra
1.566:
See: I call on the gods. Or whatever do you mean, old man?
Old man
1.567:
Look now at this man, my child, your dearest one.
Electra
1.568:
I have been looking for a long time, to see whether you have lost your mind.
Old man
1.569:
Lost my mind, because I see your brother?
Electra
1.570:
What do you mean, old man, by this word, unhoped for?
Old man
1.571:
That I see Orestes here, Agamemnon’s son.
Electra
1.572:
What mark do you see, by which I shall be persuaded?
Old man
1.573:
A scar along his brow, where he fell and drew blood one day in his father’s home when chasing a fawn with you.
Electra
1.575:
What are you saying? I see the sign of the fall.
Old man
1.576:
Then do you hesitate to embrace your dearest one?
Electra
1.577:
Not any longer, old man; for my heart is persuaded by your tokens. O you who have appeared at last, I hold you, beyond all hope.
Orestes
1.579:
And you are held by me at last.
Electra
1.580:
I never expected it.
Orestes
Nor did I hope.
Electra
1.581:
Are you that one?
Orestes
