1.0: On the sea-shore, in the Tauric Chersonese, near a temple of Artemis. Iphigenia
1.1: Pelops, son of Tantalus, coming to Pisa with swift horses, married Oenomaus’ daughter, and she gave birth to Atreus, whose children are Menelaus and Agamemnon; from him I was born,
1.5: his child Iphigenia, by the daughter of Tyndareus. Where Euripus rolls about its whirlpools in the frequent winds and twists the darkening waves, my father sacrificed me to Artemis for Helen’s sake, or so he thought, in the famous clefts of Aulis.
1.10: For there lord Agamemnon mustered his expedition of a thousand ships of Hellas, wanting to take the crown of Troy in glorious victory and avenge the outrage to Helen’s marriage, doing this favor for Menelaus.
1.15: But when he met with dreadful winds that would not let him sail, he went to burnt sacrifices, and Calchas had this to say: Lord and general of Hellas, Agamemnon, you will not set free your ships from land until Artemis has your daughter Iphigenia
1.20: as a victim. For you once vowed to sacrifice to the torch-bearing goddess the most beautiful creature brought forth that year; then your wife, Clytemnestra, bore a child in your house—ascribing the prize of beauty to me—whom you must sacrifice. And by the craft of Odysseus,
1.25: they took me from my mother, pretending a marriage with Achilles. I came to Aulis; held up high over the altar, I, the unhappy one, was about to die by the sword; but Artemis gave the Achaeans a deer in exchange for me and stole me from them; conducting me through the bright air,
1.30: she settled me here in the land of the Taurians. A barbarian rules this land of barbarians: Thoas, who runs as quickly as the flight of birds, and so he received his name for his swiftness of foot. Artemis has made me the priestess in this temple.
1.35: Here I begin the rites, which the goddess delights in, of a banquet noble in name only—I am silent as to the rest, for I fear the goddess—
1.40: But others carry out the sacrifices, not to be spoken of, within the temple of the goddess.
1.42: But the strange visions which the night brought with it, I will tell to the air, if that is any relief. I dreamed that I had left this land
1.45: to live in Argos, and to sleep in the midst of the maidens’ rooms; but the earth’s back was shaken by a tossing swell. When I escaped and stood outside, I saw the cornice of the house fall, and the whole roof hurled in ruins on the ground, from the highest pillars.
1.50: One support of my father’s house was left, I thought, and it had yellow locks of hair waving from its capital, and took on human voice. In observance of the art of slaughtering strangers that I practice here, I gave it holy water as if it were about to die, while I wept.
1.55: This is my interpretation of this dream: Orestes, whom I consecrated by my rites, is dead. For male children are the supports of the house; and those whom I purify with holy water die.

1.291: We could not see these shapes; but he alternated the sounds of sheep and howling of dogs... to send forth the Furies’ imitations.

1.300: so that the waves of the sea blossomed red with blood. And all of us, as we saw our herds falling and ravaged, took arms, blew our conch shells, and collected the neighbors; for we thought cowherds would make a poor fight of it
1.305: against well-grown and young foreigners. After a long time, our numbers were complete. But the stranger fell down, his pulsing beat of madness gone, his chin dripping with foam; when we saw him, so conveniently fallen, each of us went to work,
1.310: hurling and striking at him. The other stranger wiped off the foam and tended his body, covering him with a finely-woven robe, looking out for the attacking blows, treating his friend kindly with his care.
1.315: The stranger, now in his senses, started up from his fall and realized the surge of enemies close at hand and the present danger to them both, with a groan; we did not let up our attack with stones, pressing hard from all sides.
1.320: Then we heard his dreadful exhortation: Pylades, we shall die, but let us die with glory; draw your sword, and follow me.
1.323: But when we saw our enemies brandishing their two swords, we fled and filled up the rocky glens.
1.325: But while some would flee, others pressed on and attacked them; if they drove those back, the ones who had just given way struck them with stones again. But it was hard to believe; with so many hands, no one succeeded in hitting these offerings to the goddess.
1.330: We got the better of them with difficulty; not by daring, but by surrounding them in a circle, with stones we took away their swords; they sank on their knees to the ground, in weariness. Then we brought them to the lord of this land. He saw them, and at once
1.335:
sent them to you, for purification and slaughter. You have prayed for such sacrificial victims as these strangers, lady; if you destroy them, Hellas will make atonement for your murder and pay the penalty for the sacrifice in Aulis.
Chorus Leader
1.340:
You have told an amazing story about this madman, whoever he is, who has come from Hellas to the Black Sea.
Iphigenia
1.342: Very well. You go and bring the strangers here; the holy rites will be my concern. Exit Herdsman.
1.344: O my unhappy heart, you were gentle to strangers before,
1.345: and always full of pity, measuring out tears for the sake of our common race, whenever Hellenes came into your hands. But now, after those dreams that have made me savage, thinking that Orestes is no longer alive,
1.350: whoever comes here will find me harsh to them. This is true after all, my friends, I have realized: the unfortunate, when themselves doing badly, do not have kind thoughts towards those who are more unfortunate.
1.354: But no breeze from Zeus ever came,
1.355: or a boat, bringing Helen here, through the rocks of the Symplegedes—Helen who destroyed me, with Menelaus, so that I might avenge myself on them, setting an Aulis here against that one there, where the Danaids overpowered me and were going to sacrifice me like a calf,
1.360: and my own father was the priest.
1.361: Ah me!—I cannot forget those past evils—how often did I stroke my father’s cheek and, hanging on his knees, told him: O father, I am brought
1.365: to a shameful betrothal by you; but while you are killing me, my mother and the Argive women are singing wedding hymns, and the whole house is filled with the music of flutes; but I am being destroyed by you. For Achilles was Hades after all, not the son of Peleus,
1.370: whom you held out to me as a husband, and you brought me in a chariot to a bloody wedding by treachery. But I was modestly looking out through a fine veil, and did not take up my brother in my arms—and now he is dead—did not kiss my sister,
1.375: because I was going to the house of Peleus; I put off many embraces to another time, thinking that I would come back again to Argos.
1.378: My unhappy Orestes, if you are dead, what glories have you left, what achievements of a father!
1.380: I blame the goddess’ subtleties; whichever mortal has engaged in murder, or has touched a woman in childbirth or a corpse, she drives from her altars, thinking him impure; but she herself delights in human sacrifices.
1.385: It is not possible that Leto, the wife of Zeus, gave birth to such folly. I judge that the feast prepared by Tantalus for the gods is not to be believed, that they fed on the flesh of his son; and I think that the people here, who are themselves killers of men,
1.390:
ascribe to the goddess their sorry behavior. For I believe that no god is evil.
Chorus
1.392: Dark straits of the sea, dark, where the gadfly flying from Argos
1.395: crossed over the inhospitable wave... taking the Asian land in exchange for Europe. Whoever are the ones who left the lovely waters
1.400: of Eurotas, green with reeds, or the holy streams of Dirce, to come here, to come to the unsociable land, where, for the divine maiden, the blood of mortals stains
1.405:
the altars and columned temples?
Chorus
1.407: Did they sail the pine-wood oars with double beat of surge, over the waves of the sea,
1.410: a chariot of a ship in breezes that move the linen sails, to increase the contest of wealth for their halls? For hope is sweet, and
1.415: insatiable in mortals, to their hurt, for those who bear away the weight of wealth, wandering over the wave and crossing to barbarian cities, with one expectation. But thought of wealth comes at the wrong time for some,
1.420:
while for others it comes moderately.
Chorus
1.421: The rocks that rush together, the sleepless shores of Phineus—how did they cross them, running along the salty coast
1.425: on Amphitrite’s surge, where the fifty daughters of Nereus... the circular choruses sing,
1.430: with wind in the sails, the guiding rudder creaking under the stern, with southern breezes or by the blasts of the west wind,
1.435:
to the land of many birds, the white strand, Achilles’ lovely race-course, over the Black Sea?
Chorus
1.439: Would that, by my mistress’ prayers, Helen, Leda’s dear child,
1.440: might happen to leave Troy and come here, where she might die, crowned over her hair by the bloody water,
1.445: her throat cut by the hands of my mistress, and so pay her requital. But what a sweet message I should receive, if a sailor came from Hellas,
1.450: to put an end to my wretched slavery! For may I even in dreams be at home and in my ancestral city, the enjoyment of pleasant sleep,
1.455:
a grace we have in common with prosperity.
Chorus Leader
1.456: But here come the two youths, with tightly bound hands, the new sacrifice for the goddess; silence, my friends. These first-fruits of Hellas are indeed
1.460: approaching the temple; the herdman did not deliver a false message.
1.463: Lady Artemis, if this city carries out the rites in a way pleasing to you, accept the victims,
1.465:
which the custom among us declares to be unholy.
Iphigenia
1.467: Enough; first, it will be my care to perform well the rites of the goddess. Unbind the strangers’ hands, so that, as holy victims, they may no longer be in chains.
1.470: Then go into the temple and make ready what is necessary and customary at the present time.
1.472: (Turning to the prisoners.) Ah! Who was your mother, who gave you birth, and your father? And your sister, if you happen to have one... such two youths as she has lost,
1.475: and will be without a brother! Who knows where such fortunes will arrive? For all the gods’ affairs creep on in darkness, and no one knows evil... fate leads us on towards what we cannot know.
1.479: Unhappy strangers, where have you come from?
1.480:
For you have sailed a long time to reach this land, and you will be away from your home a long time, in the world below.
Orestes
1.482: Why do you lament these things, and mourn for the evils about to come upon us, lady, whoever you are? I do not think the one who is about to die wise,
1.485: if he wishes to conquer the fear of death by wailing, nor the one who laments when Hades is near and there is no hope of safety; for so he puts together two ills out of one, incurring a charge of folly and dying all the same; we must let fate alone.
1.490:
Do not grieve for us; for we are acquainted with the sacrifices here and we know them.
Iphigenia
1.492:
Which of you is called by the name of Pylades? I want to know this first.
Orestes
1.494:
That one, if you have any pleasure in the knowledge.
Iphigenia
1.495:
Of what city of Hellas were you born a citizen?
Orestes
1.496:
What would you gain by learning this, lady?
Iphigenia
1.497:
Are you brothers, from one mother?
Orestes
1.498:
By friendship, yes; we are not brothers by birth, lady.
Iphigenia
1.499:
What name did your father give you?
Orestes
1.500:
I might rightly be called Unfortunate.
Iphigenia
1.501:
I do not ask that; ascribe that to fortune.
Orestes
1.502:
If I die unnamed, I would not be mocked at.
Iphigenia
1.503:
Why do you begrudge this? Are you so proud?
Orestes
1.504:
You will sacrifice my body, not my name.
Iphigenia
1.505:
Can you not say what city you are from?
Orestes
1.506:
You are seeking nothing profitable, since I am going to die.
Iphigenia
1.507:
What hinders you from doing me this favor?
Orestes
1.508:
The famous Argos I claim as my native land.
Iphigenia
1.509:
By the gods, truly, stranger, were you born there?
Orestes
1.510:
Yes, from Mycenae, which was once prosperous.
Iphigenia
1.511:
Have you left your country as an exile, or by what fate?
Orestes
1.512:
My flight is in some manner willed and unwilled.
Iphigenia
1.513:
Could you then tell me something that I wish to know?
Orestes
1.514:
It will be no great addition to my own misfortune.
Iphigenia
1.515:
Indeed, I am so glad that you have come from Argos!
Orestes
1.516:
I am not; but if you are, take pleasure in it.
Iphigenia
1.517:
Perhaps you know Troy, whose fame is everywhere.
Orestes
1.518:
Would that I did not, even seen in a dream!
Iphigenia
1.519:
They say it is no more, lost to the spear.
Orestes
1.520:
It is so; you have heard nothing that has not happened.
Iphigenia
1.521:
Has Helen come back to Menelaus’ home?
Orestes
1.522:
She has; it was an unfortunate arrival for one dear to me.
Iphigenia
1.523:
And where is she? She deserves an ill turn from me also.
Orestes
1.524:
She lives at Sparta with her former bedfellow.
Iphigenia
1.525:
Creature hated by Hellas, not by me alone!
Orestes
1.526:
I have also had some benefit from the marriage of that woman!
Iphigenia
1.527:
Have the Achaeans returned, as reported?
Orestes
1.528:
How you put everything together and ask me all at once!
Iphigenia
1.529:
Before you die, I want to profit by your answers.
Orestes
1.530:
Question me, since you desire this; I will tell you.
Iphigenia
1.531:
Has a certain Calchas, a prophet, come back from Troy?
Orestes
1.532:
He is dead, as the story goes in Mycenae.
Iphigenia
1.533:
O goddess, how good that is! What about Odysseus?
Orestes
1.534:
He has not yet returned, but is alive, they say.
Iphigenia
1.535:
May he die and never achieve a return to his country!
Orestes
1.536:
Do not pray against that man; all is misery for him.
Iphigenia
1.537:
But is the son of Thetis the Nereid still alive?
Orestes
1.538:
He is not; his marriage at Aulis was in vain.
Iphigenia
1.539:
Yes, for it was a cheat, as those who experienced it know.
Orestes
1.540:
Who are you? How well you ask about Hellas!
Iphigenia
1.541:
I am from there; while still a child I was lost.
Orestes
1.542:
Then rightly you desire to know what has happened there, lady.
Iphigenia
1.543:
What about the general, who is said to be happy?
Orestes
1.544:
Who? The one I knew was not happy.
Iphigenia
1.545:
There was said to be a certain lord, Agamemnon, son of Atreus.
Orestes
1.546:
I do not know; leave this subject, lady.
Iphigenia
1.547:
No, by the gods, but tell me, stranger, to delight me.
Orestes
1.548:
The wretched man is dead, and in addition he destroyed another.
Iphigenia
1.549:
Dead? By what fate? I am unhappy!
Orestes
1.550:
Why do you mourn for this? It doesn’t concern you, does it?
Iphigenia
1.551:
I grieve for his former prosperity.
Orestes
1.552:
Yes, for he was dreadfully murdered by a woman.
Iphigenia
1.553:
O miserable the slayer... and the slain!
Orestes
1.554:
Stop now, and do not ask further.
Iphigenia
1.555:
Only this much, if the wife of the wretched man is alive.
Orestes
1.556:
She is not; she was killed by the son that she bore.
Iphigenia
1.557:
O house thrown into confusion! What was his intent?
Orestes
1.558:
To avenge on her the death of his father.
Iphigenia
1.559:
Ah! How well he exacted an evil justice!
Orestes
1.560:
Though he is just, he does not have good fortune from the gods.
Iphigenia
1.561:
Did Agamemnon leave any other children in his house?
Orestes
1.562:
He left one virgin daughter, Electra.
Iphigenia
1.563:
What else? Is there any report of the daughter who was sacrificed?
Orestes
1.564:
None, except that she is dead and does not see the light.
Iphigenia
1.565:
Unhappy girl, and also the father that killed her!
Orestes
1.566:
As a thankless favor to an evil woman, she died.
Iphigenia
1.567:
Does the dead father’s son live at Argos?
Orestes
1.568:
He lives, the miserable one, both nowhere and everywhere.
Iphigenia
1.569:
False dreams, farewell; after all, you were nothing.
Orestes
1.570: And those who are called wise divinities are not less false than winged dreams. These is much confusion, both in divine affairs and in human; but only this is a grief to the one who was not foolish, but trusted in the words of prophets
1.575:
and died—as he died to those that know.
Chorus Leader
1.576:
Ah! What about me, and my parents? Are they alive? Are they not? Who can say?
Iphigenia
1.578: Listen to me; I have come to a subject which means benefit both to you, strangers,
1.580: and to me, by your efforts. A good action is especially so, if the same matter is pleasing to all. Would you, if I should save you, go to Argos and take a report of me to my friends there, and bring a tablet,
1.585: which a captive wrote for me in pity? He did not think my hand murderous, but that the victims of the goddess, who holds these things just, die under the law. For I have had no one to go back to Argos with that message, who,
1.590: being saved, would send my letter to one of my friends. But you—if, as it seems, you are not hostile to me, and you know Mycenae and those whom I want you to know—be rescued, and have this reward, not a shameful one, safety for the sake of this small letter.
1.595:
But let him, since the city exacts it, be the offering to the goddess, separated from you.
Orestes
1.597: Stranger, you have spoken all well but this: to sacrifice him would be a heavy grief to me. I am the pilot of these misfortunes,
1.600: he sailed with me for the sake of my troubles. For it is not right for me to do you a favor and get out of danger, on condition of his death. But let it happen this way: give him the letter and he will take it to to Argos, for your well-being;
1.605:
let anyone who wishes kill me. It is most shameful for anyone to save himself by hurling his friends’ affairs into catastrophe. That man is my friend, and I wish him to live, no less than myself.
Iphigenia
1.609: O brave spirit! How you were born from some noble
1.610: stock, and are rightly a friend to your friends! May that one of my relatives who is left be such as you! For I am not without a brother, strangers, except in so far as I do not see him.
1.614: Since you wish it, I will send this man
1.615:
with the tablet, and you will die; a great eagerness for this seems to possess you.
Orestes
1.617:
Who will sacrifice me and dare such a dreadful deed?
Iphigenia
1.618:
I will; for I hold the office of this goddess.
Orestes
1.619:
It is not envied, lady, and not blessed.
Iphigenia
1.620:
But I am dedicated to necessity, which must be kept.
Orestes
1.621:
Do you yourself, a woman, sacrifice men with the sword?
Iphigenia
1.622:
No; but I sprinkle the holy water around your hair.
Orestes
1.623:
Who is the slayer? If I may ask this.
Iphigenia
1.624:
That charge belongs to those within this temple.
Orestes
1.625:
What sort of tomb will receive me, when I die?
Iphigenia
1.626:
The sacred fire within and the wide hollow of a cave.
Orestes
1.627:
Ah! Would that my sister’s hand might lay out my body!
Iphigenia
1.628: You have prayed in vain, unhappy youth, whoever you are; for she lives far from a barbarian land.
1.630: Yet indeed, since you happen to be an Argive, I too will not leave out any favor that I can do. I will set much ornament on the tomb and quench your body with yellow oil, and throw onto your funeral pyre the gleaming honey, that streams from flowers,
1.636: But I will go and bring the tablet from the temple of the goddess; take care not to bear me ill-will.
1.638: Guard them, attendants, without chains. Perhaps I will send unexpected news to one of my friends,
1.640:
whom I especially love, in Argos; and the tablet, in telling him that those whom he thought dead are alive, will report a joy that can be believed. Exit Iphigenia.
Chorus
1.644: (to Orestes.) I raise a lament for you; the drops from the holy water,
1.645:
mingled with blood, will soon take you into their care.
Orestes
1.646:
This is not a case for pity, but farewell, strangers.
Chorus
1.647:
(to Pylades.) We honor you, young man, for your happy fate, because you will tread on your native land some day.
Pylades
1.650:
An unenviable fate indeed for a friend, when his friend is to die.
Chorus
1.652: Ah, ah! You are destroyed! Alas, alas! Which is better?
1.655:
For still my mind disputes a double argument, shall I mourn for you or rather for you.
Orestes
1.658:
By the gods, Pylades, do you feel the same thing I do?
Pylades
1.659:
I do not know; I have no reply to your question.
Orestes
1.660: Who is the girl? How like a Hellene she questioned me about the labors in Ilium and the return of the Achaeans, and Calchas, wise in omens, and Achilles’ name; and how she pitied the wretched Agamemnon, and asked me about
1.665:
his wife and children! This stranger is an Argive by race, and from that land; or she would not be sending the tablet and examining these things, as if she had some share in Argos’ prosperity.
Pylades
1.669: You are not much ahead of me: I was about to say the same things you said,
1.670:
except this: all who move about in the world know what happens to kings. But I have arrived at another consideration.
Orestes
1.673:
What is it? Share it with me so that you may know better.
Pylades
1.674: It is shameful for me to live when you are dead;
1.675: I sailed together with you, and I ought to die together with you. For I will seem a coward and base in Argos and Phocis of the many mountain folds. Most will think—for most people are base—that I betrayed you and saved myself to come home alone,
1.680: or I plotted your death, in the afflictions of your house, for the sake of your kingdom, since I married your sister and heiress. I fear these things and I am ashamed; and I must breathe my last with you,
1.685:
be slaughtered with you and consumed on the pyre; because I am your friend and I fear reproach.
Orestes
1.687: Hush! I must bear my own ills, and when the grief is single, I will not bear it double. What you call vile and infamous,
1.690: would be mine, if I cause you, who have toiled with me, to die; for it is not a hardship for me, suffering as I do at the hands of the gods, to give up my life. But you are prosperous, and you have a house that is pure, not afflicted, while mine is impious and unfortunate.
1.695: If you are saved and get sons from my sister, whom I gave to you for wife, my name would remain and the whole house of my father would not be wiped out in childlessness. But go, and live, and dwell in my father’s house.
1.700: And when you come to Hellas and to Argos of the horses, I charge you, by this right hand: heap up a tomb and build a memorial for me, and let my sister give her hair and tears to the tomb. Report that I died at the hand of an Argive
1.705: woman, at an altar, purified for death. Do not ever betray my sister, when you see how lonely is my father’s house that you have joined by marriage. And now farewell; I have found you the dearest of my friends, you who have hunted with me, grown up with me,
1.710: and borne with me many miseries. Phoebus, though a prophet, has deceived me; creating his plot, he drove me far away from Hellas, ashamed of his earlier prophecies. I gave him my all and trusted in his words,
1.715:
killed my mother, and myself perish in turn.
Pylades
1.716: You will have a tomb, and I will never betray your sister’s bed, unhappy youth, since I will hold you dearer when dead than when alive. But the prophecy of the god has not destroyed you yet;
1.720:
although you stand near to slaughter. Great misfortune can offer great reversals, when it is fated; it can indeed.
Orestes
1.723:
Silence; the words of Phoebus are no benefit to me; here comes the woman out of the temple.
Iphigenia
1.725: (to the guard.) Go away and make the preparations within for those who attend to the sacrifice.
1.727: Here are the many folds of the tablet, strangers. Hear what I want in addition. No man is the same when he is in troubles
1.730:
and when he falls out of fear into courage. I am afraid that when the one who is going to take this tablet to Argos leaves this land, he will put aside my letter as worth nothing.
Orestes
1.734:
What do you want, then? What are you perplexed about?
Iphigenia
1.735:
Let him give me an oath that he will convey this letter to Argos, to the friends to whom I wish to send it.
Orestes
1.737:
And will you give in return the same words to him?
Iphigenia
1.738:
To do what, or refrain from doing? Tell me.
Orestes
1.739:
To send him from this barbarous land alive.
Iphigenia
1.740:
What you say is right; how else could he deliver it?
Orestes
1.741:
Will the king agree to this?
Iphigenia
1.742:
Yes. I will persuade the king, and I myself will put this man on the ship.
Orestes
1.743:
(to Pylades.) Swear; begin a pious oath.
Iphigenia
1.744:
(to Pylades.) You must say: I will give this to your friends.
Pylades
1.745:
I will give this letter to your friends.
Iphigenia
1.746:
And I will see you safely outside the dark rocks.
Pylades
1.747:
What god do you do you swear by, as witness to your oath?
Iphigenia
1.748:
Artemis, in whose temple I hold office.
Pylades
1.749:
And I swear by the king of heaven, revered Zeus.
Iphigenia
1.750:
But if you leave off your oath, and wrong me?
Pylades
1.751:
May I not return. What about you, if you do not save me?
Iphigenia
1.752:
May I never set foot in Argos alive.
Pylades
1.753:
Now listen to a consideration we have passed over.
Iphigenia
1.754:
But it will be something new, if it is good.
Pylades
1.755:
Give me this exception: if the ship suffers and the tablet is lost with its cargo in the waves, and I rescue myself only, may this oath not hinder me.
Iphigenia
1.759: Do you know what I will do? For many attempts hit many targets.
1.760: I will tell you what is written in the folds of this tablet for you to report to my friends. For this is secure: if you preserve the writing, itself, though silent, will speak its message; if the writing is lost in the sea,
1.765:
when you save yourself, you will save my words.
Pylades
1.766:
You have spoken well, on behalf of the gods and me. Make clear to whom I must bring this letter in Argos, and what I must say when I have heard it from you.
Iphigenia
1.769: Report to Orestes, the son of Agamemnon:
1.770:
the one slain at Aulis sends you this, Iphigenia, who is alive, though no longer alive to those there—
Orestes
1.772:
Where is she? Has she come back from the dead??
Iphigenia
1.773: The one you are looking at; don’t confuse me by your talk. Bring me to Argos, my brother, before I die.
1.775:
Take me away from the barbarian land and the sacrifices of the goddess, where I hold the office of killing foreigners.
Orestes
1.777:
Pylades, what shall I say? Where have we found ourselves?
Iphigenia
1.778:
Or I will be a curse to your house.
Pylades
1.779:
Orestes?
Iphigenia
(stopping to address Pylades.) So that you may know the name, hearing it twice.
Pylades
1.780:
O gods!
Iphigenia
Why do you invoke the gods in my affairs?
Pylades
1.781:
No reason; finish your words; my thoughts were elsewhere. Perhaps, if I question you, I will not arrive at things I cannot believe.
Iphigenia
1.783: Tell him that Artemis saved me, by giving a deer in exchange for me; my father sacrificed it,
1.785:
thinking that he drove the sword sharply into me; and she settled me in this land. This is my letter, this is the writing in the tablet.
Pylades
1.788: You have bound me with an easy oath, and sworn very well. I will not take much time
1.790: to carry out the oath I swore.
1.791:
See, Orestes, I bring you a tablet from your sister here, and give it to you.
Orestes
1.793: I do receive it, but first I will pass over the letter’s folds to take a joy that is not in words.
1.795:
(Approaching to embrace Iphigenia.) My dearest sister, with what astonishment and delight I hold you in my unbelieving arms, after learning these marvels!
Chorus Leader
1.798:
Stranger, you are wrongly defiling the attendant of the goddess, by putting your hands on her robe that should not be touched.
Orestes
1.800:
My own sister, born from my father Agamemnon, do not turn away from me, when you hold your brother and thought you never would!
Iphigenia
1.803:
You are my brother? Stop this talk! He is well known in Argos and Nauplia.
Orestes
1.805:
Unhappy girl, your brother is not there.
Iphigenia
1.806:
But did Tyndareus’ daughter, the Spartan, give birth to you?
Orestes
1.807:
Yes, and my father was Pelops’ grandson.
Iphigenia
1.808:
What are you saying? Do you have some proof of this for me?
Orestes
1.809:
I do; ask me something about our father’s home.
Iphigenia
1.810:
Well, it is for you to speak, for me to learn.
Orestes
1.811:
I will say first what I have heard from Electra. Do you know of the strife that was between Atreus and Thyestes?
Iphigenia
1.813:
I have heard of it; the quarrel concerned a golden ram.
Orestes
1.814:
Did you not weave these things in a fine-textured web?
Iphigenia
1.815:
O dearest, you are bending your course near to my heart!
Orestes
1.816:
And the image of the sun in the middle of the loom?
Iphigenia
1.817:
I wove that shape also, in fine threads.
Orestes
1.818:
And you received a ceremonial bath from your mother, for Aulis?
Iphigenia
1.819:
I know; for no happy marriage has taken that memory from me.
Orestes
1.820:
What about this? You gave locks of your hair to be brought to your mother?
Iphigenia
1.821:
As a memorial, in place of my body, in the tomb.
Orestes
1.822: What I myself have seen, I will say for proof: an old spear of Pelops, in my father’s house, which he brandished in his hand when he won Hippodamia,
1.825:
the maiden of Pisa, and killed Oenomaus; it was hung up in your rooms.
Iphigenia
1.827: O dearest, for you are my dearest, none other, I have you, Orestes,
1.830:
far from our country of Argos, my darling.
Orestes
1.831:
And I have you, who were thought to be dead. Tears, and laments mixed with joy, fill your eyes and also mine.
Iphigenia
1.834: I left you still a baby,
1.835: young in the arms of your nurse, young in the house. O my soul, you have been more fortunate than words can say.
1.840:
I have come upon things that are beyond wonder, far from speech.
Orestes
1.841:
For the rest of time, may we be fortunate with each other!
Iphigenia
1.842: O my friends, I have found an extraordinary joy; I am afraid that he will fly from my hands into the air.
1.845:
O Cyclopean hearths; o my country, dear Mycenae, I thank you for his life, for his nourishment, because you brought up this light of the house, my brother.
Orestes
1.850:
We are fortunate in our family, but in our circumstances, my sister, we were born to be unfortunate in life.
Iphigenia
1.852:
I was unhappy, I know, when my wretched father put the sword to my throat.
Orestes
1.855:
Alas! Though I was not present, I seem to see you there.
Iphigenia
1.856: O brother, when I was brought, not a bride, to the treacherous bed of Achilles;
1.860:
but beside the altar there were tears and wails. Alas for the libations there!
Orestes
1.862:
I also mourned for the daring act of our father.
Iphigenia
1.864: Fatherless was the fate I received, fatherless.
1.865:
One thing comes from another, by divine fortune.
Orestes
1.866:
Yes, if you had killed your brother, unhappy one!
Iphigenia
1.868: O wretched, in my dreadful daring!
1.870: How dreadful were the things I endured, alas, my brother! By only a little you escaped an unholy death, slain by my hands. But how will these things end? What fortune will assist me?
1.875: What way will I find to send you from this city, from slaughter, to your native Argos,
1.880: before the sword draws near to your blood? This is your business, unhappy soul, to find out. On the dry land, not in a ship?
1.885: But if you go on foot, through trackless paths and barbarian tribes, you will draw near to death.
1.890: But through the dark rocks of the narrow passage is a long way for flight by ship.
1.895:
Who, either god or mortal or something unexpected, might accomplish a way that is no way, and reveal a release from troubles for the only two children of the house of Atreus?
Chorus Leader
1.900:
It is marvelous and surpasses a fable, this event that I myself have have seen and shall relate, not as hearsay.
Pylades
1.902: When friends come into the sight of friends, Orestes, it is reasonable to embrace; but we must leave off wailing and turn to other matters:
1.905:
how we shall get the glorious name of safety and leave the foreign land. For wise men take opportunities, and do not overstep their fate to get other pleasures.
Orestes
1.909: Well said; but I think fortune will take care
1.910:
of that with us; when one is eager, divine strength is likely to be greater.
Iphigenia
1.912:
(to Pylades.) Let nothing hold me back; nor will it prevent me speaking before I first find out Electra’s fate, for you are all dear to me.
Orestes
1.915:
She lives with this man, (pointing to Pylades) and has a happy life.
Iphigenia
1.916:
What country is he from, and who is his father?
Orestes
1.917:
Strophius of Phocis is the name of his father.
Iphigenia
1.918:
He is related to me, by the daughter of Atreus?
Orestes
1.919:
He is a cousin, and my only true friend.
Iphigenia
1.920:
He was not born when my father tried to kill me.
Orestes
1.921:
He was not; for Strophius was childless for some time.
Iphigenia
1.922:
Welcome, husband of my sister!
Orestes
1.923:
And also my savior, not only a relation.
Iphigenia
1.924:
But how did you dare that dreadful deed with our mother?
Orestes
1.925:
Let us be silent on that; I was avenging my father.
Iphigenia
1.926:
What reason did she have to kill her husband?
Orestes
1.927:
Let our mother’s affairs be; nor is it good for you to hear.
Iphigenia
1.928:
I am silent; does Argos now look to you?
Orestes
1.929:
Menelaus rules there; I am an exile from my country
Iphigenia
1.930:
Our uncle has surely not maltreated our afflicted house, has he?
Orestes
1.931:
No, but fear of the Furies drives me out of the land.
Iphigenia
1.932:
That was the madness that they reported there on the shore?
Orestes
1.933:
That was not the first time that I was seen to be wretched.
Iphigenia
1.934:
I know; the goddesses were driving you for the sake of your mother.
Orestes
1.935:
So as to put a bloody bit in my mouth.
Iphigenia
1.936:
Why have you made a journey to this land?
Orestes
1.937:
I have come at the commands of Phoebus’ oracles.
Iphigenia
1.938:
To do what? Can you speak of it, or must you be silent?
Orestes
1.939: I will tell you; this is the beginning of my many troubles.
1.940: When my mother’s evil deeds, that I cannot speak of, came into my hands, I was driven to flight by the Furies’ pursuit; then Loxias sent me to Athens, to stand trial with the goddesses who may not be named.
1.945: For there is a holy tribunal there, which Zeus once established for Ares, when his hands were stained with blood-pollution. I came there... at first, no host would willingly take me in, as one hated by the gods; then some who felt shame offered me a table apart, as a guest,
1.950: themselves being under the same roof, and in silence they kept me from speaking, so that I might be apart from them in food and drink, and into each private cup they poured an equal measure of wine and had their delight.
1.955: And I did not think it right to blame my hosts, but I grieved in silence and seemed not to know, while I sighed deeply, that I was the murderer of my mother. I hear that my misfortunes have become a festival at Athens, and they still hold this custom
1.960: and the people of Pallas honor the cup that belongs to the Feast of Pitchers. When I came to the hill of Ares to stand my trial, I took one seat, and the eldest of the Furies took the other. I spoke and heard arguments on the murder of my mother,
1.965: and Phoebus saved me by bearing witness; Pallas counted out equal votes for me; and I went away victorious in my ordeal of blood. Some of the Furies who sat there, persuaded by the judgment, marked out a holy place for themselves beside this very tribunal;
1.970: but others were not persuaded by the law, and drove me always in vagabond courses until I came to the holy plain of Phoebus in turn. Stretched out before his shrine and fasting, I swore to break off my life and die there,
1.975: if Phoebus, who had destroyed me, did not save me. And then Phoebus cried out a golden voice from the tripod, and sent me here, to get the image Zeus hurled down, and set it up in Athena’s land. But what he marked out for my safety
1.980: you must help me with; for if we possess the statue of the goddess, I will be released from madness and will put you on my ship of many oars and establish you again in Mycenae. But, my beloved sister, save our father’s house and save me;
1.985:
for so I perish and all the race of Pelops, unless we take the heavenly image of the goddess.
Chorus Leader
1.987:
A terrible anger from the gods has boiled up against the race of Tantalus and drives them through torments.
Iphigenia
1.989: Before you came here, I was eager
1.990: to be in Argos and see you, my brother. Your wish is mine: to release you from torment, and restore our father’s afflicted house, for I am not angry at the one who killed me; it is my wish. I would set my hand free from your slaughter
1.995: and save our house. But I worry about concealment from the goddess and the king, when he finds the stone pedestal empty of the statue. How will I escape death? What argument will I have? But if this one thing happens all together,
1.1000: that you take the statue and bear me away on your lovely ship, the venture is a noble one. If I am separated from this, I am lost, but you might settle your affairs well and have a safe return. Indeed, I do not shrink from it, not even if I must die
1.1005:
to save you. No, for when a man dies and is gone from the home, he is longed for; but women are powerless.
Orestes
1.1007: I would not be the murderer of you as well as my mother; her blood is enough; I would rather have an equal share of life or death, in common with you.
1.1010: I will bring you home, if I myself escape from here, or if I die, I will remain here with you. Listen to what I think: if Artemis were hostile to this, how could Loxias have prophesied that I would take the statue of the goddess to Pallas’ city...
1.1015:
and see your face. Putting all these things together, I have hope of our return.
Iphigenia
1.1017:
But how may we live, and take what we want? For our return home suffers from this; but the will is present.
Orestes
1.1020:
Could we murder the king?
Iphigenia
1.1021:
A fearful suggestion, for foreigners to kill their host!
Orestes
1.1022:
But we must dare it, if it brings our safety.
Iphigenia
1.1023:
I could not; yet I approve your eagerness.
Orestes
1.1024:
What if you were to hide me secretly in the shrine?
Iphigenia
1.1025:
So that we might take advantage of the darkness and escape?
Orestes
1.1026:
Yes, for the night belongs to thieves, the light to truth.
Iphigenia
1.1027:
There are secred guards within, who will notice us.
Orestes
1.1028:
Alas, we are ruined! How can we be saved?
Iphigenia
1.1029:
I think I have a new stratagem.
Orestes
1.1030:
What is it? Let me know; share your thought.
Iphigenia
1.1031:
I will use your sorrows as my contrivance.
Orestes
1.1032:
Women are wonderfully good at devising crafty plans!
Iphigenia
1.1033:
I will say that you came from Argos after killing your mother.
Orestes
1.1034:
Make use of my troubles, if you gain by it.
Iphigenia
1.1035:
And that it is not right to sacrifice you to the goddess.
Orestes
1.1036:
With what reason? I have a suspicion.
Iphigenia
1.1037:
Because you are not pure; I will frighten what is sacred.
Orestes
1.1038:
How does this help us to seize the statue of the goddess?
Iphigenia
1.1039:
I shall want to purify you in the waves of the sea—
Orestes
1.1040:
The image that we have sailed for is still in the temple.
Iphigenia
1.1041:
I will say that I have washed that also, since you have touched it.
Orestes
1.1042:
Where? Do you mean the watery inlet of the sea?
Iphigenia
1.1043:
Where your ship is moored by its roped anchor.
Orestes
1.1044:
Will you or some other bear the image in your hands?
Iphigenia
1.1045:
I shall; it is holy for me alone to touch it.
Orestes
1.1046:
But Pylades here—how will he be assigned to our labor?
Iphigenia
1.1047:
His hands, it will be said, are stained like yours with blood-pollution.
Orestes
1.1048:
Will you do all this secretly from the king, or with his knowledge?
Iphigenia
1.1049:
I shall persuade him; I could not hide it from him.
Orestes
1.1050:
Well then, my ship, with its quick stroke of oars, is at hand.
Iphigenia
1.1051:
You must indeed take care of the rest, so that it goes well.
Orestes
1.1052: We need only one thing more, that these women conceal our plans; you approach them and find persuasive words. A woman has power over pity.
1.1055:
The rest, perhaps—. May all turn out well!
Iphigenia
1.1056: My dearest friends, I look to you; I am in your hands, whether I am to succeed, or come to nothing and lose my country, and my dear brother and dearest sister.
1.1060: And first of all, I begin my speech with this: we are women, and have hearts naturally formed to love each other, and keep our common interests most secure. Be silent for us and assist us in our flight. It is good to have trustworthy speech.
1.1065: You see how one fortune holds us three, most dear to each other, either to return to our native land, or to die. If I am saved, I will bring you safe to Hellas, so that you may share my fortune. By your right hand, I entreat you, and you, and you; (addressing different members of the Chorus.) you by your dear face,
1.1070:
by your knees, by all that is dearest to you in your home: father, mother, child, if you have children. What do you reply? Who agrees with us, or is not willing to do this—speak! For if you do not acquiesce in my words, both I and my unhappy brother must die.
Chorus Leader
1.1075:
Have courage, dear mistress, only see to your safety; I will be silent on all that you have charged me with—great Zeus be my witness.
Iphigenia
1.1078: Bless you for your words, may you be happy! It is your work now, and yours, To Orestes and Pylades to enter the temple;
1.1080: for soon the ruler of this land will come, inquiring if the sacrifice of the strangers has been carried out.
1.1082: Lady Artemis, you who saved me from my father’s slaughtering hand by the clefts of Aulis, save me now also, and these men; or through you Loxias’
1.1085:
prophetic voice will no longer be held true by mortals But leave this barbarian land for Athens with good will; it is not fitting for you to dwell here, when you could have so fortunate a city. Exeunt Iphigenia, Orestes, and Pylades.
Chorus
1.1089: Halcyon bird, you that sing your fate as a lament
1.1090: beside the rocky ridges of the sea, a cry easily understood by the wise, that you are always chanting for your husband; I, wingless bird that I am, compare
1.1095: my laments with yours, in my longing for the festivals of Hellas, and for Artemis of childbirth, who dwells beside the Cynthian mountain and the palm with delicate leaves
1.1100: and the well-grown laurel and the holy shoot of gray-green olive, Leto’s dear child, and the lake that rolls about its ripples, where the melodious swan
1.1106: O streams of tears that fell onto my cheeks, when my city was destroyed and the enemy forced me to sail,
1.1110: by their oars, by their spears! Purchased by gold, I came to a barbarian home, where I serve Agamemnon’s daughter,
1.1115: the attendant maid of the deer-killing goddess, and the altars where no sheep are sacrificed; and I envy ruin that is wretched throughout, for when you are brought up in harsh necessity, you do not suffer.
1.1120:
Misery changes; life is hard for mortals, when they are treated badly after happiness.
Chorus
1.1123: And you, lady, the Argive penteconter will bear you home;
1.1125: the wax-bound reed of the mountain god Pan, piping, will shout to the oars, and Phoebus the prophet, with the ring of his seven-stringed lyre,
1.1130: singing, will guide you well to the gleaming land of the Athenians. Leaving me here, you will go with splashing oars. In the breeze, the forestays of the ship that carries you swiftly
1.1135:
will spread out over the front beyond the prow.
Chorus
1.1138: May I come to the bright race-course, where the sun’s fire goes;
1.1140: over the chambers of my home, may I cease to flutter the wings on my back. May I take my stand in the dances of glorious marriages, where I stood as a maiden,
1.1145: twirling about in the dancing bands of other girls, away from my dear mother; rushing on to the contest of charms, the luxuriant strife of hair, I covered my cheeks with the multi-colored veil
1.1150:
and shadowed them with the locks of my hair.
Thoas
1.1153: Where is the gate-keeper of this temple, the woman of Hellas? Has she already begun the rites on the strangers?
1.1155:
Are they glowing with fire in the holy sanctuary?
Chorus Leader
1.1156:
Here she is, to tell you everything clearly, lord.
Thoas
1.1157:
Oh! Daughter of Agamemnon, why have you lifted up in your arms the statue of the goddess from its pedestal that must not be moved?
Iphigenia
1.1159:
Lord, stand there in the entrance!
Thoas
1.1160:
Iphigenia, what has happened in the temple?
Iphigenia
1.1161:
I spit out the pollution; (turning to Thoas to explain.) I say this for Holiness.
Thoas
1.1162:
What is this news in your introduction? Tell it clearly.
Iphigenia
1.1163:
The victims you caught for me are not pure, lord.
Thoas
1.1164:
What taught you this? Or are you only saying what you think?
Iphigenia
1.1165:
The image of the goddess turned back from its place.
Thoas
1.1166:
By itself, or did an earthquake turn it?
Iphigenia
1.1167:
By itself; it closed up its eyes.
Thoas
1.1168:
What was the reason? Was it the uncleanness of the strangers?
Iphigenia
1.1169:
That was the reason, and nothing else; for they have done dreadful things.
Thoas
1.1170:
What, have they killed one of the barbarians on the shore?
Iphigenia
1.1171:
They come with murder done at home.
Thoas
1.1172:
What murder? For I strongly want to know.
Iphigenia
1.1173:
They killed their mother together with their swords.
Thoas
1.1174:
Apollo! No barbarian would have dared this.
Iphigenia
1.1175:
They were driven in pursuit from all of Hellas.
Thoas
1.1176:
Is it for this that you bring the statue outside?
Iphigenia
1.1177:
Yes, to the holy air, to remove it from slaughter.
Thoas
1.1178:
How did you know the blood-pollution of the strangers?
Iphigenia
1.1179:
I questioned them, because the image of the goddess had turned back.
Thoas
1.1180:
Hellas has brought you up to be clever; how well you understood this.
Iphigenia
1.1181:
And yet they dangled a sweet lure for my heart.
Thoas
1.1182:
Reporting to you some charm of news from Argos?
Iphigenia
1.1183:
That Orestes, my only brother, is happy.
Thoas
1.1184:
So that you might save them, for the delight of their messages.
Iphigenia
1.1185:
And that my father is alive and doing well.
Thoas
1.1186:
But you turned to the goddess, with reason.
Iphigenia
1.1187:
Yes, for I hate all Hellas, which has ruined me.
Thoas
1.188:
Tell me, what shall we do with the strangers?
Iphigenia
1.1189:
We must reverence the law as it stands.
Thoas
1.1190:
But the libations and your sword are not at work?
Iphigenia
1.1191:
First I want to wash them, with holy purification.
Thoas
1.1192:
In fountain waters, or the drops of the sea?
Iphigenia
1.1193:
The sea washes away all men’s evils.
Thoas
1.1194:
They would certainly be holier victims for the goddess.
Iphigenia
1.1195:
And in this way my plans would succeed better.
Thoas
1.1196:
Doesn’t the wave beat against this very temple?
Iphigenia
1.1197:
This requires solitude; and I shall do more.
Thoas
1.1198:
Then where you wish; I do not want to see what should not be seen.
Iphigenia
1.1199:
I must purify the image of the goddess also.
Thoas
1.1200:
Yes, if a stain from the matricide has fallen on it.
Iphigenia
1.1201:
For I would not have lifted it from its base otherwise.
Thoas
1.1202:
Your piety and forethought are correct.
Iphigenia
1.1203:
Do you know what to do for me now?
Thoas
It is for you to make it known.
Iphigenia
1.1204:
Put chains on the strangers.
Thoas
Where could they escape you?
Iphigenia
1.1205:
Hellas knows no faith.
Thoas
(to his servants.) Go to get chains, attendants.
Iphigenia
1.1206:
And let them bring the strangers here.
Thoas
It will be so.
Iphigenia
1.1207:
And veil their faces with their robes.
Thoas
Before the light of the sun.
Iphigenia
1.1208:
And send some of your servants with me.
Thoas
These will attend you.
Iphigenia
1.1209:
And send someone to announce to the city—
Thoas
That what has happened?
Iphigenia
1.1210:
That all remain indoors.
Thoas
So that they do not come in contact with murder?
Iphigenia
1.1211:
Yes, for such things are polluted.
Thoas
(to a servant.) Go and announce—
Iphigenia
1.1212:
That no one come near the sight. An attendant departs.
Thoas
You are taking good care of the city
Iphigenia
1.1213:
And of the friends to whom I owe the most.
Thoas
You mean this for me.
Iphigenia
1.1214:
...
Thoas
The whole city marvels at you, with reason.
Iphigenia
1.1215:
You stay here before the shrine of the goddess.
Thoas
What shall I do?
Iphigenia
1.1216:
Purify the house with fire.
Thoas
So that you may return to find it pure.
Iphigenia
1.1217:
When the strangers come outside—
Thoas
What must I do?
Iphigenia
1.1218:
Hold your robe over your eyes.
Thoas
So that I do not receive the pollution.
Iphigenia
1.1219:
If I seem to delay too long—
Thoas
What limit of the delay should I keep in mind?
Iphigenia
1.1220:
Do not wonder at it.
Thoas
Carry out the rites of the goddess well, since you have leisure.
Iphigenia
1.1221:
May this purification fall out as I wish!
Thoas
I pray along with you.

Iphigenia
1.1222: I see the strangers coming out of the temple now, and the ornaments of the goddess and the new-born lambs, because I will wash blood-pollution away with blood, and the flash of torches and all the rest that
1.1225: I have set out as purification for the strangers and the goddess.
1.1226: I proclaim to the citizens to keep away from this pollution, if any guard of the temple is purifying his hands for the gods, or if anyone is coming to form a marriage alliance, or is weighted down by childbirth— begone, stand away, so that this defilement does not fall on anyone.
1.1230:
(Aside.) O lady, maiden daughter of of Leto and Zeus, if I cleanse the stain of murder from these men, and make the sacrifice where I ought to make it, you will dwell in a pure home, and we will be fortunate. I do not speak the rest, but I indicate it to those who know more, the gods and you, goddess. Exit Iphigenia.
Chorus

and gave the privilege back again to Loxias, and to mortals confidence in the songs of prophecy at the throne visited by many men.
Messenger
1.1284: O you that guard the temple and stand by the altar,
1.1285:
where has Thoas, the lord of this land, gone? Open the well-fastened gates, and call forth from this shrine the ruler of the land.
Chorus Leader
1.1288:
What is it, if I may speak when not commanded?
Messenger
1.1289: The two young men are gone away,
1.1290:
through the plots of Agamemnon’s daughter; they are escaping from this land, with the holy image deep within a Hellene ship.
Chorus Leader
1.1293:
What you say is incredible; but the one you want to see, the lord of the country, has gone in haste from the temple.
Messenger
1.1295:
Where? For he should know what has been done.
Chorus Leader
1.1296:
We don’t know; but go after him, and report these things to him where you find him.
Messenger
1.1298:
See, what a faithless race you women are! You also have a share in what has been done.
Chorus Leader
1.1300:
You are mad! What do we have to do the the flight of the strangers? Go as quickly as you can to the ruler’s door!
Messenger
1.1302: No! Not until this interpreter brings word if the king is inside or not. Ho there! Unbar the doors—I am speaking to those within—
1.1305:
and inform the master that I am at the gate with a burden of bad news.
Thoas
1.1307:
(appearing at the temple door.) Who is raising this clamor at the temple of the goddess, striking at the gates and sending his noise within?
Messenger
1.1309: Ah! These women told me that you were outside; they would have driven me away from the temple,
1.1310:
but you were inside after all.
Thoas
1.1311:
What advantage were they expecting and hunting after?
Messenger
1.1312: I will tell you about them later; hear what is currently at hand. The girl who presided at this altar, Iphigenia, has left the country
1.1315:
with the strangers, and takes with her the holy statue of the goddess; the purification was a cheat.
Thoas
1.1317:
What are you saying? What influence in her character brought her to this?
Messenger
1.1318:
To save Orestes; here is a marvel for you!
Thoas
1.1319:
To save whom? Clytemnestra’s son?
Messenger
1.1320:
The one whom the goddess was dedicating to herself at this altar.
Thoas
1.1321:
Marvelous! for what more can it be called?
Messenger
1.1322:
Do not think of that, but listen to me; consider it clearly and when you hear, devise a pursuit to hunt down the strangers.
Thoas
1.1325:
Speak; you have said well; for their flight is not so brief a voyage as to escape my spear.
Messenger
1.1327: When we came to the sea-shore, where Orestes’ ship was moored in hiding,
1.1330: Agamemnon’s daughter motioned to those of us you sent with the strangers’ bonds to stand far off, as if her sacrifice of purifying flame, that she had come for, were secret. But she went on alone, holding the strangers’ chains in her hands, behind them. Your servants, lord, were suspicious,
1.1335: but we allowed it. After a while, so that we might think that she was accomplishing something, she raised a shout, and chanted strange songs and spells, as if she were washing off the pollution of murder. When we had sat a long time,
1.1340: it occurred to us that the strangers, loosed from their bonds, might kill her and escape by flight. But we were afraid of seeing what we ought not, and sat in silence. But at length we all resolved to go where they were, although we were not allowed.
1.1345: There we saw a Hellene ship, winged with ready blade for the stroke, and at the oar-locks were fifty rowers with their oars; the two youths stood by the stern, freed from their chains.
1.1350: Some were holding the prow in place with poles; others were fastening the anchor from the cat-heads; others were drawing the stern-cables through their hands, and making haste to let down the ladders into the sea for the strangers. Without sparing ourselves, when we saw
1.1355: their treacherous wiles, we seized the priestess and the cables, and tried to draw the ship’s rudder-oars out through their holes. Then there was a debate: What is your reason for carrying the statue and the priestess away from the land by theft?
1.1360: Who is your father, who are you, to smuggle her away? He said: Know that I am Orestes, her brother, Agamemnon’s son, and I have come to take my sister, whom I lost from her home.
1.1364: But we held her no less,
1.1365: and were leading her to you by force, for which I received these dreadful blows on my cheeks; they had no swords, nor did we. Both the youths gave rattling blows with their fists,
1.1370: darting their limbs against our sides and breasts, so that as soon as we joined battle, we were worn out. We were fleeing to the cliff, stamped with dreadful marks, some with bloody wounds on their heads, others on their eyes;
1.1375: when we stood on the on the heights, we fought more cautiously and hurled rocks at them. But, standing on the stern, the archers with their arrows kept us off and drove us away. And now an immense swelling wave ran the ship aground,
1.1380: and the maiden was afraid to get her feet wet. Orestes bore his sister on his left arm, going into the sea and quickly up the ladder, and he set her on the ship, along with the statue of Zeus’ daughter, fallen from heaven.
1.1385: From the middle of the ship, he cried out: Sailors of Hellas, seize the ship with the oars and make the waves white with foam; for we possess those things for which we sailed the inhospitable straits, within the clashing rocks.
1.1390: They gave a cheerful shout, and struck the salt wave. The ship, while it was within the harbor, was headed for the mouth; but when it had crossed, it met with a violent swell aand was hard pressed; and the wind, rising with sudden dreadful gusts,
1.1395: forced it astern. They beat the waves strongly; but the swell was driving the ship back towards the land. Agamemnon’s daughter stood up and prayed: O daughter of Leto, bring me, your priestess, safely to Hellas
1.1400: from this barbaric land, and forgive my thefts. For you, goddess, love your brother; believe that I love mine also. The sailors shouted the paean in response to her prayer, and applied their naked shoulders
1.1405: to the oars, at the command. But the ship came nearer and nearer to the rocks; some of us rushed into the sea, others grasped the woven ropes. And I set out here to you at once, lord,
1.1410: to tell you what has happened there. But go, take chains and nets with you; for if the swell does not become calm, there is no hope of safety for the strangers.
1.1415:
Revered Poseidon, ruler of the sea, watches over Troy and is hostile to the race of Pelops; he will now allow you and your citizens, as is right, to have in your hands the son of Agamemnon and his sister; she stands convicted as betrayer of her unremembered sacrifice to the goddess in Aulis.
Chorus Leader
1.1420:
Unhappy Iphigenia, you will die with your brother, if you come again into the hands of the king.
Thoas
1.1422: All citizens of this barbarian land, hurl the reins on your horses, rush to the coast and seize what the Hellene ship
1.1425: casts forth! With the goddess’ help, be eager to hunt down these impious men! Drag the swift ships to the sea! So that by sea and with pursuit on horseback by land, you may take them; and hurl their bodies from the hard rock,
1.1430: or impale them on the stake.
1.1431:
(Turning to the Chorus.) As for you women, who knew about these plots, I will punish you later, when I am at leisure. But now in this present urgency, I will not remain still.
Athena
1.1435: Where, where are you carrying this pursuit, lord Thoas? Listen the words of Athena, who is here. Cease to follow or to send an army pouring forth; for Orestes came here, destined by the oracles of Loxias, to flee from the anger of the Furies,
1.1440: and to bring his sister to Argos and take the holy statue to my land, thus gaining a release from his present miseries. Thoas, I am speaking to you: you expect to take Orestes in the sea-swell and kill him; but Poseidon, for my sake,
1.1445: now lets him sail over the back of the waveless sea.
1.1446: And you, Orestes, attend to my commands, for you hear the goddess’ voice even though not present: go away with the statue and your sister; and when you come to Athens, built by the gods,
1.1450: there is a place on the farthest borders of the Attic land, neighbor to the ridge of Carystia, sacred, and my people call it Halae. There build a temple and set up the image in it; it will have its name from the Tauric land and from your labors,
1.1455: which you have endured, wandering through Hellas and goaded by the Furies. And mortals will in future times celebrate Artemis Tauropolos with hymns. And establish this law: whenever the people keep the festival, let a sword be held
1.1460: to a man’s throat and draw out blood, in atonement for your sacrifice, so that the goddess may have her honors, and holiness is revered.
1.1462: You, Iphigenia, must be key-holder for this goddess on the hallowed stairs of Brauron, and will die there and be buried;
1.1465: and they will dedicate adornment to you, finely-woven robes which women who have died in childbirth leave in their homes. I charge you to send these Hellene women to their country, for their correct intentions.... For I saved you
1.1470:
before also, Orestes, on Ares’ hill when the votes were equal; and this will be the custom, for the one with equal votes to win. But, son of Agamemnon, take your sister away from this land. And you, Thoas, do not be angry.
Thoas
1.1475: Lady Athena, whoever hears the words of the gods and does not obey, is not thinking rightly. I am not angry at Orestes, for going off with the goddess’ image, or at his sister; for what good is it to contend against the strength of gods?
1.1480: Let them go to your land with the statue of the goddess, and let them establish it there, with good fortune. I will send these women also to fortunate Hellas, as you bid me. And I will stop the army
1.1485:
and the ships I raised against the strangers, as you think this right, goddess.
Athena
1.1486: I commend you; for necessity rules both you and the gods.
1.1487:
Go, winds, carry the son of Agamemnon to Athens by sea; I will journey with them, and keep safe the holy image of my sister.
Chorus
1.1490: Go with good fortune, blessed in having your portion of safety.
1.1493: Pallas Athena, holy among immortals and mortals, we will do as you command.
1.1495: For we receive your voice in our ears with great and unexpected pleasure.
1.1497: Greatly revered Victory, may you occupy my life and never cease to crown me!

1.0: Scene.— Tomb of Proteus in the island of Pharos. Helen
1.1: These are the lovely pure streams of the Nile, which waters the plain and lands of Egypt, fed by white melting snow instead of rain from heaven. Proteus was king of this land when he was alive,
1.5: living on the island of Pharos and lord of Egypt; and he married one of the daughters of the sea, Psamathe, after she left Aiakos’ bed. She bore two children in his palace here: a son Theoklymenos,
1.10: and a noble daughter, her mother’s pride, called Eido in her infancy. But when she came to youth, the season of marriage, she was called Theonoe; for she knew whatever the gods design, both present and to come,
1.15: having received this honor from her grandfather Nereus.
1.16: My own fatherland, Sparta, is not without fame, and my father is Tyndareus; but there is indeed a story that Zeus flew to my mother Leda, taking the form of a bird, a swan,
1.20: which accomplished the deceitful union, fleeing the pursuit of an eagle, if this story is true. My name is Helen; I will tell the evils I have suffered. For the sake of beauty, three goddesses came to a deep valley on Mount Ida, to Paris:
1.25: Hera and Kypris, and the virgin daughter of Zeus, wishing to have the judgment of their loveliness decided. Kypris offered my beauty, if misfortune is beautiful, for Paris to marry, and so she won. Paris, the shepherd of Ida, left his ox-stalls
1.30: and came to Sparta, to have me in marriage.
1.31: But Hera, indignant at not defeating the goddesses, made an airy nothing of my marriage with Paris; she gave to the son of king Priam not me, but an image, alive and breathing, that she fashioned out of the sky and made to look like me;
1.35: and he thinks he has me—an idle fancy, for he doesn’t have me. And in turn the plans of Zeus added further troubles to these; for he brought a war upon the land of the Hellenes and the unhappy Phrygians, so that he might lighten mother earth
1.40: of her crowded mass of mortals, and bring fame to the bravest man of Hellas. So I was set up as the Hellenes’ spear-prize, to test the courage of the Trojans; or rather not me, but my name. Hermes caught me up in the folds of the air and
1.45: hid me in a cloud—for Zeus was not neglectful of me—and he set me down here in the house of Proteus, having selected the most self-controlled of all mankind, so that I might keep my bed pure for Menelaos. And so I am here, while my wretched husband
1.50: has gathered an army and gone over to the towers of Ilion to hunt down and recover me. And many lives have been lost for my sake by the streams of Skamandros; and I who have endured all this am accursed, and have in appearance betrayed my husband
1.55: and brought a great war to the Hellenes. Why then am I still alive? I heard the god Hermes declare that I would yet live in the glorious country of Sparta, with my husband—for Hermes knew I never went to Ilion—so that I would not go to bed with another man.
1.60: Well, as long as Proteus saw this light of the sun, I was safe from marriage; but now that he is hidden in the dark earth, the dead man’s son hunts after a marriage with me. But I, out of regard to my husband of long ago, am throwing myself down as a suppliant before this tomb of Proteus,
1.65:
for him to keep my bed safe for my husband, so that, if I bear a name infamous throughout Hellas, at least my body may not incur disgrace here.
Teucer
1.68: Who holds power over this fortified house? The dwelling is worthy of comparison with Ploutos’,
1.70: its royal enclosures and towering buildings. Ah! Oh gods, what sight is here? I see the hateful deadly likeness of the woman who ruined me and all the Achaeans. May the gods spurn you, so much do you look like
1.75:
Helen! If I were not in a foreign land, you would have died by this well-aimed arrow as a reward for your likeness to the daughter of Zeus.
Helen
1.78:
What is it, poor man—who are you, that you have turned away from me and loathe me for the misfortunes of that one?
Teucer
1.80:
I was wrong; I gave way to my anger more than I should, for all Hellas hates that daughter of Zeus. Forgive me for what I said, lady.
Helen
1.83:
Who are you? Where have you come from, to visit this land?
Teucer
1.84:
I am one of those unfortunate Achaeans, lady.
Helen
1.85:
Then it is no wonder that you loathe Helen. But who are you and where do you come from? Whose son should I call you?
Teucer
1.87:
My name is Teucer, my father is Telamon, and Salamis is the land that nurtured me.
Helen
1.89:
Then why are you visiting these lands of the Nile?
Teucer
1.90:
I am an exile, driven out of my native land.
Helen
1.91:
You must be unhappy! Who banished you from your fatherland?
Teucer
1.92:
My father Telamon. Could you find anyone closer to me?
Helen
1.93:
But why? This matter is surely an unfortunate one.
Teucer
1.94:
The death of my brother Aias at Troy was my ruin.
Helen
1.95:
How so? You didn’t take his life with your sword, did you?
Teucer
1.96:
He threw himself on his own sword and died.
Helen
1.97:
Was he mad? For what sensible man would dare such a thing?
Teucer
1.98:
Do you know a certain Achilleus, the son of Peleus?
Helen
1.99:
Yes; he came to woo Helen once, so I hear.
Teucer
1.100:
When he died, he left a contest for his armor to his allies.
Helen
1.101:
Well, if he did, what harm is this to Aias?
Teucer
1.102:
When someone else got the arms, he took his own life.
Helen
1.103:
Then are you ill through his suffering?
Teucer
1.104:
Yes, because I did not die together with him.
Helen
1.105:
So you went to the famous city of Ilion, stranger?
Teucer
1.106:
Yes, and by helping to sack it, I destroyed myself as well.
Helen
1.107:
Has it already been set alight and completely consumed by fire?
Teucer
1.108:
So that not even a trace of the walls is evident.
Helen
1.109:
O miserable Helen! Because of you, the Phrygians have been destroyed.
Teucer
1.110:
And also the Achaeans; great evils have been committed.
Helen
1.111:
How long is it since the city was sacked?
Teucer
1.112:
Almost seven years have gone full circle, with their harvests.
Helen
1.113:
And how much longer were you waiting at Troy?
Teucer
1.114:
For many months; the moon held its course through ten years.
Helen
1.115:
And did you capture the Spartan woman?
Teucer
1.116:
Menelaos caught her by the hair to drag her away.
Helen
1.117:
Did you yourself see the wretched creature? Or do you speak from hearsay?
Teucer
1.118:
I saw her with my own eyes, just as I see you, no less.
Helen
1.119:
Consider whether you had some fancy, sent by the gods.
Teucer
1.120:
Think of some other topic, not that woman still!
Helen
1.121:
Are you so sure this fancy was reliable?
Teucer
1.122:
I saw it with my own eyes; and the mind has sight.
Helen
1.123:
Is Menelaos already at home with his wife?
Teucer
1.124:
No; he is neither in Argos nor by the streams of the Eurotas.
Helen
1.125:
Alas! This is evil news for those to whom you bring it.
Teucer
1.126:
He is said to have disappeared with his wife.
Helen
1.127:
Wasn’t there the same passage for all the Argives?
Teucer
1.128:
Yes; but a tempest scattered them in every direction.
Helen
1.129:
On which surface of the salty ocean?
Teucer
1.130:
While they were crossing the Aegean in mid-channel.
Helen
1.131:
And from that time does no one know of Menelaos’ arrival?
Teucer
1.132:
No one; but throughout Hellas he is reported to be dead.
Helen
1.133:
I am wholly lost. Is the daughter of Thestius alive?
Teucer
1.134:
You speak of Leda? She is dead and gone, indeed.
Helen
1.135:
It wasn’t Helen’s disgraceful fame that killed her, surely?
Teucer
1.136:
Yes, they say she tied a noose around her noble neck.
Helen
1.137:
Are the sons of Tyndareus still alive or not?
Teucer
1.138:
They are dead, and not dead: it is a double story.
Helen
1.139:
Which report is the stronger? I am so unhappy at these evils!
Teucer
1.140:
Men say that they are gods in the likeness of stars.
Helen
1.141:
That is good news; but what is the other story?
Teucer
1.142: That they killed themselves because of their sister. But enough of such talk! I do not need to grieve twice. As to why I came to this royal palace,
1.145: wanting to see the prophetess Theonoe, you be my patron, so I might obtain an oracle: how I should steer a favorable course to the island of Cyprus, where Apollo has declared I am to live, giving it the island name of
1.150:
Salamis in honor of that fatherland over there.
Helen
1.151: The voyage itself will explain that, stranger; leave this land and escape, before the son of Proteus, the ruler of this land, catches sight of you; now he is away with his trusty hounds tracking his savage quarry to the death;
1.155:
for he kills every visitor from Hellas that he catches. Do not seek to learn his reason, and I will not say; for how could I help you?
Teucer
1.158: Lady, you have spoken well. May the gods grant you a return for your kindness!
1.160:
Although you have a body like Helen’s, your heart is not like hers, but very different. May she die miserably, and never reach the streams of Eurotas! But may you always have good fortune, lady.
Exit Teucer. Helen
1.164: Oh, as I begin the great lament of my great distress,
1.165:
what mourning shall I strive to utter? or what Muse shall I approach with tears or songs of death or woe? Alas!
Helen
1.167: Winged maidens, virgin daughters of Earth, the Sirens, may you come to my mourning
1.170: with Libyan flute or pipe or lyre, tears to match my plaintive woes; grief for grief and mournful chant for chant, may Persephone send choirs of death
1.175:
in harmony with my lamentation, so that she may receive as thanks from me, in addition to my tears, a paean for the departed dead beneath her gloomy roof.
Chorus
1.180: and on the tangled grass, I happened to be drying purple robes in the sun’s golden blaze near the young reed shoots; from my mistress, from where she cried aloud her misery,
1.185: I heard a sound, a mournful song not fit for the lyre, because she was then shrieking, lamenting with her wails; just as a Naiad nymph, who sends a song of woe ringing over the hills, cries out, under the rocky hollows, with screams
1.190:
at the rape of Pan.
Helen
1.191: Oh! Oh! Maidens of Hellas, the prey of barbarian sailors! An Achaean sailor
1.195: came, he came bringing tears upon tears to me. Ilion has been destroyed and is left to the enemy’s fire through me, the death-giver, through my name, full of suffering.
1.200: Leda sought death by hanging, in anguish over my disgrace. My husband, after much wandering in the sea, has died and is gone;
1.205: and Castor and his brother, twin glory of their native land, have vanished, vanished, leaving the plains that shook to their galloping horses,
1.210:
and the schools of reed-fringed Eurotas, scene of youthful labors.
Chorus
1.211: Alas, alas! for your mournful fate and destiny, lady! You were fated, fated to have a life full of pain, when Zeus begot you on your mother,
1.215: shining through the air on the wings of a snow-white swan. What evil is not yours? What life have you not endured? Your mother is dead;
1.220: the twin beloved sons of Zeus do not enjoy happiness; and you do not see your fatherland, while through the cities a rumor goes, mistress, which hands you over
1.225:
to the bed of a barbarian; your husband has lost his life in the salty waves, and never again will you bring glee to your father’s halls and Athene of the Bronze House.
Helen
1.229: Ah! Who was it, either from Phrygia
1.230: or from Hellas, who cut the pine that brought tears to Ilion? From this wood the son of Priam built his deadly ship, and sailed by barbarian oars
1.235: to my home, to that most ill-fated beauty, to win me as his wife; and with him sailed deceitful and murderous Kypris, bearing death for the Danaans.
1.240: Oh, unhappy in my misfortune! But Hera, the holy beloved of Zeus on her golden throne, sent the swift-footed son of Maia. I was gathering fresh rose leaves in the folds of my robe,
1.245: so that I might go to the goddess of the Bronze House; he carried me off through the air to this luckless land, and made me an object of miserable strife, of strife between Hellas and the sons of Priam. And my name
1.250:
beside the streams of Simois bears a false rumor.
Chorus Leader
1.253:
You have sorrows, I know; but it is best to bear as lightly as we can the necessary evils of life.
Helen
1.255: Dear friends, to what a fate am I yoked? Did my mother bear me as a wonder to mankind?
1.260: My life and all I do is a wonder, partly because of Hera, and partly my beauty is to blame. If only I could be rubbed out like a painting, and have again in turn a plainer form instead of beauty, and the Hellenes would have forgotten the evil fate that I now have,
1.265: and would remember what part of my life is not evil, as they now remember what is.
1.267: When someone looks to one event only, and is ill-treated by the gods, it is hard, but all the same it can be borne. But I am involved in countless troubles.
1.270: First, although I never acted wrongly, my good name is gone. And this trouble is stronger than the reality, if someone incurs blame for wrongs that are not his own. Next, the gods have removed me from my native country to barbarian habits, and bereft of friends
1.275: I have become a slave although I am free by birth; for among barbarians all are slaves except one. And the only anchor of my fortunes is gone, the hope that my husband would come one day and free me of my woes—he is dead, he no longer exists.
1.280: My mother is dead, and I am called her murderer—unjustly, but that injustice is mine to bear; while the one who was born the glory of the house, my daughter, is growing gray as a virgin, without a husband; and those two Dioskouroi, called the sons of Zeus, are no more.
1.285: But with all my misfortunes, I am as good as dead in my circumstances, though not in fact. And this is the last evil of all: if ever I should come home, I would be shut out by barred doors, for people would think I was that Helen of Troy, coming back with Menelaos.
1.290: If my husband were still alive, we could have recognized each other by recourse to tokens which are evident to us alone. But now this is not so, and he can never be saved.
1.293: Why then do I still live? What fortune do I have left? Shall I choose marriage in exchange for evils,
1.295: and live with a barbarian man, seated at his sumptuous table? But whenever a husband she hates lives with a woman, her own body is also hateful to her. It is best to die; how could this not be well done?
1.300: For I have come to such a depth of misery; other women have good fortune from their beauty,
1.305:
but the same thing has destroyed me.
Chorus Leader
1.306:
Helen, do not suppose that stranger who came here, whoever he was, has spoken the whole truth.
Helen
1.308:
And yet he said very clearly that my husband was dead.
Chorus Leader
1.309:
Many words might be said in falsehood also.
Helen
1.310:
And the opposite of falsehood is clear in its truth.
Chorus Leader
1.311:
You are carried towards misfortune instead of what is good.
Helen
1.312:
Yes, for terror has embraced me and leads me to the thing I fear.
Chorus Leader
1.313:
How much goodwill is there in this house for you?
Helen
1.314:
All are my friends, except the one who hunts me in marriage.
Chorus Leader
1.315:
Then do you know what you should do? Leave your seat at the monument—
Helen
1.316:
What sort of word of advice are you coming to?
Chorus Leader
1.317: Go inside and question the daughter of the sea-nymph, Theonoe, who knows all things, about your husband, whether he is still alive, or has left the light of day;
1.320: and when you know for certain, rejoice or be full of mourning, according to your fortune. Before you know anything correctly, what good would it do you to grieve? But be persuaded by me; leave this tomb and join the girl;
1.325:
when you have someone in this house from whom you can learn the whole truth, why do you look further? And I myself want to go in and ask about the prophecies of the maiden with you; for, truly, women ought to help each other.
Helen
1.330:
Dear friends, I welcome your advice. Come in, come into the house, to learn within about my struggles.
Chorus
1.334:
You are calling on one who is wholly willing.
Helen
1.335:
Oh, what an unhappy day! What tearful word shall I hear, unhappy as I am?
Chorus
1.338:
Do not be a prophetess of sorrow, dear friend, anticipating lamentation.
Helen
1.340: What has my poor husband suffered? Does he see the light and the sun’s chariot and the paths of the stars? Or does he have a lasting fate
1.345:
among the dead beneath the earth?
Chorus
1.346:

towards my own dear brother, and throw my arms about my darling’s neck, so long, poor boy! an exile. How distinguished he is with his golden weapons, old man, flashing like the morning rays!
Old servant

He will come to this house, under truce, to fill your heart with joy.
Antigone
1.171:

Old servant
1.173:
That, lady, is the prophet Amphiaraus; with him are the victims, earth’s bloodthirsty streams.
Antigone
1.175:
Daughter of the sun with dazzling zone, O moon, you circle of golden light, how quietly, with what restraint he drives, goading first one horse, then the other! But where is the one who utters those dreadful insults against this city?
Old servant
1.180:
Capaneus? There he is, calculating how he may scale the towers, taking the measure of our walls up and down.
Antigone
1.182: O Nemesis, and roaring thunder-peals of Zeus and blazing lightning-bolts, oh! put to sleep his presumptuous boasting!
