Never, never, Lady Artemis, golden-haired child of Zeus, may I endure that slavery.
Old servant
1.193: My child, go inside, and stay beneath the shelter of your maiden chamber, now that you have had
1.195: your wish and seen all that you wanted; for a crowd of women is coming toward the royal palace, as confusion enters the city. Now women by nature love scandal; and if they get some slight handle for their gossip
1.200:
they exaggerate it, for women seem to have pleasure in saying nothing wholesome about each other. Exeunt Antigone and the old servant.

1.205: to be a slave to Phoebus in his halls, where he dwells under the snow-swept peaks of Parnassus; through the Ionian sea I sailed in the waves,
1.210:
over the unharvested plains, in the gusts of Zephyrus that ride from Sicily, sweetest music in the sky.

1.215: as beauty’s gift for Loxias, to the land of Cadmus I came, sent here to the towers of Laius, the home of my kin, the famous sons of Agenor.

for the service of Phoebus.

1.235:

suffers any mischance, Phoenicia’s realm will share it. Ah me! our blood is one; we are all children of Io, the horned maid; these sorrows I claim as mine.

1.260:

and I am called Polyneices by the people of Thebes.

1.301: Maidens, I hear your Phoenician voice, and my old feet drag their tottering steps. O my son,

1.355:

1.385:
No, question me, leave out nothing; for your will, mother, is my pleasure too.

Well then, first I ask you what I long to have answered. What is it, to be deprived of one’s country? Is it a great evil?
Polyneices

Polyneices
1.391:
One thing most of all; he cannot speak his mind.

1.392:

Polyneices
1.393:

Jocasta
1.394:

Polyneices
1.395:

Jocasta
1.396:
Hope, they say, is the exile’s food.

Yes, hope that looks so fair; but always in the future.

Polyneices

Jocasta

Sometimes I would have enough for the day, and sometimes not.

1.402:
Didn’t your father’s friends and guests assist you?
Polyneices
1.403:
Seek to be prosperous; friends are nothing in misfortune.
Jocasta
1.404:

Polyneices
1.405:

Jocasta
1.406:
Man’s dearest treasure, it seems, is his country.
Polyneices
1.407:
You could not name how dear it is!
Jocasta

Polyneices
1.409:
Loxias gave Adrastus an oracle.
Jocasta
1.410:

Polyneices
1.411:

1.412:

1.413:

1.414:

Polyneices
1.415:
It was night when I reached the porch of Adrastus.
Jocasta
1.416:

Polyneices
1.417:
Yes; and then another exile came there.
Jocasta
1.418:

1.419:

Polyneices
1.421:

Polyneices
1.423:

Polyneices

As yet I have no fault to find with it.
Jocasta

and of all things in the world it has the greatest power. This I have come to secure at the head of my great army; for a man well-born but poor is worth nothing.

arbitration between us, by which you persuaded me to admit this man under truce within the walls.

Polyneices
1.469: The words of truth are naturally simple,
1.470: and justice needs no subtle interpretations, for it has a fitness in itself; but the words of injustice, being sick in themselves, require clever treatment. I provided for his interests and mine in our father’s house, being anxious to escape the curse

1.480: doing others harm and suffering it myself, as is now the case. But he, after consenting to this and calling the gods to witness his oath, has performed none of his promises, but is still keeping the sovereignty in his own hands together with my share of our heritage.
1.484: And now I am ready to take my own
1.485: and dismiss the army from this land, receiving my house in turn to dwell in, and once more restore it to him for an equal period, instead of ravaging our country and bringing scaling-ladders against the towers,
1.490: as I shall attempt to do if I do not get my rights. I call the gods to witness that spite of my just dealing in everything I am being unjustly robbed of my country, a most unholy act. I have made my points, mother, without stringing together

words to entangle you, but urging a fair case, I think, in the judgment of the wise and the simple.
Chorus Leader
1.497:
To me, although I was not born and bred in Hellas, your words seem full of sense.

He says the Argive army intend at once to wind about

Across those trenches, to fight at once.
Creon
1.715:
Our forces are small, while theirs are plentiful.
Eteocles
1.716:
I know well they are brave in argument.

1.717:
Argos has some weight among the Hellenes.
Eteocles
1.718:
Never fear! I will soon fill the plain with their dead.
Creon
1.719:
I could wish it so; but I see great difficulties in this.
Eteocles
1.720:
I will not keep my army within the walls.
Creon
1.721:

Eteocles
1.722:
Do you then want me to turn to some other way?

1.723:
Yes, to every one, before running the risk once for all.
Eteocles
1.724:

1.725:

1.726:

1.727:

1.728:

1.729:

1.730:

1.731:

Eteocles

Creon

They have seven men, I hear—
Eteocles
1.738:

Eteocles

Eteocles

1.5: Tantalus, the reputed son of Zeus, flies in the air, quailing at the rock which looms above his head; paying this penalty, they say, for the shameful weakness he displayed in failing to keep a bridle on his lips, when admitted by gods, though he was a man,
1.10: to share the honors of their feasts like one of them.
1.11: He begot Pelops, the father of Atreus, for whom the goddess, when she had carded her wool, spun a web of strife—to make war with his own brother Thyestes. But why need I retrace that hideous tale?
1.15: Well, Atreus slew Thyestes’ children and feasted him on them. Atreus, now; I pass over intermediate events; from Atreus and Aerope of Crete were born the famous Agamemnon, if he really was famous, and Menelaus. Now Menelaus married Helen,
1.20: the gods’ abhorrence; while lord Agamemnon married Clytemnestra, notorious in Hellas; and we three daughters were born: Chrysothemis, Iphigenia, and myself, Electra; also a son Orestes; all from that one accursed mother,
1.25: who slew her husband, after snaring him in an inextricable robe. Her reason a maiden’s lips may not declare, and so I leave it unclear for the world to guess at. What need for me to charge Phoebus with wrong-doing? Though he persuaded Orestes
1.30: to slay his own mother, a deed that few approved. Still it was his obedience to the god that made him kill her; I had a share in the murder, in so far as a woman could,
1.34: After this my poor Orestes, wasting away in a cruel disease,
1.35: lies fallen on his couch, and it is his mother’s blood that drives him round and round in frenzied fits; I am ashamed to name the goddesses, whose terrors are chasing him—the Eumenides. It is now the sixth day
1.40: since the body of his murdered mother was committed to the cleansing fire; since then no food has gone down his throat, nor has he washed his skin; but wrapped in his cloak he weeps in his lucid moments, whenever the fever leaves him;
1.45: at other times he bounds headlong from his couch, as a colt when it is loosed from the yoke. This city of Argos has decreed that no man give us shelter in home or hearth, or speak to matricides like us; and this is the fateful day on which the Argives will take a vote,
1.50: whether we are both to die by stoning. There is, it is true, one hope of escape from death: Menelaus has landed from Troy; his fleet now crowds the haven of Nauplia where he has come to anchor on the shore, returned at last from Troy
1.55: after ceaseless wanderings; but Helen, that so-called lady of sorrows, he has sent on to our palace, waiting for the night, lest any of those parents whose sons died at Troy might see her if she went by day, and set to stoning her.
1.60: Within she sits, weeping for her sister and the calamities of her family, and yet she has still some solace in her woe; for Hermione, the child she left at home when she sailed for Troy, the maid whom Menelaus brought from Sparta
1.65: and entrusted to my mother’s keeping, is still a cause of joy to her and a reason to forget her sorrows.
1.67: I am watching each approach, until I see Menelaus arriving; for unless we find some safety from him, we have only a feeble anchor to ride on otherwise.
1.70:
A helpless thing, an unlucky house!
Helen
1.71: Daughter of Clytemnestra and Agamemnon, unhappy Electra, a maiden for so long, how is it with you and your brother, this ill-starred Orestes who slew his mother?
1.75: For referring the sin as I do to Phoebus, I incur no pollution by addressing you; and yet I am truly sorry for the death of my sister Clytemnestra, whom I never saw after I was driven by heaven-sent frenzy to sail as I did to Ilium;
1.80:
but now that I am parted from her, I bewail our misfortunes.
Electra
1.81: Helen, why should I speak of that which your own eyes can see?
1.83: Beside his wretched corpse I sit, sleepless—for corpse he is, so faint his breath—
1.85:
not that I reproach him with his sufferings; but you are highly blessed and your husband too.
Helen
1.88:
How long has he lain in this way on the couch?
Electra
1.89:
Ever since he spilt his mother’s blood.
Helen
1.90:
Unhappy wretch! unhappy mother! what a death she died.
Electra
1.91:
Unhappy enough to succumb to his misery.
Helen
1.92:
By the gods, would you hear me a moment, maiden?
Electra
1.93:
Yes, with such leisure as this watching over a brother leaves.
Helen
1.94:
Will you go for me to my sister’s tomb?
Electra
1.95:
Would you have me seek my mother’s tomb? Why?
Helen
1.96:
To carry an offering of hair and a libation from me.
Electra
1.97:
Isn’t it right for you to go to the tomb of one you love?
Helen
1.98:
No, for I am ashamed to show myself in Argos.
Electra
1.99:
A late repentance surely for one who left her home so shamefully then.
Helen
1.100:
You have told the truth, but your telling is not kind to me.
Electra
1.101:
What is this supposed shame before the eyes of Mycenae that possesses you?
Helen
1.102:
I am afraid of the fathers of those who lie dead at Ilium.
Electra
1.103:
Good cause for fear; your name is on every tongue in Argos.
Helen
1.104:
Then free me of my fear and grant me this favor.
Electra
1.105:
I could not bear to look upon my mother’s grave.
Helen
1.106:
And yet it would be shame indeed for servants to bear these offerings.
Electra
1.107:
Then why not send your daughter Hermione?
Helen
1.108:
It is not good for maidens to go into a crowd.
Electra
1.109:
And yet she would be repaying her dead foster-mother’s care.
Helen
1.110: You have told the truth and have convinced me, maiden. Calling. Hermione, my child, come out, before the palace. Take these libations and these tresses of mine in your hands, and go pour round Clytemnestra’s tomb
1.115: a mingled cup of honey, milk, and frothing wine; then stand upon the heaped-up grave, and say this: Helen, your sister, sends you these libations as her gift, fearing herself to approach your tomb from terror of the Argive mob and bid her harbor kindly thoughts
1.120: towards me and you and my husband; towards these two wretched sufferers, too, whom the gods have destroyed. And promise that I will pay in full whatever funeral gifts are due from me to a sister. Now go, my child, and hurry;
1.125:
and soon as you have made the libations at the tomb, think of your return. Exit Helen.
Electra
1.126: O human nature, how great an evil you are in men! and what salvation, too, to those who have a goodly heritage there.
1.128: Did you see how she cut off her hair only at the ends, to preserve its beauty? She is the same woman as of old.
1.130: May the gods hate you! for you have proved the ruin of me and my brother and all Hellas.
1.132: Alas! here are my friends once more, coming to unite their plaintive dirge with mine; they will soon put an end to my brother’s peaceful sleep, and cause my tears to flow
1.135: when I see him in frenzy.
1.136: The Chorus of Argive Maidens enters quietly. The following lines between Electra and the Chorus are chanted responsively. Chorus
1.140:
Hush, hush! let your footsteps fall lightly! not a sound!
Electra
1.142:
Go further from his couch, further, I beseech you!
Chorus
1.145:
Ah, ah! Speak like the breath of a slender reed-pipe, my dear, I pray.
Chorus
1.147:
See, how soft and low I drop my voice.
Electra
1.148: Yes, do so; approach now, softly, softly!
1.150:
Give me an account of why you have come here. For at last he has lain down, and sleeps.
Chorus
1.153:
How is he? You give us an account, my dear; what has happened, what misfortune?
Electra
1.155:
He is still breathing, but his moans grow feeble.
Chorus
1.156:
What are you saying? turning to Orestes. Unhappy Orestes!
Electra
1.158:
You will kill him, if you disturb him from the sweet sleep he now enjoys.
Chorus
1.160:
Poor sufferer, for his hateful deeds, inspired by a god!
Electra
1.162: Ah, misery! Injustice it was, after all, from an unjust mouth, when Loxias on the tripod of Themis
1.165:
decreed my mother’s most unnatural murder.
Chorus
1.166:
Do you see? He stirs beneath his robe!
Electra
1.167:
Alas! Your noisy chatter has roused him from his sleep.
Chorus
1.169:
No, I think he is asleep.
Electra
1.170:
Leave us, go away from the house! circle back again! cease this noise!
Chorus
1.173:
He is asleep.
Electra
You are right. O Lady Night,
1.175: giver of sleep to hard-working mortals, come from Erebus, come, wing your way to the palace of Agamemnon.
1.180: For with misery and woe we are lost, we are gone.
1.181: There! To the Chorus. that noise again! Do be still and keep the sound of your voice
1.185:
away from his couch; let him enjoy his sleep in peace, my dear!
Chorus
1.187:
Tell me, what end of troubles awaits him.
Electra
1.188:
Death, death; what else? For he has no desire for food.
Chorus
1.190:
Then his destiny is already clear.
Electra
1.191:
Phoebus offered us up for sacrifice, when he ordered the pitiable, unnatural murder of our mother, who killed our father.
Chorus
1.194:
It was just.
Electra
But it was not well done.
1.195: You killed and were killed, my mother! and you have slain a father and your own children;
1.200: for we are dead or as good as dead. You are in your grave, and the greater part of my life is spent in weeping and wailing,
1.205:
and tears at night; unmarried, childless, I drag out forever a joyless existence.
Chorus Leader
1.208: Electra, you are nearby; see whether your brother has not died without your knowing it;
1.210:
for I do not like his utter prostration.
Orestes
awaking refreshed
1.211: Sweet charm of sleep, savior in sickness, how sweetly you came to me, how needed! Revered forgetfulness of troubles, how wise a goddess you are, and invoked by every suffering soul!
1.215:
Addressing Electra. Where have I come from? How am I here? For I have lost all previous recollection and remember nothing.
Electra
1.217:
My dearest, how glad I was to see you fall asleep! Do you want me take you in my arms and lift your body?
Orestes
1.219: Take, oh! take me in your arms, and from this sufferer’s mouth
1.220:
and eyes wipe off the flakes of foam.
Electra
1.221:
There! The service is sweet, and I do not refuse to tend a brother’s limbs with a sister’s hand.
Orestes
1.223:
Prop me up, your side to mine; brush the matted hair from my face, for I see dimly.
Electra
1.225:
Ah, poor head, how dirty your hair! How savage you look, remaining so long unwashed!
Orestes
1.227:
Put me once more upon the couch; whenever the madness leaves me, I am unnerved and weak.
Electra
1.229: As she lays him down. There! His couch is welcome to the sick man,
1.230:
a painful possession, but a necessary one.
Orestes
1.231:
Set me upright once again, turn my body round; it is their helplessness that makes the sick so hard to please.
Electra
1.233:
Will you set your feet upon the ground and take a step at last? Change is always pleasant.
Orestes
1.235:
Oh, yes; for that has a semblance of health; and the semblance is preferable, though it is far from the truth.
Electra
1.237:
Hear me now, my brother, while the Furies permit you to use your senses.
Orestes
1.239: You have news to tell; if it is good, you do me a kindness;
1.240:
but if it tends to my hurt, I have suffered enough.
Electra
1.241:
Menelaus, your father’s brother, has come; his ships are moored in Nauplia.
Orestes
1.243:
What did you say? Has he come to be a light in our troubles, a man of our own family, who owes gratitude to our father?
Electra
1.245:
He has come, and is bringing Helen from the walls of Troy—accept this as proof of what I say.
Orestes
1.247:
If he had returned alone in safety, he would be more enviable; but if he is bringing his wife, he has come with great mischief.
Electra
1.249: Tyndareus begot a race of daughters notorious for blame,
1.251:
Then you be different from that evil brood, for you can be; and not only in words, but also in heart.
Electra
1.253:
Ah! brother, your eye is growing wild, and in a moment you are turning mad again, when you were just now sane.
Orestes
starting up wildly
1.255:
Mother, I implore you! Do not shake at me those maidens with their bloodshot eyes and snaky hair. Here they are, close by, to leap on me!
Electra
1.258:
Lie still, poor sufferer, on your couch; your eye sees nothing, you only imagine that you recognize them.
Orestes
1.260:
O Phoebus! they will kill me, the hounds of hell, death’s priestesses with glaring eyes, the dreadful goddesses.
Electra
1.262:
I will not let you go; but with arms twined round you, I will prevent your piteous leaping.
Orestes
1.264: Let me go! you are one of my Furies,
1.265:
and are gripping me by the waist to hurl me into Tartarus!
Electra
1.266:
Alas for me! What aid can I find, when we have Heaven’s forces set against us?
Orestes
1.268: Give me my horn-tipped bow, Apollo’s gift, with which he told me to ward off the goddesses,
1.270: if ever they sought to scare me with wild transports of madness.
1.271: A mortal hand will wound one of them, unless she departs from my sight. Don’t you hear me? Don’t you see the feathered arrows springing out from my far-shooting bow? What!
1.275: Do you linger still? Mount the sky on your wings, and blame those oracles of Phoebus.
1.276: Ah! why am I raving, gasping? Where, oh! where have I leapt, from my couch? Once more the storm is past, I see a calm.
1.280: Sister, why do you weep, your head wrapped in your robe? I am ashamed that I should make you a partner in my sufferings and distress a maiden like you through my sickness. Do not waste away over my troubles; for though you consented to it, yet I was the one that spilled
1.285: our mother’s blood. I blame Loxias, for urging me on to do a deed most unholy, encouraging me with words but not in deed. I believe that, if I had asked my father to his face whether I must slay my mother,
1.290: he would have strongly entreated me, by this beard, never to plunge a sword into her throat, since he would not regain his life, and I, poor wretch, would accomplish such evil!
1.294: And now, my sister, unveil your face
1.295: and cease to weep, despite our misery. Whenever you see me give way to despair, it is for you to calm and soothe the terrors and distorted fancies of my brain. Whenever sorrow comes to you, I must be at your side and give you comforting advice;
1.300: for to help our friends like this is noble.
1.301: Go in the house now, my poor sister; lie down and close your sleepless eyes; take food and bathe your body. For if you leave me or fall sick from nursing me,
1.305:
I am lost. You are my only ally; I am deserted by all the rest, as you see.
Electra
1.307: I will not leave you; with you I will choose to live and die; for it is the same: if you die, what shall I, a woman, do? How shall I escape alone,
1.310: with no brother, or father, or friends? Still, if you think it right, I must do your bidding. But lie down upon your couch, and do not pay too great heed to the terrors and alarm that scare you from your rest; lie still upon your pallet. For even if you are not sick, but only think you are,
1.315:
this brings weariness and perplexity to mortals. Exit Electra.
Chorus
1.316: Ah! ah! you goddesses swiftly careering on your wings, whose lot it is to hold a revel, not with Bacchic rites,
1.320: in tears and groans; you black-skinned avenging spirits, that dart along the spacious air, exacting a penalty for blood, a penalty for murder, I beg you, I beg you!
1.325: Allow the son of Agamemnon to forget his wild whirling frenzy.
1.327: Alas for the toils which you, poor wretch, strove after to your ruin, when you heard the voice from the tripod, proclaimed by Phoebus,
1.330:
at his sanctuary, where the hollows are called the navel of the earth.
Chorus
1.332: O Zeus! What pity, what deadly struggle is here,
1.335: hurrying you on, the wretch on whom some avenging fiend is heaping tears upon tears, bringing to the house your mother’s blood, which drives you raving mad?
1.340: Great prosperity is not secure among mortals. I lament, I lament! But some divine power, shaking it to and fro like the sail of a swift ship, plunges it deep in the waves of grievous affliction, violent and deadly as the waves of the sea.
1.345:
For what other family must I still revere, rather than the one from a divine marriage, from Tantalus.
Chorus Leader
1.348: And see, a king draws near, lord Menelaus; from his magnificence it is plain to see
1.350: that he belongs to the blood of the Tantalids.
1.352: All hail! you that set out with a thousand ships to Asia’s land; good fortune is your friend,
1.355:
for you have accomplished, with divine aid, all that you prayed for.
Menelaus
1.356: O my home, some joy I feel to see you again on my return from Troy, but I also grieve at the sight; for never have I seen another house more closely encircled by dire affliction.
1.360: For I learned Agamemnon’s fate and the death he died at his wife’s hands, as I was trying to put in at Malea; when the sailors’ prophet, the truthful god Glaucus, Nereus’ seer, brought the news to me from the waves;
1.365: he stationed himself in full view and told me this: Menelaus, your brother lies dead, plunged in a fatal bath, the last his wife will ever give him. My sailors and I wept greatly at his words. When I arrived at Nauplia,
1.370: my wife already on the point of starting here, I was expecting to give a fond embrace to Orestes, Agamemnon’s son, and his mother, thinking that they were doing well, when I heard from a sailor the unholy murder of Tyndareus’ child.
1.375:
And now tell me, young ladies, where to find the son of Agamemnon, who dared such evil. For he was a baby in Clytemnestra’s arms when I left my home to go to Troy, so that I would not recognize him if I saw him.
Orestes
Staggering towards him from the couch.
1.380:
Menelaus, I am Orestes, whom you are asking about. I will of my own accord inform you of my sufferings. But as my first portion, I clasp your knees as a suppliant, giving you prayers from the mouth of one without the suppliant’s bough; save me, for you have come at the crisis of my troubles.
Menelaus
1.385:
O gods, what do I see? What living corpse greets my sight?
Orestes
1.386:
You are right; I am dead through misery, though I still gaze upon the light.
Menelaus
1.387:
How savage the look your unkempt hair gives you, poor wretch!
Orestes
1.388:
It is not my looks, but my deeds that torture me.
Menelaus
1.389:
Your tearless eyes glare dreadfully!
Orestes
1.390:
My body is gone, though my name has not deserted me.
Menelaus
1.391:
Unsightly apparition, so different from what I expected!
Orestes
1.392:
Here I am, the murderer of my wretched mother.
Menelaus
1.393:
I have heard, spare your words; evils should be seldom spoken.
Orestes
1.394:
I will be sparing; but the deity is lavish of woe in my case.
Menelaus
1.395:
What ails you? what is your deadly sickness?
Orestes
1.396:
My conscience; I know that I am guilty of a dreadful crime.
Menelaus
1.397:
What do you mean? Wisdom is shown in clarity, not in obscurity.
Orestes
1.398:
Grief especially has ruined me—
Menelaus
1.399:
Yes, she is a dreadful goddess, yet are there cures for her.
Orestes
1.400:
And fits of madness, the vengeance of a mother’s blood.
Menelaus
1.401:
When did your madness begin? Which day was it?
Orestes
1.402:
On the day I was heaping the mound over my poor mother’s grave.
Menelaus
1.403:
When you were in the house, or watching by the pyre?
Orestes
1.404:
As I was waiting by night to gather up her bones.
Menelaus
1.405:
Was any one else there, to help you rise?
Orestes
1.406:
Pylades who shared with me the bloody deed, my mother’s murder.
Menelaus
1.407:
You are sick from phantom shapes; what sort?
Orestes
1.408:
I seemed to see three maidens, black as night.
Menelaus
1.409:
I know whom you mean, but I do not want to name them.
Orestes
1.410:
Yes, for they are revered; you were well-informed, to avoid naming them.
Menelaus
1.411:
Are these the ones that drive you to frenzy, with the curse of kindred blood?
Orestes
1.412:
Oh! the torment I endure from their pursuit!
Menelaus
1.413:
It is not strange, if those who have done dreadful things should suffer them.
Orestes
1.414:
But I have a way to recover from these troubles.
Menelaus
1.415:
Do not speak of death; that is not wise.
Orestes
1.416:
It is Phoebus, who commanded me to kill my mother.
Menelaus
1.417:
Showing a strange ignorance of what is fair and right.
Orestes
1.418:
We are slaves to the gods, whatever those gods are.
Menelaus
1.419:
And does Loxias not help your affliction?
Orestes
1.420:
He will in time; this is the nature of gods.
Menelaus
1.421:
How long is it since your mother breathed her last?
Orestes
1.422:
This is the sixth day; her funeral pyre is still warm.
Menelaus
1.423:
How soon the goddesses arrived to avenge your mother’s blood!
Orestes
1.424:
I am not clever, but I am by nature a true friend to my friends.
Menelaus
1.425:
Does your father give you any help at all, for your avenging him?
Orestes
1.426:
Not yet; I call delay the equal of inaction.
Menelaus
1.427:
How do you stand in the city after that deed of yours?
Orestes
1.428:
I am so hated that no one will speak to me.
Menelaus

Orestes
1.430:
No, for wherever I go, the door is shut against me.
Menelaus

Which citizens are driving you from the land?
Orestes
1.432:
Oeax, who refers to my father his reason for hating Troy.
Menelaus

Orestes
1.434:
That was nothing to do with me; yet I am destroyed for three reasons.

Who else? Some of the friends of Aegisthus, I suppose?
Orestes

They insult me, and the city listens to them now.
Menelaus

Will the city allow you to keep the scepter of Agamemnon?
Orestes
1.438:

Menelaus

Orestes

A vote will be taken against us today.
Menelaus

Orestes
1.442:
Death by stoning at the hands of the citizens.
Menelaus
1.443:
Then why not cross the border and try to escape?
Orestes
1.444:
Because we are encircled by men fully armed.
Menelaus
1.445:
Private foes or Argive troops?
Orestes

All the citizens, so that I may die; it is shortly told.
Menelaus
1.447:
Poor wretch! you have arrived at the extremity of woe.
Orestes
1.448: In you I have hopes of escape from my troubles. But since you have come with good fortune,
1.450: share with your friends, who are wretched, your prosperity; do not hold aside that goodness for yourself alone; but partake of troubles in your turn, and so pay back my father’s kindness to those who have a claim on you. For such friends as desert us in adversity

are friends in name but not in deed.
Chorus Leader
1.456:
And here is Tyndareus, the Spartan, struggling with aged step, clad in black robes, with his hair cut short in mourning for his daughter.
Orestes
1.459: Menelaus, I am ruined. See, Tyndareus
1.460: approaches us, the man of all others I most shrink from facing, because of the deed I have done. For he nursed me when I was small, and lavished on me many a fond caress, carrying me about in his arms as the son of Agamemnon; and so did Leda;
1.465: for they both honored me no less than the Dioscuri.

Ah me! my wretched heart and soul, it was a sorry return I made them! What darkness can I find for my face? What cloud can I spread before me in my efforts to escape the old man’s eye?
Tyndareus

1.475:
and clasp his hand, as a friend whom at last I see again.
Menelaus
1.476:
Hail, old man, rival of Zeus for a bride!
Tyndareus
1.477: All hail to you, Menelaus, my kinsman!

Menelaus, are you speaking to that godless wretch?
Menelaus
1.482:
And why not? He is the son of one whom I loved.
Tyndareus

This is his son, this creature here?
Menelaus

Yes, his son; if he is in misfortune, he ought to be honored.
Tyndareus

1.486:

Tyndareus

Menelaus
1.488:

Tyndareus
1.489:

Menelaus
1.490:

it would be shameful for two old men to fall down. But let that pass, for we must serve Bacchus, the son of Zeus. Beware lest Pentheus bring trouble to your house, Kadmos; I do not speak in prophecy, but judging from the state of things; for a foolish man speaks foolishness.
Chorus

1.375: insolence against Bromius, the child of Semele, the first deity of the gods at the banquets where guests wear beautiful garlands? He holds this office, to join in dances,
1.380: to laugh with the flute, and to bring an end to cares, whenever the delight of the grape comes at the feasts of the gods, and in ivy-bearing banquets
1.385:
the goblet sheds sleep over men.
Chorus
1.386: Misfortune is the result of unbridled mouths and lawless folly; but the life of quiet
1.390: and wisdom remain unshaken and hold houses together. Though they dwell far off in the heavens the gods see the deeds of mortals.
1.395: But cleverness is not wisdom, nor is thinking on things unfit for mortals. Life is short, and on this account the one who pursues great things does not achieve that which is present. In my opinion,
1.400:
these are the ways of mad and ill-advised men.
Chorus
1.402: Would that I could go to Cyprus, the island of Aphrodite, where the Loves, who soothe
1.405: mortals’ hearts, dwell, and to Paphos, fertilized without rain by the streams of a foreign river flowing with a hundred mouths. Lead me there, Bromius, Bromius, god of joy who leads the Bacchae,
1.410: to Pieria, beautiful seat of the Muses, the holy slope of Olympus. There are the Graces, there is Desire; there it is
1.415:
lawful for the Bacchae to celebrate their rites.
Chorus
1.417: The god, the son of Zeus, delights in banquets, and loves Peace, giver of riches,
1.420: goddess who nourishes youths. To the blessed and to the less fortunate, he gives an equal pleasure from wine that banishes grief. He hates the one who does not care about this:
1.425: to lead a happy life by day and friendly night and to keep his wise mind and intellect away from over-curious men.
1.430:
What the common people think and adopt, that would I accept.
Enter a servant Servant

1.435: for which you sent us, nor have we set out in vain. This beast was docile in our hands and did not withdraw in flight, but yielded not unwillingly. He did not turn pale or change the wine-dark complexion of his cheek, but laughed and allowed us to bind him and lead him away.
1.440: He remained still, making my work easy, and I in shame said: Stranger, I do not lead you away willingly, but by order of Pentheus, who sent me. And the Bacchae whom you shut up, whom you carried off and bound in the chains of the public prison,

1.450:
full of many wonders. You must take care of the rest.
Pentheus
1.451: Release his hands, for caught in the nets he is not so swift as to escape me. But your body is not ill-formed, stranger, for women’s purposes, for which reason you have come to Thebes.
1.455: For your hair is long, not through wrestling, scattered over your cheeks, full of desire; and you have a white skin from careful preparation, hunting after Aphrodite by your beauty not exposed to strokes of the sun, but beneath the shade.
1.460:
First then tell me who your family is.
Dionysus
1.461:
I can tell you this easily, without boasting. I suppose you are familiar with flowery Tmolus.
Pentheus
1.463:
I know of it; it surrounds the city of Sardis.
Dionysus
1.464:
I am from there, and Lydia is my fatherland.
Pentheus
1.465:
Why do you bring these rites to Hellas?
Dionysus
1.466:
Dionysus, the child of Zeus, sent me.
Pentheus
1.467:
Is there a Zeus who breeds new gods there?
Dionysus
1.468:
No, but the one who married Semele here.
Pentheus
1.469:
Did he compel you at night, or in your sight?
Dionysus
1.470:
Seeing me just as I saw him, he gave me sacred rites.
Pentheus
1.471:
What appearance do your rites have?
Dionysus
1.472:
They can not be told to mortals uninitiated in Bacchic revelry.
Pentheus
1.473:
And do they have any profit to those who sacrifice?
Dionysus
1.474:
It is not lawful for you to hear, but they are worth knowing.
Pentheus
1.475:
You have counterfeited this well, so that I desire to hear.
Dionysus
1.476:
The rites are hostile to whoever practices impiety.
Pentheus
1.477:
Are you saying that you saw clearly what the god was like?
Dionysus
1.478:
He was as he chose; I did not order this.
Pentheus
1.479:
Again you diverted my question well, speaking mere nonsense.
Dionysus
1.480:
One will seem to be foolish if he speaks wisely to an ignorant man.
Pentheus
1.481:
Did you come here first, bringing the god?
Dionysus
1.482:
All the barbarians celebrate these rites.
Pentheus
1.483:
Yes, for they are far more foolish than Hellenes.
Dionysus
1.484:
In this at any rate they are wiser; but their laws are different.
Pentheus
1.485:
Do you perform the rites by night or by day?
Dionysus
1.486:
Mostly by night; darkness conveys awe.
Pentheus
1.487:
This is treacherous towards women, and unsound.
Dionysus
1.488:
Even during the day someone may devise what is shameful.
Pentheus
1.489:
You must pay the penalty for your evil contrivances.
Dionysus
1.490:
And you for your ignorance and impiety toward the god.
Pentheus
1.491:
How bold the Bacchant is, and not unpracticed in speaking!
Dionysus
1.492:
Tell me what I must suffer; what harm will you do to me?
Pentheus
1.493:
First I will cut off your delicate hair.
Dionysus
1.494:
My hair is sacred. I am growing it for the god.
Pentheus
1.495:
Next give me this thyrsos from your hands.
Dionysus
1.496:
Take it from me yourself. I bear it as the ensign of Dionysus.
Pentheus
1.497:
We will guard your body within, in prison.
Dionysus
1.498:
The god himself will release me, whenever I want.
Pentheus
1.499:
Yes, when you call him, standing among the Bacchae.
Dionysus
1.500:
Even now he see my sufferings from close by.
Pentheus
1.501:
Where is he? He is not visible to my eyes.
Dionysus
1.502:
Near me; but you, being impious, do not see him.
Pentheus
1.503:
To attendants Seize him; he insults me and Thebes!
Dionysus
1.504:
I warn you not to bind me, since I am in my senses and you are not.
Pentheus
1.505:
And I, more masterful than you, bid them to bind you.
Dionysus
1.506:
You do not know why you live, or what you are doing, or who you are.
Pentheus
1.507:
I am Pentheus, son of Echion and Agave.
Dionysus
1.508:
You are well-suited to be miserable in your name.
Pentheus
1.509: Go. To attendants Shut him up near the horse
1.510:
stable, so that he may see only darkness. To Dionysus Dance there; and as for these women whom you have led here as accomplices to your crimes, we will either sell them or, stopping their hands from this noise and beating of skins, I will keep them as slaves at the loom.
Dionysus
1.515:
I will go, for I need not suffer that which is not necessary. But Dionysus, who you claim does not exist, will pursue you for these insults. For in injuring us, you put him in bonds.
Chorus
1.520: venerable Dirce, happy virgin, you once received the child of Zeus in your streams, when Zeus his father snatched him up from the immortal fire and saved him in his thigh,
1.525: crying out: Go, Dithyrambus, enter this my male womb. I will make you illustrious, Bacchus, in Thebes, so that they will call you by this name.
1.530: But you, blessed Dirce, reject me with my garland-bearing company about you. Why do you refuse me, why do you flee me? I swear by the cluster-bearing
1.535:
delight of Dionysus’ vine that you will have a care for Bromius.
Chorus
1.537: What rage, what rage does the earth-born race show, and Pentheus,
1.540: once descended from a serpent—Pentheus, whom earth-born Echion bore, a fierce monster, not a mortal man, but like a bloody giant, hostile to the gods.
1.545: He will soon bind me, the hand-maid of Bromius, in chains, and he already holds my fellow-reveler within the house, hidden in a dark prison.

1.555:
and restrain the insolence of the blood-thirsty man.
Chorus

1.570: whirling Maenads, leaving Lydias, giver of wealth to mortals, the father who they say fertilizes the land of beautiful horses with

within Io! Hear my voice, hear it, Io Bacchae, Io Bacchae!
Chorus
1.578:
Who is here, who? From what quarter did the voice of the Joyful one summon me?
Dionysus
1.580:
Io! Io! I say again; it is I, the child of Zeus and Semele.
Chorus
1.582:
Io! Io! Master, master! Come now to our company, Bromius.
Dionysus
1.585:
Shake the world’s plain, lady Earthquake!
Chorus

1.590:
Revere him. —We revere him! —Did you see these stone lintels on the pillars falling apart? Bromius cries out in victory indoors.
Dionysus
1.594: Light the fiery lamp of lightning!
1.596: Oh! Oh! Do you not see the the fire, do you not perceive, about the sacred tomb of Semele, the flame that Zeus’ thunderbolt left?
1.600:
Cast on the ground your trembling bodies, Maenads, cast them down, for our lord, Zeus’ son, is coming against this palace, turning everything upside down.
Enter Dionysus Dionysus
1.604: Barbarian women, have you fallen on the ground
1.605:
so stricken with fear? You have, so it seems, felt Bacchus shaking the house of Pentheus. But get up and take courage, putting a stop to your trembling.
Chorus Leader
1.608:
Oh greatest light for us in our joyful revelry, how happy I am to see you—I who was alone and desolate before.
Dionysus
1.610:
Did you despair when I was sent to fall into Pentheus’ dark dungeon?
Chorus Leader
1.612:
How not? Who was my guardian, if you met with misfortune? But how were you freed, having met with an impious man?
Dionysus
1.614:
By myself I saved myself easily, without trouble.
Chorus Leader
1.615:
Did he not tie your hands in binding knots?
Dionysus
1.616: In this too I mocked him, for, thinking to bind me, he neither touched nor handled me, but fed on hope. He found a bull by the stable where he took and shut me up, and threw shackles around its knees and hooves,
1.620: breathing out fury, dripping sweat from his body, gnashing his teeth in his lips. But I, being near, sitting quietly, looked on. Meanwhile, Bacchus came and shook the house and kindled a flame on his mother’s tomb. When Pentheus saw this, thinking that the house was burning,
1.625: he ran here and there, calling to the slaves to bring water, and every servant was at work, toiling in vain. Then he let this labor drop, as I had escaped, and snatching a dark sword rushed into the house. Then Bromius, so it seems to me—I speak my opinion—
1.630: created a phantom in the courtyard. Pentheus rushed at it headlong, stabbing at the shining air, as though slaughtering me. Besides this, Bacchus inflicted other damage on him: he knocked his house to the ground, and everything was shattered into pieces, while he saw my bitter chains. From fatigue,
1.635: dropping his sword, he is exhausted. For he, a man, dared to join battle with a god. Now I have quietly left the house and come to you, with no thought of Pentheus. But I think—at any rate I hear the tramping of feet inside—he will soon come to the front of the house. What will he say after this?
1.640:
I shall easily bear him, even if he comes boasting greatly. For it is the part of a wise man to practice restrained good temper.
Enter Pentheus Pentheus
1.642: I have suffered terrible things; the stranger, who was recently constrained in bonds, has escaped me. Ah!
1.645:
Here is the man. What is this? How do you appear in front of my house, having come out?
Dionysus
1.647:
Stop, and put a stop to your anger.
Pentheus
1.648:
How have you escaped your chains and come outside?
Dionysus
1.649:
Did I not say—or did you not hear—that some one would deliver me?
Pentheus
1.650:
Who? You are always introducing strange explanations.
Dionysus
1.651:
He who produces the rich-clustering vine for mortals.
Pentheus
Dionysus
1.652:
You reproach Dionysus for what is his glory.
Pentheus
1.653:
I order you to close up all the towers around.
Dionysus
1.654:
Why? Do gods not pass over walls too?
Pentheus
1.655:
You are wise, wise at least in all save what you should be wise in.
Dionysus
1.656:
I was born wise in all that I should be. Enter a messenger Listen first to the words of this man, who has come from the mountain to bring you some message. I will await you, I will not try to escape.
Messenger
1.660:
Pentheus, ruler of this land of Thebes, I have come from Kithairon, where the bright flakes of white snow never melt.
Pentheus
1.663:
What important news do you come to bring?
Messenger
1.664: Having seen the holy Bacchae, who
1.665: goaded to madness have darted from this land with their fair feet, I have come to tell you and the city, lord, that they are doing terrible things, beyond marvel. I wish to hear whether I should tell you in free speech the situation there or whether I should repress my report,
1.670:
for I fear, lord, the quickness of your mood, your keen temper and your too imperious disposition.
Pentheus
1.672: Speak, as you will have immunity from me in any case. For it is not right to be angry with the just. The more you tell me terrible things about the Bacchae,
1.675:
the more I will punish this one here who taught the women these tricks.
Messenger
1.677: The herds of grazing cattle were just climbing up the hill, at the time when the sun sends forth its rays, warming the earth.
1.680: I saw three companies of dancing women, one of which Autonoe led, the second your mother Agave, and the third Ino. All were asleep, their bodies relaxed, some resting their backs against pine foliage,
1.685: others laying their heads at random on the oak leaves, modestly, not as you say drunk with the goblet and the sound of the flute, hunting out Aphrodite through the woods in solitude. Your mother raised a cry,
1.690: standing up in the midst of the Bacchae, to wake their bodies from sleep, when she heard the lowing of the horned cattle. And they, casting off refreshing sleep from their eyes, sprang upright, a marvel of orderliness to behold, old, young, and still unmarried virgins.
1.695: First they let their hair loose over their shoulders, and secured their fawn-skins, as many of them as had released the fastenings of their knots, girding the dappled hides with serpents licking their jaws. And some, holding in their arms a gazelle or wild
1.700: wolf-pup, gave them white milk, as many as had abandoned their new-born infants and had their breasts still swollen. They put on garlands of ivy, and oak, and flowering yew. One took her thyrsos and struck it against a rock,
1.705: from which a dewy stream of water sprang forth. Another let her thyrsos strike the ground, and there the god sent forth a fountain of wine. All who desired the white drink scratched the earth with the tips of their fingers and obtained streams of milk;
1.710: and a sweet flow of honey dripped from their ivy thyrsoi; so that, had you been present and seen this, you would have approached with prayers the god whom you now blame. We herdsmen and shepherds gathered in order to
1.715: debate with one another concerning what strange and amazing things they were doing. Some one, a wanderer about the city and practised in speaking, said to us all: You who inhabit the holy plains of the mountains, do you wish to hunt
1.720: Pentheus’ mother Agave out from the Bacchic revelry and do the king a favor? We thought he spoke well, and lay down in ambush, hiding ourselves in the foliage of bushes. They, at the appointed hour, began to wave the thyrsos in their revelries,
1.725: calling on Iacchus, the son of Zeus, Bromius, with united voice. The whole mountain revelled along with them and the beasts, and nothing was unmoved by their running. Agave happened to be leaping near me, and I sprang forth, wanting to snatch her,
1.730: abandoning the ambush where I had hidden myself. But she cried out: O my fleet hounds, we are hunted by these men; but follow me! follow armed with your thyrsoi in your hands! We fled and escaped
1.735: from being torn apart by the Bacchae, but they, with unarmed hands, sprang on the heifers browsing the grass. and you might see one rending asunder a fatted lowing calf, while others tore apart cows.

1.745: dragged down by countless young hands. The garment of flesh was torn apart faster then you could blink your royal eyes. And like birds raised in their course, they proceeded along the level plains, which by the streams of the Asopus

1.765: And they returned where they had come from, to the very fountains which the god had sent forth for them, and washed off the blood, and snakes cleaned the drops from the women’s cheeks with their tongues. Receive this god then, whoever he is,
1.770:
into this city, master. For he is great in other respects, and they say this too of him, as I hear, that he gives to mortals the vine that puts an end to grief. Without wine there is no longer Aphrodite or any other pleasant thing for men.
Chorus Leader

I fear to speak freely to the king, but I will speak nevertheless: Dionysus is inferior to none of the gods.
Pentheus

the Bacchae. For it is indeed too much if we suffer what we are suffering at the hands of women.

than kick against his spurs in anger, a mortal against a god.

Pentheus

Dionysus

Pentheus
1.803:

Dionysus

Pentheus
1.805:

Dionysus
1.806:

Pentheus
1.807:

Dionysus
1.808:

Pentheus
1.809:
To a servant Bring me my armor. To Dionysus And you, stop speaking.
Dionysus
1.810:

Pentheus
1.812:
Certainly. I’d give an enormous amount of gold for that.
Dionysus
1.813:

Pentheus

I would be sorry to see them in their drunkenness.
Dionysus

Pentheus

Dionysus

Pentheus

Dionysus

Pentheus
1.820:

Pentheus

Dionysus
1.823:

Pentheus
1.824:

Dionysus
1.825:

Pentheus
1.826:
How can your advice to me be well carried out?
Dionysus

1.828:

1.829:

1.832:

Pentheus
1.834:

Dionysus
1.835:

Pentheus
1.838:
True. We must go first and spy.
Dionysus
1.839:

Pentheus
1.840:

Dionysus
1.841:

Pentheus
1.842:

Dionysus
1.844:
It will be so; in any case I am ready.
Pentheus
1.845:
I will go in. For either I will go bearing arms, or I will obey your counsels.
Dionysus
1.848: Women, the man is caught in our net. He will go to the Bacchae, where he will pay the penalty with his death. Dionysus, now it is your job; for you are not far off.

Dionysus, who is in fact a god, the most terrible and yet most mild to men.
Chorus
1.862: Shall I move my white foot in the night-long dance, aroused to a frenzy,
1.865: throwing my head to the dewy air, like a fawn sporting in the green pleasures of the meadow, when it has escaped a fearful chase beyond the watchers
1.870: over the well-woven nets, and the hunter hastens his dogs on their course with his call, while she, with great exertion and a storm-swift running, rushes along the plain by the river, rejoicing
1.875: in the solitude apart from men and in the thickets of the shady-foliaged woods. What is wisdom? Or what greater honor do the gods give to mortals than to hold one’s hand
1.880:
in strength over the head of enemies? What is good is always dear.

1.882: Divine strength is roused with difficulty, but still is sure. It chastises those mortals
1.885: who honor folly and those who in their insanity do not extol the gods. The gods cunningly conceal the long pace of time and

1.900:
in strength over the head of enemies? What is good is always dear.

1.60: with burnt-sacrifice, binding themselves by this curse: whoever wins the child of Tyndareus for wife, they will assist that man, in case a rival takes her from his house and goes his way, robbing her husband of his rights; and march against that man in armed array and raze his city to the ground,
1.66: Now when they had once pledged their word and old Tyndareus with no small cleverness had beguiled them by his shrewd device, he allowed his daughter to choose from among her suitors the one towards whom the sweet breezes of Aphrodite might carry her.

1.0:
VARIOUS VOICES.
It is a cloudy but moonlight night on the plain before Troy. The Trojans and their allies have won a decisive victory and are camping on the open field close to the Greek outposts. The scene is in front of a rude tent or hut that has been set up for HECTOR, the Trojan leader. A watch-fire burns low in front. Far off at the back can be seen rows of watch-fires in the Greek camp. The road to Troy is in front to the left; the road to Mount Ida leads far away to the right. All is silence; then a noise outside. Enter tumultuously a band of Trojan Pickets.

1.330:
Master, dost think already that our foe
Is ta’en?
HECTOR.
1.331:
I do. To-morrow’s light will show.
LEADER.
1.332:
Have care. Fate often flings a backward cast.
HECTOR.
1.333: I hate the help that comes when need is past...
1.336: Howbeit, once come, I bid him welcome here
1.337: As guest—not war-friend; guest to share our cheer.
1.338:
The thanks are lost, he might have won from us.
LEADER.
1.334:
My general, to reject an ally thus
Must needs make hatred.
SHEPHERD.
1.335:
The mere sight of those
I saw would sure cast fear upon our foes.
HECTOR.
(yielding reluctantly, with a laugh)
1.339:
Ah, well; thy words are prudent; and (To SHEPHERD) thine eyes
See glorious things. With all these panoplies
1.340: Of gold that filled our Shepherd’s heart with joy,
1.341:
Bid Rhesus welcome, as war-friend to Troy.
Exit SHEPHERD; HECTOR returns to his tent, amid the joy of the soldiers.
CHORUS.
1.342: Now Adrasteia be near and guard
1.343: Our lips from sin, lest the end be hard!
1.344: But he cometh, he cometh, the Child of the River!
1.345: The pride of my heart it shall roll unbarred.
1.346: We craved thy coming; yea, need was strong
1.347: In the Hall of thy lovers, O child of Song;
1.348: Thy mother the Muse and her fair-bridged River
1.349:
They held thee from us so long, so long!
CHORUS.
1.351: By Strymon’s torrent alone she sang,
1.352: And Strymon shivered and coiled and sprang;
1.353: And her arms went wide to the wild sweet water,
1.354: And the love of the River around her rang.
1.355: We hail thee, Fruit of the River’s seed,
1.356: Young Zeus of the Dawn, on thy starry steed!
1.357: O ancient City, O Ida’s daughter,
1.358:
Is God the Deliverer found indeed?
CHORUS.
1.360: And men shall tell of thee, Ilion mine,
1.361: Once more a-harping at day’s decline,
1.362: ’Mid laughing of lovers and lays and dances
1.363: And challenge on challenge of circling wine?
1.364: When the Greek is smitten that day shall be,
1.365: And fled to Argolis over the sea:
1.366: O mighty of hand, O leader of lances,
1.367:
Smite him, and heaven be good to thee!
CHORUS.
1.370: Thou Rider golden and swift and sheer,
1.372: The car like flame where the red shield leapeth,
1.373: The fell white steeds and the burning spear!
1.374: No Greek shall boast he hath seen thy face
1.375: And danced again in the dancing place;
1.376: And the land shall laugh for the sheaves she reapeth,
1.377:
Of spoilers dead by a sword from Thrace.
Enter RHESUS in dazzling white armour, followed by his CHARIOTEER and Attendants. The CHARIOTEER carries his golden shield. The CHORUS break into a shout of All Hail! LEADER.
1.379: All hail, great King! A whelp indeed
1.380: Is born in Thracia’s lion fold,
1.381: Whose leap shall make strong cities bleed.
1.382: Behold his body girt with gold,
1.383: And hark the pride of bells along
1.384:
The frontlet of that targe’s hold.
CHORUS.
1.385:
A God, O Troy, a God and more!
’Tis Ares’ self, this issue strong
1.386: Of Strymon and the Muse of song,
1.387:
Whose breath is fragrant on thy shore!
Re-enter HECTOR. RHESUS.
1.388: Lord Hector, Prince of Ilion, noble son
1.389:
Of noble sires, all hail! Long years have run
Since last we greeted, and ’tis joy this day
1.390: To see thy fortunes firm and thine array
1.391: Camped at the foe’s gate. Here am I to tame
1.392:
That foe for thee, and wrap his ships in flame.
HECTOR.
1.393: Thou child of Music and the Thracian flood,
1.394: Strymonian Rhesus, truth is alway good
1.395: In Hector’s eyes. I wear no double heart.
1.396: Long, long ago thou shouldst have borne thy part
1.397: In Ilion’s labours, not have left us here,
1.398: For all thy help, to sink beneath the spear.
1.399: Why didst thou—not for lack of need made plain!—
1.400: Not come, not send, not think of us again?
1.401: What grave ambassadors prayed not before
1.402: Thy throne, what herald knelt not at thy door?
1.403: What pride of gifts did Troy not send to thee?
1.404: And thou, a lord of Barbary even as we,
1.405:
Thou, brother of our blood, like one at sup
Who quaffs his fill and flings away the cup,
Hast flung to the Greeks my city! Yet, long since,
1.406: ’Twas I that found thee but a little prince
1.407: And made thee mighty, I and this right hand;
1.408: When round Pangaion and the Paiôn’s land,
1.409: Front against front, I burst upon the brood
1.410: Of Thrace and broke their targes, and subdued
1.411: Their power to thine. The grace whereof, not small,
1.412: Thou hast spurned, and when thy kinsmen, drowning, call,
1.413:
Comest too late. Thou! Others there have been
These long years, not by nature of our kin..
1.414: Some under yon rough barrows thou canst see
1.415: Lie buried; they were true to Troy and me;
1.416:
And others, yet here in the shielded line
Or mid the chariots, parching in the shine
1.417:
Of noonday, starving in the winds that bite
Through Ilion’s winter, still endure and fight
1.418:
On at my side. ’Twas not their way, to lie
On a soft couch and, while the cups go by,
1.419: Pledge my good health, like thee, in Thracian wine.
1.420: I speak as a free man. With thee and thine
1.421:
Hector is wroth, and tells thee to thy face.
RHESUS.
1.422: Thy way is mine, friend. Straight I run my race
1.423: In word and deed, and bear no double tongue.
1.424: I tell thee, more than thine my heart was wrung,
1.425: Yea, angered past all durance, thus to stay
1.426:
Back from thy battles. ’Twas a folk that lay
Hard on my borders, Scythians of the north;
1.427: Just when my host for Troy had started forth,
1.428: They fell upon our homes. I had reached the coast
1.429:
Of the Friendless Sea and purposed to have crossed
My Thracians there. We turned; and all that plain
1.430: Is trampled in a mire of Scythian slain
1.431: Ploughed by our spears, and blood of Thrace withal
1.432: Not stinted. This it was that drowned thy call
1.433: For help and held me back from Ilion’s need.
1.434:
I broke their power; the princes of their breed
I took to hostage, made their elders swear
1.435: To bring my house due tribute, year by year,
1.436: Then, never lagging, crossed the Pontus mouth,
1.437: Marched by long stages through Bithynia south
1.438: And here am come... not drunken with the feast,
1.439: As thou wouldst have me be, not lulled to rest
1.440: In golden chambers. In this harness hard
1.441: I have borne my nights of winter storm that starred
1.442: The Euxine into ice and scared the strong
1.443: Paionians. Long I have been, but not too long
1.444: To save thee yet. Friend, this is the tenth year
1.445: Thou labourest on unceasing, with no clear
1.446:
Vantage; day creeps by day, and Ares throws
The same red dice for thee and for thy foes.
1.447: Now, hear my vow. Before one day’s eclipse
1.448: I swear to break their wall, to burn their ships
1.449: And slay their princes. On the second day
1.450: I leave this soil and take my homeward way,
1.451:
Thy pains relieved. No Trojan of the land
Need move, nor turn the buckler in his hand.
1.452: Alone my late-comers will turn the tide
1.453:
And smite your Greeks, for all their bitter pride.
CHORUS.
The Trojan soldiers, who have been listening with delight, here break out in irrepressible applause.
1.457: From those proud lips the Wrath that none may bear!
1.460: Now, nor in days of yore,
1.461: Prince like to thee, so valiant and so fair.
1.464: Or face thy lance? May I but stand that day
1.466:
Broken beneath thy steel,
And once in blood his many murders pay!
RHESUS.
1.467: Yea, more atonement thou shalt take from me
1.468: For this slow help.—May Adrasteia see
1.469:
My heart and pardon!—When we two have set
Troy free from these who compass her with hate,
1.470: Soon as the Gods have had their first-fruits, I
1.471: With thee will sail—so help me Zeus on high!—
1.472: And sack all Hellas with the sword, till these
1.473:
Doers of deeds shall know what suffering is.
HECTOR.
1.474: By heaven, could I once see this peril rolled
1.475: Past us, and live in Ilion as of old,
1.476: Untrembling, I would thank my gods! To seek
1.477: Argos and sack the cities of the Greek-
1.478:
’Twere not such light work as thou fanciest.
RHESUS.
1.479:
These Greeks that face thee, are they not their best?
HECTOR.
1.480:
We seek not better. These do all we need.
RHESUS.
1.481:
When these are beaten, then, we have done the deed.
HECTOR.
1.482:
Lose not thy path watching a distant view.
RHESUS.
1.483:
Thou seem’st content to suffer, not to do?
HECTOR.
1.484: I have a kingdom large by mine own right..
1.485: What station will best please thee in this fight
1.486: To ground the targe and stablish thine array?
1.487:
Right, left, or midmost in the allies? Say.
RHESUS.
1.488: ’Twould please me best to fight these Greeks alone.
1.489: Yet, if ’twould irk thine honour not to have thrown
1.490: One firebrand on the ships with me, why, then
1.491:
Set us to face Achilles and his men.
HECTOR.
1.492:
Achilles? Nay, his spear ye cannot meet.
RHESUS.
1.493:
How so? Fame said he sailed here with the fleet.
HECTOR.
1.494: He sailed, and he is here. But some despite
1.495:
’Gainst the great King now keeps him from the fight.
RHESUS.
1.496:
Who next to him hath honour in their host?
HECTOR.
1.497: Next, to my seeming, Ajax hath the most,
1.498: Or Diomede.—But Odysseus is a tough
1.499: And subtle fox, and brave; aye, brave enough.
1.500: No man of them hath harmed us more than he.
1.501: He climbed here to Athena’s sanctuary
1.502:
One night, and stole her image clean away
To the Argive ships. Yes, and another day,
1.503: Guised as a wandering priest, in rags, he came
1.504:
And walked straight through the Gates, made loud acclaim
Of curses on the Greek, spied out alone
1.505: All that he sought in Ilion, and was gone—
1.506: Gone, and the watch and helpers of the Gate
1.507: Dead! And in every ambush they have set
1.508: By the old Altar, close to Troy, we know
1.509:
He sits—a murderous reptile of a foe!
RHESUS.
1.510: No brave man seeks so dastardly to harm
1.511: His battle-foes; he meets them arm to arm.
1.512: This Greek of thine, this sitter like a thief
1.513: In ambush, I will make of him my chief
1.514: Care. I will take him living, drive a straight
1.515: Stake through him, and so star him at the Gate
1.516:
To feed your wide-winged vultures. ’Tis the death
Most meet for a lewd thief, who pillageth
1.517:
God’s sanctuary, or so we hold in Thrace.
HECTOR.
(making no answer)
1.518: Seek first some sleep. There still remains a space
1.519: Of darkness.—I will show the spot that best
1.520: May suit you, somewhat sundered from the rest.
1.521: Should need arise, the password of the night
1.522:
Is Phoebus: see your Thracians have it right.
Turning to the Guards before he goes.
1.523: Advance beyond your stations, men, at some
1.524: Distance, and stay on watch till Dolon come
1.525: With word of the Argives’ counsel. If his vow
1.526:
Prosper, he should be nearing us by now.
Exeunt HECTOR and RHESUS and Attendants. The Guards, who have been below, come forward sleepily from the camp fire, and sit watching by HECTOR’S tent. CHORUS.
1.527: Say, whose is the watch? Who exchanges
1.528: With us? The first planets to rise
1.530: Move low on the margin of heaven,
1.531:
And the Eagle is risen and ranges
The mid-vault of the skies.
ANOTHER.
1.532: No sleeping yet! Up from your couches
1.533: And watch on, the sluggards ye are!
1.534:
The moon-maiden’s lamp is yet burning.
THIRD GUARD.
1.535: Oh, the morning is near us, the morning!
1.538:
Who drew the first night-watch?
ANOTHER.
1.539:
’Twas one Koroibos, called the Mygdon’s Son.
THE GUARD.
1.540:
And after?
THE OTHER.
The Mount Taurus men
1.541: Had second watch: from them again
1.542:
The Mysians took it. We came then.
A GUARD.
1.543: ’Tis surely time. Who will go tell
1.544: The fifth watch? ’Tis the Lycians’ spell
1.545:
By now; ’twas thus the portions fell.
ANOTHER.
1.547: Nay, hearken! Again she is crying
1.549: Of the face of dead Itys that stunned her,
1.550:
Of grief grown to music and wonder:
Most changeful and old and undying
The nightingale calls.
ANOTHER.
1.551: And on Ida the shepherds are waking
1.552: Their flocks for the upland. I hear
1.553:
The skirl of a pipe very distant.
ANOTHER.
1.554: And sleep, it falls slow and insistent.
1.556:
Of dawn is so near.
DIVERS GUARDS
(talking).
1.557: Why have we still no word nor sign
1.558:
Of that scout in the Argive line?
ANOTHER.
1.559:
I know not; he is long delayed.
ANOTHER.
1.560: God send he trip not on the blade
1.561:
Of some Greek in an ambuscade!
ANOTHER.
It may be. I am half afraid.
LEADER.
1.562: Our time is past! Up, men, and tell
1.563: The fifth watch. ’Tis the Lycians’ spell
1.564:
Now, as the portions fairly fell.
The Guards pass out to waken the Lycians. The stage is empty and dark except for the firelight, when a whisper is heard at the back. Presently enter ODYSSEUS and DIOMEDE in dull leather armour, DIOMEDE carrying at his belt DOLON’S wolf-skin and mask. ODYSSEUS.
1.565: Diomede, hist!—A little sound of arms
1.566:
Clanking... or am I full of void alarms?
DIOMEDE.
1.567: No. ’Tis some horse tied to the chariot rail
1.568: That clanks his chain.—My heart began to fail
1.569:
A moment, till I heard the horse’s champ.
They steal on further, keeping in the shadow. ODYSSEUS.
1.570:
Mind—in that shade—the watchers of the camp.
DIOMEDE.
1.571:
I keep in shadow, but I am staring hard.
ODYSSEUS.
1.572:
Thou know’st the watchword, if we stir some guard?
DIOMEDE.
1.573:
Phoebus. ’Twas the last sign that Dolon gave.
They creep forward in silence to the entrance of HECTOR’S tent. ODYSSEUS.
1.574:
Now, forward!
They dash into the tent, swords drawn; then return.
God! All empty as the grave!
DIOMEDE.
1.575: Yet Dolon told us Hector’s couch was made
1.576:
Just here. For none but him I drew this blade.
ODYSSEUS.
1.577:
What means it? To some ambush is he gone?
DIOMEDE.
1.578:
Maybe, to work some craft on us at dawn.
ODYSSEUS.
1.579:
He is hot with courage when he is winning, hot.
DIOMEDE.
1.580: What must we do, Odysseus?—He was not
1.581:
Laid where we thought him, and our hopes are lost.
ODYSSEUS.
1.582: Back to our own ship-rampart at all cost!
1.583: The God who gave him victory saves him still.
1.584:
We cannot force Fortune against her will.
DIOMEDE.
1.585: Could we not find Aeneas? Or the bed
1.586:
Of Paris the accurst, and have his head?
ODYSSEUS.
1.587: Go by night searching through these lines of men
1.588:
For chiefs to kill? ’Twere death and death again.
DIOMEDE.
1.589: But to go empty back—what shame ’twill be!—
1.590:
And not one blow struck home at the enemy!
ODYSSEUS.
1.591: How not one blow? Did we not baulk and kill
1.592: Dolon, their spy, and bear his tokens still?
1.593:
Dost think the whole camp should be thine to quell?
DIOMEDE takes DOLON’S wolf-mask off his belt and hangs it in HECTOR’S tent, then turns. DIOMEDE.
1.594:
Good. Now for home! And may the end be well!
As they turn there appears at the back a luminous and gigantic shape, the Goddess ATHENA. ATHENA.
1.595: What make ye, from these sleepers thus to part
1.597: If Hector be not granted you to slay
1.598: Nor Paris? Little know ye what great stay
1.599: Of help is found for Troy. This very night
1.600: Rhesus is come; who, if he see the light
1.601:
Of morning, not Achilles nor the rack
Of Ajax’ spear hath power to hold him back,
1.602: Ere wall and gate be shattered and inside
1.603: Your camp a spear-swept causeway builded wide
1.604: To where beached galleys flame above the dead.
1.605: Him slay, and all is won. Let Hector’s head
1.606: Sleep where it lies and draw unvexèd breath;
1.607:
Another’s work, not thine, is Hector’s death.
ODYSSEUS.
1.608: Most high Athena, well I know the sound
1.609: Of that immortal voice. ’Tis ever found
1.610: My helper in great perils.—Where doth lie
1.611:
Rhesus, mid all this host of Barbary?
ATHENA.
1.613: Full near he lies, not mingled with the host
1.614: Of Troy, but here beyond the lines—a post
1.615: Of quiet till the dawn, that Hector found.
1.616: And near him, by his Thracian chariot bound,
1.617: Two snow-white coursers gleam against the wan
1.618: Moon, like the white wing of a river swan.
1.619: Their master slain, take these to thine own hearth,
1.620: A wondrous spoil; there hides not upon earth
1.621:
A chariot-team of war so swift and fair.
ODYSSEUS.
1.622: Say, Diomede, wilt make the men thy share,
1.623:
Or catch the steeds and leave the fight to me?
DIOMEDE.
1.624: I take the killing, thou the stablery:
1.625: It needs keen wit and a neat hand. The post
1.626:
A man should take is where he helpeth most.
ATHENA.
1.628: This tent. Methinks he knoweth from the guard
1.629:
Some noise of prowling Argives hither blown.
DIOMEDE.
1.630:
Comes he alone or with his guards?
ATHENA.
1.631:
Alone;
Toward Hector’s quarters, as I deem, he plies
1.632:
His message. He hath heard some tale of spies.
DIOMEDE.
1.633:
Then he shall be the first dead Trojan!
ATHENA.
1.634:
No;
Beyond the ordainèd end thou canst not go.
1.635: Fate hath not willed that Paris by thy deed
1.636: Shall die; it is another who must bleed
1.637:
To-night. Therefore be swift!
Exeunt ODYSSEUS and DIOMEDE.
For me, my guise
Shall melt and change in Alexander’s eyes,
Yea, till he dream ’tis Cypris, his delight
1.638: And help in need, that meets him in the night,
1.639: And soft shall be my words to him I hate.
1.640: So speak I; but on whom my spell is set
1.641:
He hears not, sees not, though so near I stand.
She becomes invisible where she stands. Enter PARIS. PARIS.
1.642: Ho, Hector! Brother! General of the land!
1.643: Sleepest thou still? We need thy waking sight.
1.644: Our guards have marked some prowler of the night,
1.645:
We know not if a mere thief or a spy.
ATHENA becomes visible again, but seems changed and her voice softer. ATHENA.
1.646:
Have comfort thou! Doth not the Cyprian’s eye
Mark all thy peril and keep watch above
1.647: Thy battles? How shall I forget the love
1.648: I owe thee, and thy faithful offices?
1.649: To crown this day and all its victories,
1.650: Lo, I have guided here to Troy a strong
1.651: Helper, the scion of the Muse of song
1.652:
And Strymon’s flood, the crownèd stream of Thrace.
PARIS.
(standing like one in a dream)
1.653:
Indeed thy love is steadfast, and thy grace
Bounteous to Troy and me. Thou art the joy
1.654: And jewel of my days, which I to Troy
1.655: Have brought, and made thee hers.—O Cyprian,
1.656: I heard, not clearly,—’twas some talk that ran
1.657: Among the pickets—spies had passed some spot
1.658: Close by the camp. The men who saw them not
1.659:
Talk much, and they who saw, or might have seen,
Can give no sign nor token. It had been
1.660:
My purpose to find Hector where he lay.
ATHENA.
1.661: Fear nothing. All is well in Troy’s array.
1.662:
Hector is gone to help those Thracians sleep.
PARIS.
1.663: Thy word doth rule me, Goddess. Yea, so deep
1.664:
My trust is, that all thought of fear is lost
In comfort, and I turn me to my post.
ATHENA.
1.665: Go. And remember that thy fortunes still
1.666: Are watched by me, and they who do my will

1.668:

1.669: Back, back, ye twain! Are ye in love with death?
1.670: Laertes’ son, thy sword into the sheath!
1.671: Our golden Thracian gaspeth in his blood;
1.672: The steeds are ours; the foe hath understood

1.674:

(amid the tumult)
1.675: Ha! Ha!—At them! At them! After them! Down

1.679:
Rascal thieves, the sort that crawl

I have them! I have caught them!
CAPTAIN
(to ODYSSEUS).

(indignantly).
1.683:

1.684:
Stop! Give the watchword quick, before I have thy body on my pike.

(in a tone of authority).
1.685:
Halt every man and have no fear!
CAPTAIN.
Come, gather round. Be quick to strike.
ODYSSEUS
(to CAPTAIN).

1.687:
Hold back all!
VOICES.
No more holding back!
ODYSSEUS
(as they attack him).
What, strike an ally in the field?

1.688:
Then give the watchword!
ODYSSEUS.
Phoebus.
CAPTAIN.
Right. Ho, every man hold back his spear!—
1.689:
Then know’st thou where the men are gone?
ODYSSEUS.
We saw them running, somewhere here.

Off every one upon their track!
A MAN.
Or should we rouse the army?
CAPTAIN.

No;
To stir the allies in the night and make more panic!

1.692: Who was the man that passed?
1.694:
Even as I held him fast,
Laughed, and I loosed my hold?
1.695: Where shall I find him now?
1.696: What shall I deem of him,
1.697: To steal thro’ the guards a-row,
1.698:
Quaking not, eye nor limb,
On thro’ the starlight dim?

1.702:
What man hath seen his face?
What was his name or race,
1.703:
What the high God by whom his sires have sworn?

(talking).
1.704: This night must be Odysseus’ work, or whose?—

1.707: What else? It seems he hath no fear

Of such as we!—Whom praise ye there?
Whose prowess? Say!—Odysseus.—Nay,
1.709:
Praise not the secret stabbing of a thief!

1.711:
Up thro’ the city throng,
Foam on his lips, a-cold,

His face grimed and scored,
